1500: Urban marine environments are increasingly recognised as critical for conservation research, particularly as wide-ranging apex predators adapt to human-altered coastal habitats. This study examines elasmobranch composition and temporal trends in Hulhumalé, Maldives, using visual encounter data (April 2023-March 2025) collected by local dive guides who received training in photo and video data collection. Across dives, nine shark and ray species were recorded, including IUCN Red List threatened taxa such as the critically endangered great hammerhead shark (Sphyrna mokarran), bottlenose wedgefish (Rhynchobatus australiae) and bowmouth guitarfish (Rhina Ancylostoma). Spinner sharks (Carcharhinus brevipinna) dominated observations, showing clear seasonal peaks, followed by tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) and bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas), present year-round, and sicklefin lemon sharks (Negaprion acutidens). A moderate positive association was detected between monthly dive effort and overall shark sightings (Spearman’s ρ=0.49, p=0.0175), while the Kruskal-Wallis test detected no significant lunar phase effect for C. brevipinna or G. cuvier. Sightings occurred along a reef area adjacent to persistent anthropogenic pressures, reflecting global patterns of “urban-adapted” taxa persisting near coastlines with favourable conditions. These findings highlight the ecological relevance of urban reef systems and support the need for longer-term monitoring, regulatory dive protocols, with potential inclusion of such sites within national monitoring programs and future assessments under frameworks such as the Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRA) criteria. Beyond its findings, this study also highlights the invaluable role of tourism stakeholders in advancing citizen-led science.

1502: Science communication is a fundamental pillar of conservation, specially for improving the negative or non-existent public opinion about sharks in Spain and other countries. For this reason, the Proyecto AtracTibu —a science communication strategy aimed at countering negative public perception and deficient knowledge about sharks— was developed. The project involved the creation of unique educational resources, and was implemented in a Secondary Education classroom using a Service-Learning methodology. This initiative combined the inclass incubation of small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula) eggs, with other educational activities including interviews, games, booklets, dissections and workshops. It concluded with an outreach phase led by students, making them protagonists of their own learning and advocates for shark conservation, while engaging local media and the mayor of their municipality. The project’s effectiveness was statistically mesured and evaluated. Students’ knowledge and awareness was assesed before, immediately after, and one year following the project’s completion, while satisfaction among students and teachers was recorded through perception surveys. The results revealed a significant, long-term improvement in both learning and awareness among participants, along with a high level of satisfaction. Results demonstrate the effectiveness of the project’s strategy in generating a paradigm shift regarding stigmatized species, presenting it as a replicable and viable tool for future initiatives. Moreover, the project produced a freely accesible repertoire of shark-related educational resources to counteract the widespread misinformation that threatens these animals. Therefore, Proyecto AtracTibu demonstrates that well-adapted outreach strategies is an excellent tool for conserving this threatened animals and improving its public perception.

1504: Deep waters (50 to 2,000m) around the Cayman Islands were surveyed using deep-sea baited remote underwater videos (BRUVs). Over a two-year period (2022-2024), this study documented new locality records of two deep-water sharks, the blurred lantern shark (Etempoterus bigelowi) and the roughskin dogfish (Centroscymnus owstonii), and a school of scalloped hammerheads (Sphyrna lewini) below 200m depth. The blurred lantern shark was previously known only from a few records in the Western and South Atlantic Ocean and the roughskin dogfish appears to have a patchy global distribution from incidental catch records. In this study, three different individuals of the blurred lantern shark were recorded on deep-sea BRUVs across two separate deployments between 653m – 668m off Grand Cayman and multiple roughskin dogfish individuals were observed on footage at 1,054m off Little Cayman, marking the first record of both species in the Cayman Islands and the Caribbean Sea. While the scalloped hammerhead shark is characterised by its occurrence in large schools, over the past decade observations of such have drastically declined in the Atlantic Ocean. Using deep-sea BRUVs, this study documented a school of 11-13 individual scalloped hammerheads in deep water (> 200m depth) off Grand Cayman, the first of its kind locally recorded since the 1970s. These observations expand our minimal knowledge of deep-water species diversity and distribution; and provide evidence of scalloped hammerheads re-occupying the area, appearing to select deeper waters to school.

1506: Whale sharks Rhincodon typus frequently associate with anchored lift-net fishing platforms (bagans) in Indonesia, yet residency and short-range movements around these fisheries are poorly quantified. We combined direct observations with photo-identification (Photo-ID) across two focal areas in East Kalimantan (Derawan Islands and Talisayan) between September 2014 and March 2023. Surveys were conducted during evening fishing operations (18:00–22:00), totaling survey days and visits to bagan platforms; whale sharks were present and successfully photo-identified during visits. We compiled a catalogue of uniquely identified individuals, strongly male-biased (6 females; 5%). Estimated total lengths spanned ~2–7 m (mean 4.75 ± 0.86 m), with a modal size of ~4.5 m, indicating predominance of juveniles. Using lagged identification rate (LIR) models fit in SOCPROG with QAIC model selection and bootstrap resampling (n = 1,000), the best-supported parameterized model estimated a mean of 21.1 whale sharks (SE 7.4; 95% CI 6.6–33.3) present in the study area at any one time, with individuals spending on average 19.2 days (95% CI 1.2–144.2) within and 34.9 days (95% CI 7.0– 437.6) outside the area between visits. Daily mortality or permanent emigration was low (0.00053 day⁻¹; 95% CI 1.0×10⁻⁵–8.2×10⁻⁴). Adjusted residency, accounting for survey effort, was 34.7 days·yr⁻¹ (residency index = 0.095). These results confirm a juvenile-dominated, male-biased aggregation with repeated short-term residency around bagan platforms, highlighting the need for local management guidelines that integrate fisheries operations and wildlife-tourism practices.

1507: Several threatened, migratory elasmobranchs carry out important life cycle phases in shallow shelf waters. An example is the bentho-pelagic tope (Galeorhinus galeus); a critically endangered, highly mobile, pan-global species observed to migrate throughout Europe. It is thought that coastal waters in the Irish Sea are important for tope parturition and feeding. Although, their large-scale migrations in the Irish Sea are described, data on local coastal movements in the western Irish Sea is limited. This study used a large acoustic array (37 receivers), covering ~61 km along the coast, deployed from June 2023 – May 2024, to describe the movement of tope around a small windfarm (7 x 3.6 MW turbines) and the surrounding area. Nine mature tope (i.e., > cm) were tagged (Innovasea V13 and V16s) in September/October 2023. Eight tope were detected after release, with 4007 detections in total. Of these, two male individuals were responsible for detections on the turbine receivers. Overall, male tope were detected in the array more often than females (M: 3757, F:250). Regardless of detection frequency, all individuals had reduced/no detections in the winter and an increase in detections in the spring. Three individuals were detected across the Irish Sea on the UK coast in Swansea Bay. These findings indicate coastal presence, widespread movement and seasonal migration of tope in the Irish Sea, which aligns with previous PSAT data. Additional presence and movement analysis is underway to support sensitive marine spatial planning in the area.

1509: Although the general population is becoming increasingly familiar with the presence of elasmobranchs in the ecosystems where they carry out their daily activities, there is still widespread ignorance about their biology, ecology and behaviour. In this context, researchers are currently seeking to deepen their knowledge of these emblematic species, addressing aspects such as habitat use, sexual segregation and their movement patterns, whether horizontal or vertical. Several species of elasmobranchs frequent the coastal areas of the Canary Islands, with the angel shark (Squatina squatina) and the butterfly ray (Gymnura altavela) being some of the most common. With the aim of improving knowledge about the latter species, the Rays of Paradise Project has been developing an annual acoustic tagging programme since 2019 on the islands of Gran Canaria and Tenerife, complemented by the installation of acoustic receivers along the coastline of both islands. To date, individuals have been tagged, in Gran Canaria and in Tenerife, and a total of acoustic receivers have been installed between the two islands. The records obtained indicate that Spiny butterfly rays (G. altavela) remain present on the coasts of both islands throughout the year, refuting the initial hypothesis that suggested a movement towards deep waters or areas after their seasonal disappearance from shallow waters. Furthermore, no significant differences have been observed between receivers, suggesting a relatively homogeneous distribution of the species along the island coasts.

1511: The true scale and intensity of global fisheries activity as well as anticipated biodiversity loss are being revealed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List assessment process. I draw on key data products from the global reassessment of 1,199 species in Class Chondrichthyes – sharks, rays, and chimaeras. These data provide arguably the first comprehensive assessments of the national regional and global assessments of the world’s fisheries through the lens of the bycatch of intrinsically sensitive, functionally important and economically valuable wildlife. From these data we can (1) identify systemic biases and inequalities in global fisheries data, (2) shortfalls in the management of non-target species and the application of the Ecosystem Approach to Fisheries Management, as well as (3) the degree to which global trade flows are driving national unsustainability. From this comprehensive authoritative data-driven view we can identify priorities and set the agenda for global fisheries and trade regulation improvement for the next decade.

1515: Guitarfishes represent one of the most threatened groups of elasmobranchs globally, with populations declining due to intense, often unregulated fishing pressure, widespread coastal habitat degradation, and a lack of species-specific conservation concern. Their fine-scale information on their habitat use and trophic ecology remains scarce in the Northern Indian Ocean. This study investigates the ecological linkage between benthic prey availability and feeding habitat selection of three guitarfish species (Glaucostegus obtusus, Glaucostegus granulatus, and Glaucostegus younholeei) along the intertidal zones of the Cox’s Bazar coast, Bangladesh. Systematic field surveys will be assessed to quantify the composition, density, and spatial heterogeneity of benthic macroinvertebrate assemblages that represent potential prey resources. A habitat suitability model will be developed by combining environmental factors (salinity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, and tidal exposure) with prey availability to identify regions that are most likely to sustain feeding activity. Preliminary findings indicate strong associations between benthic prey abundance and intertidal areas heavily utilized by artisanal fishers, suggesting ecological dependence and potential vulnerability to habitat disturbance and bycatch. The endangered guitarfish species in the Bay of Bengal will benefit from the vital feeding habitats and evidence-based management plans that the model's outputs will provide. This study offers crucial recommendations for national conservation and spatial management planning and is among the first habitat-based evaluations to connect prey availability with guitarfish distribution in Bangladesh.
1516: Identifying and protecting nursery habitats for reef-associated sharks is essential for conserving threatened populations. Although blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus, Near Threatened) are widespread across Malaysian reefs, their early life ecology remains poorly understood. Chagar Hutang Bay (CHB), within Redang Island marine park, was recently designated as one of Malaysia’s first Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) due to its potential role as a nursery. Following Heupel’s criteria for characterizing shark nursery areas, we used complementary approaches, including baited remote underwater video surveys (BRUVs), drone tracking and transects, conventional mark–recapture, and passive acoustic telemetry to characterize juvenile habitat use, their residency and site fidelity within the bay. BRUV and drone surveys consistently recorded significantly higher juvenile abundance along shallow shoreline habitats, with none detected in deeper forereef areas. Mark–recapture efforts yielded a 33.3% recapture rate, with a mean 56.4 ± 42.5 days at liberty, with one individual recaptured at days. Acoustic telemetry revealed a mean residency period of 46.2 ± 43.4 days, including two individuals detected for ≥ days. Integrating mark–recapture and acoustic data increased the estimated residency periods of dually tagged sharks. Acoustic detections revealed diel detection peaks in early morning and late afternoon, and a stronger site fidelity to the bay’s western side. These results confirm CHB as a spatially restricted nursery for neonate blacktip reef sharks. They provide empirical support for its ISRA designation and offer guidance for reefshark conservation management within Malaysia’s marine park network.

1517: The historical and contemporary presence of the Critically Endangered (IUCN Mediterranean & European assessment) great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) in French waters remains poorly documented and fragmented. While sporadic evidence exists in the Mediterranean Sea, archival records from the French Atlantic coast are almost nonexistent. This project represents the first initiative specifically dedicated to identifying, compiling, and analyzing historical and contemporary traces of C. carcharias along the French Atlantic coastline. In the Mediterranean, various types of historical material have been reported in the literature and informal records, including preserved jaws from private collections, archived photographs, and verified recent observations, highlighting that systematic archival research can reveal cryptic or unpublished data. In contrast, for the Atlantic coast, no official dataset currently exists. To address this gap, we: (1) conduct targeted investigations in museums and private collections via direct curator contact or online public calls; (2) consult fisheries committees and professional fishers; and (3) review historical scientific and grey literature, as well as journalistic archives. By integrating all information into a unified database, the project aims to refine understanding of the historical and current distribution of C. carcharias along the French Atlantic coast and initiate a first tissue sampling effort. Beyond documenting occurrence, the project aims to support future international collaboration and guide field investigations to validate potential key areas. We kindly invite stakeholders with any material, imagery, or records to contact the team.

1518: Neotropical freshwater stingrays (Potamotrygoninae) are restricted to the main South American river basins and are an important component of the Neotropical aquatic biodiversity. Mostly known for being highly valued in the aquarium trade due to their attractive polychromatic dorsal color patterns and feared for inflicting sting wounds, these stingrays have been subject to increasing unprecedented threats and conservation challenges. Fisheries, targeting potamotrygonins for food, ornamental or recreational purposes, or as bycatch in other fisheries, and negative fishery (mutilation or killing and discard) pose similar threats as to their marine counterparts. Habitat modification or loss, associated with fragmentation, degradation, or even significant changes in water physicochemical characteristics, are among the major threats for these stingrays. Some of the habitat degradation processes indirectly affect habitat conditions, such as deforestation, forest fires, damming, dredging and livestock impacts. The full understanding or measuring the consequences of these indirect habitat impacts still require further studies. The effects of contaminants from various sources, including metals, metalloids, hydrocarbon residues, elemental mercury applied in gold mining activities, and agricultural pesticides runoff are also considered as threats for this group, especially for endemics or for species in areas highly exposed to them. Furthermore, climate change effects comprising changes in riverine hydrological cycles and severe and long-lasting droughts only add another layer of emerging and growing-in-intensity challenges for the Potamotrygoninae. Conversely, unlike other freshwater organisms, invasive aquatic species seem to pose limited or no threat to potamotrygonins, mainly because of their top to meso-predator position in riverine trophic webs.

1520: Identification of potential “lifeboats” (i.e., critical areas for recovery) for sawfish has been outlined in the IUCN-Global Strategy for the Conservation of Sawfish. In the United States, Everglades National Park and Ten Thousand Islands National Wildlife Refuge, have been protected for decades from development and commercial fishing, and represent the largest expanse of mangrove forest in North America. These areas represent core habitat for smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata; therefore, any population increase would hypothetically be detected there first before appearing in other areas of their range. While identification of critical areas is valuable for conservation of threatened and endangered species, monitoring of relative abundance, is often challenged by a lack of data. We conducted a meta-analysis of all available information on relative abundance of juvenile smalltooth sawfish within a proposed “lifeboat” for this species. Relative abundance trends were standardized using generalized linear mixed models and combined into a single time series through a Bayesian hierarchical framework. Overall relative abundance has increased since 1989 to the early 2020s. Moreover, monitoring studies in areas outside of these protected zones indicate a stable or decreasing trend in juvenile sawfish abundance. These results lend credence to the value of identification of “lifeboats” and protected areas as tools for recovery of sawfish. While results are encouraging, recovery will require that long-term habitat protections remain in place.

1521: The reintroduction of spurdog (Squalus acanthias) into the UK seafood market following the lifting of its zero Total Allowable Catch (TAC) and prohibited species status (2010–2023) presents a unique opportunity to examine the ecological, social, and economic dimensions of managing a recovering shark fishery. Once heavily depleted, spurdog are now being landed and utilised for meat under newly established catch limits, offering valuable insights into how conservation measures transition into sustainable use frameworks. This study explores how regulatory measures, market dynamics, and industry perceptions interact to shape this process, drawing on interviews with fishers and processors engaged in the UK shark supply chain. Results reveal that despite a cautious reopening, the domestic market for spurdog meat remains limited and sensitive to fluctuations in demand, with competition from North American imports and processing challenges constraining growth. Stakeholders recognise that regulatory adjustments alone cannot ensure sustainability or viability without parallel investment in consumer awareness, transparent supply chains, and equitable economic returns. By integrating ecological recovery with market and social considerations, this research highlights the complexities of reintroducing a previously prohibited shark species to trade. The findings contribute to broader discussions on how adaptive, ecosystem-based management and responsible consumption can support the dual goals of species conservation and socioeconomic resilience in shark fisheries.

1522: Reliable age estimation and understanding life histories of chondrichthyans are necessary for management. Conventional age estimation relies on counting bands in calcified structures, though their accuracy is increasingly debated. A review of the last years of age and growth papers revealed persistent methodological issues, limited validation, small validation sample sizes, and inconsistent periodicity in band formation. A constraining factor for validation is the high costs and time required for mark recapture methods, and robust sample sizes can be challenging for threatened and wide-ranging species. To address the limitations of conventional methods, we explore novel geochemical approaches to improve estimation of age, focused on elemental and isotopic characterisation of vertebral bioapatite in Speartooth Shark, Glyphis glyphis, and Winghead Shark, Eusphyra blochii. The vertebrae of G. glyphis were analysed to test if bioapatite strontium (Sr) concentrations and isotopic variation could be used for age validation. We found banded Sr and isotopic variations that were directly linked to predictable, seasonal rainfall. This established a temporal link between Sr bands and seasonality. Notably, these bands did not correspond one-to-one with conventional age bands. This provides proof of concept that elements with predictable seasonal fluctuations can indicate age. In E. blochii, elemental mapping of pregnant individuals revealed maternal partitioning and evidence of growth cessation when gravid, providing new insight into physiological processes responsible for ‘missing time’ in adult vertebrae. This highlights the potential of elements and isotopes to objectively age, and validate age estimates in species where conventional methods may be inadequate.

1523: Early life is a critical bottleneck for shark survival; yet, the physiological challenges of this stage remain poorly understood. Within dynamic reef environments, young sharks face both abiotic pressures, such as fluctuating temperatures, and biotic influences, including competition and predation, that shape growth, energy balance, and survival. In oviparous elasmobranchs, such as the epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium ocellatum), transitioning from yolk dependence to feeding marks a major metabolic reorganisation requiring precise energy allocation. Using oxygen uptake rates as a proxy, we quantified baseline energetic costs (standard metabolic rate; SMR) and the metabolic response to feeding (specific dynamic action; SDA), in recently-hatched sharks. We further tested the effect of ecologically realistic temperatures (25, 28, and 31°C) across early development. Sharks with longer intervals between yolk depletion and first feeding had higher SMR – each week increasing SMR by ~20% – supporting the “critical feeding period” hypothesis. Total SDA costs also increased over time after first feeding. As sharks grew, SMR became more sensitive to elevated temperatures – increasing by as much as 18% – which was also reflected in reduced body mass. Collectively, findings indicate that maximum energetic capacity remains fixed during early ontogeny, but higher maintenance costs may limit the energy available for digestion and growth. If young epaulette sharks already operate near their aerobic ceiling, additional abiotic and biotic pressures could be detrimental. Indeed, as ocean warming intensifies, these compounded energetic constraints are likely to elevate early-life mortality, restrict developmental performance, and ultimately influence population resilience for reef-associated sharks.

1528: Laboratory-based studies have contributed substantially to our understanding of metabolic mechanisms that underpin the physiology, behaviour, and ecology of elasmobranchs. Although oxygen consumption measured using respirometry is the standard method to measure metabolic rates of elasmobranchs, inherent limitations have resulted in a lack of estimates for many species, particularly those that are large and highly mobile. To investigate a new physiological proxy, this study sought to validate a differential model that estimates routine metabolic rate (RMR) from rates of change in body temperature. Intermittent respirometry was used to measure oxygen consumption of Heterodontus portusjacksoni implanted with temperature sensors that measured concurrent water and body temperature. A positive correlation between RMR estimated from oxygen consumption and body temperature demonstrated the potential of the novel method. The differential model was applied to a ~4.12day time series of body temperature for a 3.54m total length, free-swimming Carcharodon carcharias. Intraspecies comparison revealed that precision of RMR estimates increased when body temperature was modelled over a broader range of temperature changes and activities. The accuracy of temperature sensors was more important for smaller elasmobranchs that display body temperatures more similar to ambient water temperature. Hence, the sensitivity of the differential model favours the estimation of metabolic rates for free-swimming elasmobranchs during routine behaviours, and for large, highly mobile elasmobranchs. This demonstrates strong potential for the conventional use of body temperature as a proxy for estimating metabolic rate, improving the availability and accuracy of field estimates for elasmobranchs that are unsuitable for traditional laboratory studies.

1529: Shark meat is widely traded globally, including in Australia, where it is typically sold under the label ‘flake’. While the use of the flake label is recommended for gummy shark (Mustelus antarcticus) and New Zealand rig (Mustelus lenticulatus), there is no mandatory legislation defining the species that can be sold as flake. We surveyed flake products across the supply chain in southern Australia, and using DNA barcoding found that only 22% was one of the recommended species. Furthermore, over half of the samples (53%) were ambiguously labelled, with no species information but included threatened species like school shark (Galeorhinus galeus), shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) and smooth hammerhead (Sphyrna zygaena). This poor labelling standard or practice limits both consumers' abilities to make informed decisions and poses challenges for sustainable fisheries management. To address this, we investigated rapid and cost-effective alternatives for species identification that can be easily applied in the field, during monitoring or compliance checks, including isothermal genetics (Loop Mediated Isothermal Amplification assays) and Raman spectroscopy. Both techniques showed promise for accurate species identification, as well as for identifying products requiring confirmatory sequencing when species do not match recommended types. Overall, these tools can allow presumptive, in-field testing of species being traded (from landing to import/export and across the supply chain) to strengthen conservation management and regulatory oversight on the capture trade of threatened shark species.

1531: Climate change is increasingly interacting with overfishing and habitat loss to erode the resilience of sharks and rays, yet global, multispecies climate‐risk syntheses remain scarce to inform management. We apply an updated Integrated Risk Assessment for Climate Change (IRACC) to shark and ray species spanning six ecological groups (freshwater/estuarine, coastal/inshore, reef, shelf, pelagic, bathyal). Combining exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity, we integrate six climatic stressors (warming, acidification, deoxygenation, sea-level rise, altered freshwater input, extreme weather) with three anthropogenic pressures (overfishing, habitat degradation, plastic pollution), drawing on IUCN Red List assessments, FishBase and the primary literature (2010–2024). Mean vulnerability scores increased relative to Chin et al. (2010) (Δ = +0.16 ± 0.06), with the largest rises in nearshore taxa. Of the species classified as highly vulnerable (score ≥ 23), >90% occupy freshwater/estuarine or coastal/inshore habitats; sawfishes, river sharks and heavily exploited coastal hammerheads consistently rank among the most at-risk taxa. Bathyal and pelagic species generally exhibit lower climate exposure but heightened sensitivity to expanding deoxygenation and targeted fisheries. These results identify shallow estuaries, mangroves and nearshore nurseries as global convergence zones of climate and anthropogenic risk, and provide a transparent evidence base for prioritising species and places in conservation planning. We outline how IRACC-derived rankings can guide climate-smart marine protected areas, spatially and temporally adaptive fishery closures, and restoration of blue-carbon nursery habitats, thereby operationalising global targets (e.g. SDG 14) into concrete management actions for elasmobranch conservation under accelerating climate change.

1532: Apex predators shape marine ecosystems by influencing prey populations and mediating energy across habitats. Understanding their diet is key to revealing how they connect species and ecosystems, particularly in vulnerable habitats that support endangered species. Shark Bay, Western Australia, features the world’s largest seagrass beds, which sustain threatened marine megafauna such as loggerhead and green turtles, and dugongs. Tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier), likely preys on these species playing a key role in structuring the community. In 2011, a severe marine heatwave caused an extensive seagrass loss, leading to declines in green turtle and dugong sightings. However, tiger shark catch rates remained stable, indicating potential dietary shifts. As generalist predators, tiger sharks are capable of exploiting multiple habitats and food webs, likely adapting their foraging strategies to target specific prey in different environments. This study investigates predator-prey dynamics by determining the dietary habits of tiger sharks and assessing how shifts in prey availability and distribution influence predator behaviour and ecosystem health. Tissue samples from tiger sharks, dugongs, turtles, fish, sea snakes, dolphins, and invertebrates were analysed using two complementary biochemical tracers (stable isotopes and fatty acids) to characterize shark’s diets. It is expected that Shark Bay tiger sharks derive energy from both seagrass-associated and pelagic food webs, exhibiting opportunistic feeding at the population level but potential individual specialization. These results advance our understanding of megafauna interactions in a fragile ecosystem at catastrophic risk from climate change, providing valuable insights for adaptive management and conservation of World Heritage marine habitats.

1534: Sharks regularly interact with fishing vessels at Cocos (Keeling) Islands (CKI), leading to high rates of depredation. This human-wildlife conflict results in costly loss of target catch and gear for artisanal fishers, extra mortality for target species, and growing negative attitudes towards sharks. Initial community consultation and engagement activities highlighted the need for testing suitable mitigation methods to reduce depredation levels at CKI. As such, we codesigned a study to test the effectiveness and practicality of a shark deterrent device currently available on the market and designed to mitigate fisher-shark interactions (RPELX) in demersal line fishing. A randomised experimental design was used to test the RPELX against a control treatment during days of fishing. In total, fish were caught across fishing sessions. Grey reef sharks (Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos) were the main species responsible for depredation. Results of a Generalised Linear Model indicated that treatment and skipper had a significant effect on the number of fish depredated, with the RPELX reducing the probability of depredation events by 63%. Using the RPELX device also substantially reduced shark bycatch and loss of fishing gear to the environment. Further community consultation suggested improvements to the device’s design to promote better uptake and recommended a new prototype for pelagic fishing. Overall, the RPELX device can provide environmental and socioeconomic benefits to the marine ecosystem, the local artisanal fishery and the community at CKI, by enabling improved human-shark coexistence. Further testing is recommended in other line fisheries around the world.

1536: Shark populations are declining globally, yet many aspects of their physiology and life history remain poorly understood. Most of the understanding and management of sharks is based on our knowledge of their biology and interactions with other macroorganisms. Sharks live, however, in association with microorganisms which have critical roles in their health and function. Understanding how their associated microbiota change with ontogeny can give insight into evolutionary processes of their microbial symbiosis and the susceptibility of sharks to disease during early development. We examined ontogenetic shifts in the microbiota of the oviparous Port Jackson shark (Heterodontus portusjacksoni) by characterising microbial communities associated with embryos, neonates, and adults using 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Microbial composition differed markedly among life stages, and no microbiota were detected in the egg albumen. We define the pioneer microbiota in this shark species and discuss potential mechanisms of microbial transmission, including both horizontal and vertical pathways. Our findings offer the first detailed assessment of microbial dynamics across the vulnerable early life stages of the Port Jackson shark and provide a foundation for understanding microbial contributions to shark developmental physiology. These insights may have broader relevance for other oviparous shark species and conservation initiatives such as ex-situ breeding programs.

1537: Predator-prey interactions fundamentally shape ecosystem dynamics and, by extension, our understanding of ecological processes. However, objectively quantifying these interactions— particularly among wild marine predators — remains a significant challenge. Large sharks are renowned for their stealth-based hunting strategies, often relying on stalking and rapid ambush to overcome prey defences and enhance predation success. We report a rare and fortuitous observation of a predation event involving a tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier), captured from the perspective of its prey: an adult flatback turtle (Natator depressus) equipped with an animalborne video camera in nearshore coastal waters off northern Western Australia, 2020. The resulting footage offers a striking view of the turtle deploying a full suite of known anti-predator behaviours, effectively preventing the shark’s typical reliance on stealth and surprise. Nevertheless, the shark persisted and ultimately succeeded in predating the turtle. A detailed, quantitative account of the interaction was obtained by encoding the behaviours of both predator and prey from the video. This instance of scientific naturalism — featuring a freeranging predator operating under its’ own volition in its natural environment — provides a valuable contribution to our understanding of tiger shark hunting strategies. We explore key themes including predator detection capabilities, decision-making processes, individual risktaking, behavioural trade-offs, and the ethical considerations surrounding animal tagging. Ultimately, we highlight how modern biologging technologies significantly advance our capacity to study natural behaviours of wild animals in situ, offering deeper insights into the complexity of predator-prey dynamics.

1538: The mobulid rays of Japan are amongst the least understood populations globally, despite the region hosting the world’s oldest photo-identification catalogue for manta rays. In 2024, increasing reports of mobulid bycatch in coastal set-net fisheries and evidence of mishandling highlighted an urgent need for coordinated conservation efforts. In response, the Japan Manta Project was established to integrate community-driven conservation, scientific research, and local capacity building across the Ryukyu Archipelago. To date, we have deployed satellite tags on six individuals (two Mobula birostris and four M. alfredi) providing the first insights on vertical and horizontal movement behaviours of mobulids in Japan. These data will help clarify movement patterns, habitat use, and potential connectivity among island groups. We have also collected several biological data and tissue samples from set-net fisheries, representing multiple species (M. tarapacana, M. thurstoni, M. mobular, and M. alfredi), forming the foundation for future population structure and population connectivity analyses. Beyond field research, the project prioritises collaborative engagement with local fishers, dive operators, schools, and local community organisations. These activities include educational workshops, photo-ID training, youth outreach, and the co-development of best-practice guidelines for handling and reporting mobulid encounters. Together, these interdisciplinary efforts aim to build the first comprehensive, community-anchored mobulid conservation program in Japan, improve our scientific understanding of local populations and create a long-term framework that empowers coastal communities to participate directly in the protection of these culturally and ecologically important species.

1539: In the current biodiversity crisis, sharks, rays, and chimaeras are threatened with an elevated risk of extinction. Our understanding of the consequences of this potential biodiversity loss is limited, partially due to data deficiencies. Trait-based ecology is a promising remedy for overcoming data-limitation and developing insights and predictions for data-poor species. In sharks, recent research has revealed a relationship between gill slit height (oxygen uptake) and tail shape (oxygen expenditure) where species with higher caudal fin aspect ratios have proportionally longer gill slits. The relationship between morphology and metabolism in rays is largely unexplored and presents a unique challenge. Sharks swim by caudal propulsion, as do some rays such as guitarfishes. Rays have two additional swimming modes: pectoral undulation (e.g. wiggling by stingrays) and pectoral oscillation (e.g. flapping by manta rays). Here, we examine the relationship between gill slit height and fin morphology from museum specimens from species (~30% of rays). We use Bayesian mixed-effects models and find that the morphological trait most correlated to gill slit height varies by swimming style. For example, caudal fin aspect ratio is positively related to gill slit height for caudal propulsion species, but is an incompatible trait for pectoral undulation species. Instead, we find a positive relationship between gill slit height and length to the apex (widest point of the disc) for pectoral undulators. This trait-based approach opens the door to understanding how morphology underpins ecological function and extinction risk for all rays.

1540: Oceanic manta rays (Mobula birostris) are widely distributed, highly mobile elasmobranchs whose populations are declining due to targeted and incidental fishing pressure. However, fundamental knowledge of their population dynamics and movements across the Indian Ocean remains limited. Using a long-term photo-identification dataset spanning 1996–2025 and data from three miniPAT satellite tags, this study provides the first comprehensive assessment of M. birostris demographics, spatial distribution, and seasonal occurrence in the Republic of Maldives. A total of 1,107 individuals were identified from 1,200 sightings across of the country’s geographical atolls. The recorded population was dominated by adults (93.6%) and exhibited a male-biased sex ratio (1F:1.14M). Sightings peaked between December and April, particularly in March–April, coinciding with the transition of the South Asian Monsoon, and were highly concentrated at Fuvahmulah Atoll in the south of the archipelago (84% of all sightings). Low re-sighting rates (7.4%) and limited evidence of long-term residency suggest that the Maldives may serve as a migratory waypoint rather than a core habitat for this species. Preliminary satellite-tracking data indicate variable short-term movements, including migrations beyond the Maldivian Exclusive Economic Zone, potentially exposing individuals to unregulated fisheries in international waters. These findings highlight the transboundary nature of M. birostris movements and the limitations of national protection alone. Strengthened regional cooperation, enhanced enforcement of existing conservation measures, and improved monitoring of fisheries interactions are essential to safeguard this endangered species across the central Indian Ocean.

1541: Human-wildlife interactions are increasingly recognized as critical components of effective conservation strategies for threatened marine species. As human activities expand across marine environments, understanding where and how people interact with marine fauna becomes essential for equitable and sustainable area-based management. This study presents a case-study focusing on two endangered guitarfish species, the blackchin guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) and the common guitarfish (Rhinobatos rhinobatos), along Israel’s Mediterranean coastline, illustrating how this approach can inform broader chondrichthyan conservation. Using citizen science data from the MECO (Mediterranean Environments Citizen Observatories) project, we mapped encounter locations by species, life stage, sex, and activity type (e.g., diving, snorkeling, angling, etc.). We conducted a gap analysis comparing current and planned marine protected areas against conservation goals. Marxan optimization was used to identify priority conservation areas under four scenarios combining guitarfish habitat targets (30% and 50%) with conservation targets for human recreational activities. Results showed uneven protection among demographic groups: adult male blackchin guitarfish were closest to current 30% protection goals, while juveniles of both species had the lowest protection levels. Priority areas consistently clustered in the central and south-central coastline, overlapping with zones of intense recreational use. By integrating human activity data into spatial prioritization, our framework demonstrates how social and ecological dimensions can be jointly addressed in conservation planning. While applied here to guitarfish, this approach can be readily adapted to other chondrichthyan species, offering a scalable model for advancing inclusive, data-driven area-based management aligned with global biodiversity and ocean governance goals.

1546: Population growth rate (rmax) is a key species-specific trait that determines the intrinsic sensitivity to threatening processes, the limits of exploitation, and risk of extinction. Metabolic models explain population growth rate with maximum body mass and environmental temperature (and depth), but does not consider reproductive investment in offspring size or number. However, life history theory suggests species with larger offspring have lower population growth rates. We used a combination of predictive bayesian linear modelling with structured equation modelling to determine the causal relationships between environment, morphology, and population growth rate. We found that rmax is positively related to temperature, activity level, and maximum body size, such that large highly active species in tropical surface waters have high rmax (e.g.). We also found that rmax is negatively related to offspring mass, gill slit height, and dissolved oxygen. The positive relationship between rmax and maximum body size is only apparent after incorporating offspring size in the model suggesting that offspring size is a function of maximum size and that rmax is actually better estimated with offspring size rather than maximum size. Our results suggest that the investment in the size of a species’ offspring has a very strong trade off with population growth rate, such that species that invest in larger (and likely fewer) offspring will have reduced population growth rates and be more sensitive to overexploitation. Our work highlights the trade-off between slow and vulnerable life histories with potentially decreased juvenile natural mortality rates.

1547: Shark depredation is an increasing concern worldwide, leading to cryptic mortality of target species, loss of fishing gear and revenue, retaliatory actions towards sharks, and tension between stakeholder groups. Since 2018, we have collaborated with marine park managers and the local community of Lord Howe Island, ~600 km from the Australian mainland, to develop practical measures for reducing shark depredation and its associated negative impacts. Spatio-temporal mapping of Galapagos shark home ranges and residency patterns, combined with fishing vessel activity, has identified overlap hotspots where depredation is more likely to occur. Additionally, changes in shark behaviour and residency were recorded at a fish waste dumping site. We developed best-practice guidelines in consultation with the community to reduce depredation, which include: avoidance of overlap hotspots, fishing shallower or deeper than the core depth range of Galapagos sharks recorded through acoustic tracking, switching to jigs and lures instead of bait, diversifying target species, and establishing a waste management system to use fish waste instead of discarding it at sea. Testing of three electromagnetic line-mounted deterrent devices has shown reductions in bites on the bait and depredation of hooked fish by up to 55% and 83%, respectively, and revealed practical considerations to improve usability of these devices during line fishing. The holistic approach co-developed during this research is promoting coexistence between humans and sharks and can serve as a model to guide management of depredation in other areas where this humanwildlife conflict is growing.

1548: Sharks and rays are a clade of high evolutionary, ecological, economic, and cultural significance, and yet they are one of the most threatened taxa groups in the marine environment. Despite this, there remains a lack of molecular resources for this class to assist with their conservation. The tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier) is a Near Threatened (IUCN), keystone species distributed circumglobally that is under substantial pressure from human impacts, making it a high priority for management worldwide. We sequenced and characterised a high-quality reference genome assembly for the tiger shark and used it to dive deeper into the evolution and ancient demographic history of this species. We investigated how effective population size and inbreeding (heterozygosity and runs of homozygosity) has changed over millions of years to infer how this species has responded to past global events, and hence potential responses to accumulating threats. Through this, we also explored the genetic mechanisms that have made this species so resilient as the last surviving member of its family.

1551: Large sharks are an important attraction for public aquaria, with aquariums have a duty to provide a platform for and to create public awareness about. The Two Oceans Aquarium, Cape Town, South Africa, has displayed ragged-tooth sharks, Carcharias taurus, since 1995 as an ambassador species for education and conservation programmes. Since 2004, sharks that have become too large for the exhibit have been released back into the wild. In 2012, a tagging programme was initiated, and since then, male and female sharks have been acoustically tagged and released after spending an average of and days, respectively on display, aiming to assess their survivability post-release, and whether their movements mirror their wild counterparts. Overall, 81% of the sharks were detected over 000 times, confirming survival post-release, with males (1075 days) and females (1172 days) being detected for a similar number of days. Both sexes showed some degree of northward movements during winter months, returning to the south coast during summer. Sharks were also recorded spending time in both the Knysna (females) and Breede (males) estuaries. Importantly, released sharks were recorded in the same regions and spent similar amounts of time in these regions as wild tagged sharks. This suggests that sharks kept in an aquarium environment for up to 8.5 years are able to reintegrate back into the wild. This further strengthens the Two Oceans Aquariums release programme of ragged-tooth sharks back into the wild population and that it could be adapted to other shark species.

1552: Despite a widespread traditional belief in Sri Lanka that eating shark meat boosts breast milk production, there is no empirical evidence to support this claim. Therefore, a total of participants, including pregnant and lactating mothers registered at the Maternal and Child Health Clinics in Angunakolapelessa, Hambantota, and Tangalle in Sri Lanka's southern province, were interviewed from November to December 2023. Additionally, mothers at the Maternal and Child Health Clinics in Ratnapura, Sabaragamuwa Province, were interviewed from October to November 2025. When a participant provided multiple responses, each response was considered a separate entry. Among participants, 70% (n=281) heard that shark meat consumption enhances lactation. Furthermore, 38% (n=153) believed it, 46% (n=185) did not, and 16% were uncertain. The percentage of participants who had heard this belief varied significantly across towns (χ²(8, N = 400) = 1410.20, p < 0.001). Although Ratnapura is a more inland region, 47% of participants believed this, accounting for 11% of all respondents. When asked about the sources of societal influence on this belief, 61% (n=244) cited their parents, 31% (n=125) mentioned grandparents, and 18% (n=72) pointed to healthcare professionals. However, when asked about the most trusted or reliable factors influencing their decision to consume shark meat for lactation, 58% (n=233) indicated advice from healthcare professionals, 33% (n=133) referenced experiences shared by other mothers, and 21% (n=84) referred to cultural or traditional beliefs. Overall, 35% (n=141) of participants reported consuming shark meat during the study period specifically to promote lactation.

1553: Captures of sharks and rays in Sabah, Malaysia, whether targeted or accidental, has led to changes in species composition and abundance, and population declines. Market surveys at major landing sites record near-daily instances of shark and ray landings, but little is known of the location of the interactions, and of captures that are not landed at the major markets. Many small scale fishers bring their catch back to their villages with small jetties, and any shark and ray captures from these fisheries remain unrecorded and unquantified. A major challenge in managing shark and ray bycatch is the lack of knowledge of when and where these species are captured at sea. To address this concern we set out to understand the time and space relationships with bycatch of sharks and rays on trawl vessels via the deployment of electronic monitoring systems (on-board, GPS-linked camera systems). We quickly realised that commercial options were either too expensive or linked to data download and processing contract terms which were unsuitable for our needs. We therefore designed, built and gradually refined our own home-built, low cost time lapse cameras and have used them continuously since 2020 to document bycatch in Malaysian waters. From small cylindrical self-contained units on 3D-printed brackets to rectangular units using stainless steel brackets and external batteries and solar panels, our camera system have evolved into a low-cost robust datacollection tool that has led to the design of several ISRAs and Malaysia’s first elasmobranch time-area closure.
1554: Fieldwork skills are a crucial attribute for many marine scientists. In other disciplines, positive fieldwork experiences are linked to increased productivity, strong collaborations and a greater connection to the natural world, while negative field experiences can cause significant psychological stress and disrupt career trajectories. While safe fieldwork opportunities are fundamental to both individual wellbeing and scientific progress, we lack data to assess the impact of fieldwork culture on marine and shark science. To deepen our understanding, we used an online survey to compare the positive and negative experiences of marine science fieldworkers. Positive experiences led to greater self-confidence, future career ambitions in the field and further fieldwork opportunities, while negative experiences related to poor psychological safety, reduced feelings of value and, in some cases, the decision to leave marine science altogether. Inappropriate behaviour was common across field experiences and was unrelated to the presence of a code of conduct. A step change is required across the community to effectively mitigate the consequences of inappropriate behaviour at marine field stations, including the provision of appropriate reporting structures. Our results indicate that fieldworkers idealise safe and supportive learning environments. By drawing on pre-existing guidelines and describing tools we have developed in response to our survey results, we signpost the options available for researchers at all career stages to contribute to driving positive fieldwork culture. Together, this work emphasises the value of positive fieldwork environments and provides clear steps for researchers and field leaders to follow.

1556: Effective conservation of sharks and rays in the Maldives relies not only on legislation but on the meaningful engagement of the fishers who share their habitats. Despite national bans on shark and ray fisheries, incidental capture, trade pressures, and limited awareness continue to challenge protection efforts. Recognising this, the Maldives Manta Conservation Programme (MMCP) has spent over a decade building partnerships with local fishers and communities to foster understanding, trust, and co-management approaches to elasmobranch conservation. Through fisher interviews, participatory monitoring, and collaborative outreach across multiple atolls, the MMCP has gathered valuable socio-ecological insights into bycatch dynamics, fisher perceptions, and species encounter trends. Community-led initiatives, such as mobulid sighting networks, and participatory workshops on the ecological and economic value of sharks and rays, have demonstrated the potential of fisher involvement to improve compliance and enhance data quality in remote regions. This study synthesises key lessons learned from these long-term engagement efforts, identifying barriers to participation as well as strategies that have proven effective in aligning conservation goals with local livelihoods. Findings highlight how integrating traditional knowledge with citizen science can inform management decisions and build a stronger social foundation for elasmobranch conservation in the Maldives. More broadly, this work underscores the importance of trust-based, participatory approaches in ensuring that conservation outcomes for sharks and rays are ecologically meaningful, socially equitable, and locally sustainable.

1557: Is protecting a shark species on paper enough? South Africa was the first country to protect white sharks, an important move guided by a precautionary approach in recognition of the species’ ecological and economic value despite limited data on population status. Unfortunately, several lines of evidence suggest an ongoing population reduction, arguing that the protection of white sharks is simply on paper and that the white shark population is likely in decline. Is protecting ecological important areas on paper enough? South Africa increased the footprint of its MPA estate from 0.4 to 5% in 2019. Unfortunately, there is limited management in most South African MPAs and in some, ongoing commercial activities are not sanctioned without public intervention. Nevertheless, these are not only South Africa’s problems. Around the world many counties face similar challenges of good legislation with limited enforcement. We would like to propose a multifaceted framework of strategies (research, media, legal…) to support the changes needed to address this challenge at both national and international levels.

1558: Since 2009, the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation (ISSF) has engaged tropical tuna fishers from over countries through participatory Skippers Workshops. These workshops bring together scientists and fishers of all ranks—shipowners, captains, officers, engineers, and crew—mainly from purse seine fleets, but also longline, to discuss ways to reduce bycatch of endangered species, with a strong focus on elasmobranchs. Over years of face-to-face interaction has built trust and enabled collaboration on research to develop and test shark and ray mitigation measures before, during, and after sets. Many successful solutions originated from fishers’ ideas shared during workshops or trials at sea. Once proven effective, these practices are disseminated across fleets, encouraging voluntary adoption— even before regulations—because they are peer-driven and practical. This model of bridging science and fishing communities has demonstrated that co-designed solutions foster positive change. We believe the Skippers Workshop approach can be scaled from local artisanal fleets to global industrial operations, promoting sustainable practices for shark and ray conservation worldwide.

1559: The giant freshwater whipray (Urogymnus polylepis) is a globally endangered large ray, inhabiting major river and estuarine systems in Bangladesh, notably the Sundarbans and Ganges basin. The species faces significant population declines primarily due to artisanal fisheries, habitat degradation, and unregulated trade, but have critical knowledge gap throughout its range including Bangladesh. This study integrates available knowledge on the distribution, habitat, threats, fisheries interaction, trade and conservation status in Bangladesh highlighting the data gap. Catch and landing records shows the species is regularly being caught in estuaries and upstream of the large rivers using gillnets, set-bag nets, and longline hooks mainly targeting on large bony fishes. Data shows that the seemingly declined catches and reduced availability, possibly increased demand, and the rarity of the trophy-sized individuals have elevated the market prices, creating a scarcity-driven premium. The tendencies of taking meat to nation-wide premium fish markets, online sellers, and supermarkets is increasing. The Wildlife (Conservation and Security) Act, 2012, provide strict safeguards for this species under schedule I, as killing, trade or consumption is not permitted. However, major challenges include the lack of knowledge and awareness about the species, socio-economic dependence on fisheries, and enforcement gaps. Considering its unique habitat requirements and high risk of overexploitation, the findings of this study will support more effective conservation of this species through understanding its distribution and threats, and through evidence-based conservation planning strategies.

1560: Manta rays are iconic and enigmatic species, yet major gaps remain in understanding their trophic ecology. Tissue sampling and satellite/acoustic tag deployments may prove difficult in many locations due to concerns regarding the negative effects on manta ray tourism from invasive tag placements or biopsies. Even where permits are possible, the high costs of tagging can limit sample sizes and the breadth of ecological insights. While manta mucus has been used successfully in multiple DNA studies, and a previous fatty acid and isotope study, the accuracy of mucus isotopes for reflecting diets, and the timeframe over which the diet is represented (turnover time), has yet to be validated. Initial results suggest a DTDF of +2.0 ‰ (depending on diet quality), an isotopic half-life of days, and a % turnover time of days, thereby defining the temporal window represented by mucus samples. These findings demonstrate that isotopic analyses of mucus from captive mantas offer significant potential for advancing understanding of the trophic ecology of wild manta ray populations through noninvasive mucus sampling.

1563: The angelshark (Squatina squatina), listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN, persists in only a few regions of its former range, with the Canary Islands representing one of its last strongholds. Despite this, knowledge on the species’ spatial ecology, behavioural patterns, and response to environmental change remains limited, constraining effective conservation actions. Using acoustic telemetry, we conducted two complementary studies within La Graciosa Marine Reserve (Spain) between 2018 and 2024 to investigate these aspects of angelshark biology. Between 2018–2022, adults (32 males, females) were tracked, revealing clear sexual and spatial segregation. Males exhibited higher activity, broader ranges, and greater use of deep-water habitats (>80 m), whereas females showed higher site fidelity to shallow zones, likely associated with reproduction and refuge. Diel variation indicated increased nocturnal activity and social segregation by sex. From 2021–2024, acoustic and environmental data were integrated to assess the effects of temperature anomalies and thermal extremes. Females displayed greater thermal sensitivity, with a possible upper thermal threshold close to 22.5C, while males remained coastal during the breeding season (November– December) regardless of temperature. These findings emphasize the need to integrate sexspecific behaviour and environmental variability into conservation planning. In the face of accelerating climate change, adaptive or dynamic marine protected areas (MPAs), activated during predictable thermal or reproductive events, could enhance the resilience and effectiveness of conservation strategies for S. squatina populations across the northeastern Atlantic.

1566: Photoperiod is a fundamental environmental cue that sets circadian clocks, shapes development, behaviour, and metabolic regulation; however, its role during oviparous elasmobranch embryogenesis remains largely unexplored. The epaulette shark, Hemiscyllium ocellatum, is a small reef-associated oviparous species known for its resilience to environmental stressors, making it a valuable model for examining early-life developmental plasticity. We compared embryos reared under baseline light-dark photocycle (12L:12D), to complete darkness (0L:24D), to test whether the absence of light cues alters the timing and coordination of key morphological, respiratory, and energetic milestones. Under baseline conditions, embryogenesis progressed through seven distinct stages over approximately fourand-a-half months, with the longest stage occurring in the first half of development. Towards the end of stage four, and the midpoint of development, embryos transitioned from tail-driven ventilation to buccal pumping, a key shift in respiratory strategy. This shift was followed by significant growth, pigment formation and hatch positioning, as well as a late-stage phase of rapid yolk mobilisation. Ongoing comparisons of embryos reared in constant darkness (0L:24D) indicate potential shifts in the timing of ventilatory transition, and differences in how yolk reserves are allocated relative to growth. 1567: Drifting longline bycatch remains a global challenge to sustainable fisheries and, in particular, a major threat to pelagic sharks. These species are highly vulnerable to overexploitation, and effective management requires understanding their spatial distribution and the factors influencing their catch rates. Shark bycatch per unit effort (BPUE) data were obtained from the Spanish observer program for pelagic longline fisheries between 2018 and 2024 (N = 3170 sets). We developed statistical and machine learning models to identify the key drivers influencing catch rates and mortality of the three species with the most comprehensive datasets, Prionace glauca, Isurus oxyrinchus and Alopias superciliosus, integrating a broad set of biological, environmental, and operational predictors, with particular attention to mesoscale oceanographic features. We further estimated absolute bycatch and mortality levels by combining model predictions with fishing effort data used as a proxy for total fleet activity. Our preliminary results revealed clear spatiotemporal patterns in shark bycatch and highlighted the strong influence of mesoscale ocean features in shaping bycatch hotspots. By improving our understanding of the environmental and operational factors that determine shark-fishery encounters and outcomes, this study provides valuable insights to inform adaptive management strategies aimed at minimizing shark bycatch in a dynamic ocean environment.

1570: Sharks and rays are ecologically important taxa that face global declines primarily due to overfishing. Marine protected areas (MPAs) are widely used for biodiversity conservation, yet their effectiveness for elasmobranchs remains debated. 1574: Targeted and incidental capture of pelagic sharks and rays in tuna and billfish fisheries remains a major challenge for the sustainable management of these fisheries. Tuna Regional Fisheries Management Organizations (tRFMOs) have a legal mandate to conserve associated and dependent species while ensuring the long-term sustainability of target stocks. In particular, the International Tuna for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) recently extended its mandate to include the management of oceanic sharks and rays. To understand ICCAT´s current elasmobranch policy management framework, we identified all shark - and ray - related Conservation and Management Measures (CMMs) adopted between 2004 and 2025. The CMMs were classified according to the mitigation component addressed within the bycatchmanagement hierarchy (avoid, minimize, remediate, offset). Thirteen binding CMMs were identified. Most focus on data collection and reporting, and post-capture mortality, through finning bans, safe-handling and release protocols, and retention and landing prohibitions for various sharks and rays species (oceanic whitetip, hammerheads - except Sphyrna Tiburo, bigeye threshers, silky sharks, whale shark, mobula rays). Other measures establish catch and retention limits and rebuilding plans for blue shark and shortfin mako, respectively. ICCAT currently lacks measures targeting avoidance, such as gear modifications or spatial-temporal management, despite being recognized as effective mitigation measures. However, their implementation can be challenging due to species-specific performance and operational tradeoffs for fishing fleets as well as real-time information gaps. Future work will identify nationallevel policies and regulations across ICCAT Contracting Parties to evaluate how domestic measures align with and reinforce ICCAT CMMs.

1576: Freshwater ecosystems are severely imperiled, with freshwater megafauna populations having globally declined by 88% since 1970. Within Asia, the Mekong River is a stronghold of freshwater megafauna, although a range of anthropogenic pressures impact populations. In order to better understand the severity and spatial characteristics of threats for each of the Mekong’s freshwater megafauna species (inclusive of dolphins, rays, fish, and turtles), a vulnerability assessment framework was adapted and applied to the Mekong. From this, we aim to outline species relative conservation priorities, and key drivers of decline at the river, country, and species-specific levels. Specifically, we aim to understand how the relative vulnerabilities of the Mekong’s two freshwater rays, Mekong Stingray, Hemitrygon laosensis, and the Giant Freshwater Whipray, Urogymnus polylepis, differ to other sympatric megafauna. A literature review of freshwater vulnerability assessments was conducted to identify the most suitable threats and how they are best integrated into the assessment. Critically Endangered and Endangered Mekong megafauna were identified using the IUCN Red List, along with their distributions, biological traits, and threats. Primary literature and global databases were used to inform threat severity, through either quantitative or qualitative data. Species were then assessed across the components of exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity to determine an overall vulnerability ranking. Outcomes of the study will include 1) a prioritization of species and threats to inform future management in the Mekong, 2) a comprehensive framework that will be adaptable to other tropical river systems, and 3) increased understanding of vulnerability between freshwater megafauna groups.

1577: Effective science communication requires tailoring messages to resonate with the audience. Over the past three years, the Save Our Seas Foundation Shark Education Centre (SOSFSEC) has developed an innovative educational resource specifically for high school learners in underresourced communities of the Western Cape, South Africa. Recognising the scarcity of educational materials that the learners can take home, SOSFSEC developed a graphic novel focused on ocean connection, environmental responsibility, and community interdependence. The novel links conservation issues with social history, acknowledging the disparities in education, livelihoods, and environmental access faced by young people in South Africa today. Its development was an iterative process involving input from the entire SOSFSEC team, including children, youth groups, creatives, and experts in education, marine science, and science communication. Throughout, the English-language storyline and script emphasised cultural sensitivity by integrating local dialects and contextual elements to enhance the reading experience. Ultimately, the goal is for the graphic novel to be read and shared by families and communities, offering entertainment, strengthening emotional and intellectual bonds with the ocean, and inspiring action and ocean stewardship. This case study highlights a storytelling approach that is inclusive and has the potential to address the historical exclusion of local indigenous communities from marine conservation discussions.

1578: Rapid ocean change and overfishing threaten the persistence of many marine predators. The blue shark (Prionace glauca) is the most widely distributed and heavily fished shark species globally. It is also particularly vulnerable to ocean warming and deoxygenation due to its ectothermic physiology and highly active predatory behaviour, making it an ideal model for investigating how pelagic predators facing environmental and anthropogenic pressures can adapt and persist. Yet, previous studies used few markers or reduced-representation approaches that mostly capture neutral variation, thus limiting the ability to detect fine-scale population structure and demographic trends in highly mobile species. Here, we address this limitation by applying, for the first time, whole-genome sequencing to blue sharks to investigate genetic diversity and structure across biogeographical regions in the Atlantic and Mediterranean. Linkage disequilibrium decay analyses revealed low LD across the genome, consistent with high recombination rates and no signals of recent bottlenecks. Similarly, population structure analyses showed no detectable genetic structure, supporting a largely panmictic population with unrestricted gene flow in the Atlantic and Mediterranean, contrasting with patterns suggested by recent genome-scan results. Building on these results, we are expanding the analysis to explore possible signals of local differentiation and reconstruct the species’ recent demographic history. We will also discuss future opportunities to integrate genomics with ecological data to strengthen shark conservation. This study provides the most comprehensive genomic assessment to date of the species’ current genetic status and offers a foundation for predicting how it may respond to future ocean conditions.

1580: Fishing is culturally significant across most coastal communities but poses several environmental and human health challenges. These include the overharvesting of key stocks and the potential contamination of food-fish by agricultural or industrial runoff. Saudi Arabia has highly industrialized coastlines but the accumulation of environmental toxins in local fisheries species is poorly studied. I assess mercury concentrations in commercially targeted bony fish (226 individuals from species) and bycaught Elasmobranchs (252 individuals from species) collected from fish markets and landing sites distributed across the northern, central, and southern Saudi Arabian Red Sea. Observed mercury concentrations correlated strongly with the size and trophic level of sampled species, with large predators (including all assessed sharks) exhibiting contamination up to two orders of magnitude higher than their herbivorous counterparts. Models based on the observed mercury contamination indicated that a single gram serving of some large predators could contain more than the recommended weekly dose of mercury without providing any discernable nutritional benefit over consuming less-toxic herbivores. Mercury concentrations were also positively correlated with the market price and overfishing vulnerability of a given species. Eating smaller, low trophic level fish is therefore cheaper, more ecologically sustainable, and less toxic. Shark fishing is illegal within Saudi Arabian waters, yet sales of poached or bycaught animals persist in some markets. Highlighting the health risks associated with shark consumption may help reduce local demand and may ultimately be more effective than fining suppliers.

1581: Directional asymmetry (DA) is a widespread yet often overlooked feature of animal morphology. Here, we report a consistent right-biased asymmetry in the crystalline lenses of the thornback ray Raja clavata. Across individuals sampled from the Strait of Sicily, 24% exhibited lens asymmetry, and in all cases, the right lens was larger. This pattern, supported by binomial and distributional tests, represents the first evidence of population-level ocular DA in this species. Body size and age emerged as the primary correlates of asymmetry: the odds of exhibiting DA increased significantly with body weight, whereas the effects of sex and sampling site were not significant. The prevalence of asymmetry thus appears to rise with age and ontogenetic growth. Two non-exclusive mechanisms may account for this pattern. First, the association with positive allometry (b = 3.33) suggests that right-lens enlargement could reflect a functional or developmental lateralisation, potentially conferring a visual or ecological advantage to larger individuals. Alternatively, the same right-lens bias could arise through an age-related pathological process, such as oxidative or osmotic lens swelling preceding cataract formation, consistent with asymmetric physiological wear. These findings reveal a novel case of morphological lateralisation in an elasmobranch and highlight the need for comparative, histological, and functional approaches to disentangle adaptive asymmetry from lateralised senescence in the visual system of R. clavata. This pattern represents the first evidence of population-level ocular lateralisation in an elasmobranch.

1584: The reproductive ecology of Mobulid rays remains poorly understood, largely due to their low fecundity, wide-ranging movements, and the scarcity of in situ observations. 1587: Whale shark behaviour in Indonesia can be studied at fine scale because sharks regularly interact with bagan liftnet fisheries. This interaction enables safe deployment and recovery of long-duration multi-sensor biologging device, providing continuous datasets that are rarely achievable for large pelagic species. These deployments revealed a previously undocumented deep foraging strategy in Saleh Bay. Sharks spent 6–12 hours at >180 m, performing repeated vertical oscillations with steep ascent pitch, slow speeds, and high activity. The kinematics indicate filter feeding under high drag, likely targeting dense sergestid layers that migrate downslope at dawn. This represents the first detailed evidence of sustained mesopelagic foraging in whale sharks. Comparative foraging behaviour from Cenderawasih Bay shows strong regional contrasts. Saleh Bay sharks displayed pronounced diel vertical migration linked to daytime deep foraging, while Cenderawasih sharks alternated between weak reverse DVM in coastal waters and crepuscular deep movements offshore. These differences suggest behavioural flexibility shaped by prey structure and predictable human-driven foraging opportunity from the presence of bagan fishery operation. This work positions Indonesia as a natural laboratory for studying predator dynamics at depth. The tagging platform provides rare access to hidden foraging strategies in a large filter feeder and strengthens the role of biologging in understanding movement, energetics, and habitat use across contrasting environments.

1589: Manta and devil rays (collectively, mobulids) are circumglobal, planktivorous pelagic rays. Mobulids are declining globally due to targeted and non-targeted capture.
