1590: Changing ocean conditions, including climate change, are altering the habitats of marine elasmobranchs. As many elasmobranchs exert top-down controls within the ecosystem, it is imperative that we understand how those changes may already be impacting this vital group of organisms and predict how they will respond in future conditions to improve management practices. Developing conservation strategies for highly migratory shark species can be more challenging than non-migratory species due to their large home ranges and low reproductive output. By utilizing acoustic detections of tagged spiny dogfish (Squalus acanthias) and sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus) and available oceanographic parameters, such as sea water temperature, chlorophyll a, dissolved oxygen, salinity, and CDOM (colored dissolved organic matter), we are building a spatial probability model that determines how oceanographic variables influence the distribution and habitat use of highly migratory shark species. Furthermore, by examining a cold-adapted species (S. acanthias) and warm-adapted species (C. plumbeus), we are working to identify how species with different temperature preferences may have varied responses to variability and changes in the environment. One of the early results from our model indicates that sea surface temperature may predict the presence of S. acanthias. Additional model outputs will be presented here that indicate optimal oceanographic conditions favoring the presence of highly migratory shark species. This will allow us to identify possible management zones that overlap with their preferred habitat and improve the conservation of these migratory organisms as a whole.
1591: Effective conservation of elasmobranchs requires a reciprocal relationship between scientists and managers, in which scientific research informs policy decisions, and, equally, management needs actively shape research priorities. In Hawai‘i, NOAA Fisheries managers and scientific researchers have developed a collaborative framework demonstrating how this two-way integration can advance recovery of the oceanic whitetip shark (Carcharhinus longimanus), listed as Threatened under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. Since its listing, the oceanic whitetip shark has been the focus of a coordinated effort to ensure that management decisions are informed by the best available science and that research is explicitly designed to address management needs. Researchers from the Hawaii Community Tagging Program, a communitybased shark tagging program focused on oceanic whitetip movements and habitat preferences, have worked closely with NOAA Fisheries managers throughout recovery planning and implementation. Together, they have aligned research priorities with recovery objectives and incorporated management-driven questions into funding proposals and study designs, producing valuable outcomes. Emerging data suggest early signs of population recovery for oceanic whitetip sharks in the Western and Central Pacific. As numbers begin to increase, managers face new challenges, including rising fishery interactions and depredation events that carry economic and operational impacts for local fisheries. Addressing these issues requires adaptive, science-driven management that supports recovery while minimizing socioeconomic impacts. This case study highlights how proactive, reciprocal engagement between scientists and managers can translate knowledge into action, inform adaptive management, and serve as a replicable model for other regions and species facing similar conservation challenges.

1592: Understanding chondrichthyan health condition and post-release mortality is critical for developing effective bycatch mitigation strategies. Yet such data remain scarce, as standardized health assessment methods are lacking and monitoring post-release mortality through tagging remains costly, logistically difficult, and often ineffective, particularly for deepwater species. We present a standardized, low-cost health assessment toolkit designed to quantify the physical, behavioural, and physiological responses of chondrichthyans to capture stress, enabling correlations with post-release mortality and optimising specimen selection for tagging studies. The protocol integrates rapid onboard indices of external condition and reflex impairment with haematological, gasometric, and biochemical blood analyses, allowing consistent and comparable assessments across taxa and fishing operations. The toolkit was applied to 1,294 individuals from species and families of sharks, rays, and chimaeras, primarily demersal deepwater species, captured in a New Zealand fisheries-independent trawl survey. A subset of specimens was monitored in onboard tanks to assess short-term mortality. Results reveal that specific physical and behavioural indicators, together with key blood parameters including haematocrit, lactate, and pH, are strongly associated with mortality probability, shedding light into the physiological mechanisms driving capture stress. The relative importance of these predictors was modelled to provide a mechanistic framework for estimating post-release mortality across taxa. The toolkit is currently being tested on pelagic sharks captured by commercial longliners and monitored using satellite tagging to expand and cross-validate taxonomic applicability. Overall, this toolkit provides a practical framework for integrating health and mortality assessments into bycatch monitoring programmes, advancing adaptive management and chondrichthyan conservation.

1593: Sri Lanka’s fisheries monitoring relies on observer programmes, tracking a fleet of approximately 50,000 artisanal vessels, catching different elasmobranch species (sharks and rays), operating from harbours and beaches. Environmental DNA (eDNA) offers a transformative monitoring approach by providing species inventories from residual DNA shed by organisms into the environment. To date the approach has primarily been used for describing ecological communities, but it also has potential to support bycatch and illegal wildlife trade monitoring. This study assessed the potential for eDNA isolated from fishing nets, and boat wastewater to characterize catch compositions and identify overlooked species, particularly elasmobranchs. We also addressed factors affecting eDNA detections not observed in the catch. The study worked with two open-hull coastal fishing boats (OFRP) and four multiday deep-sea fishing boats (IMUL) operating in Valaichchenai, Sri Lanka. Three eDNA capture methods alongside observational records were used: metaprobes (custom-made roll of gauze tied to a hollow perforated spherical probe) attached to fishing gear; metaprobes secured within the boat; and boat wastewater filtered through 0.45μm filter paper. Consecutive, concurrent observational catch records were made for boats to evaluate eDNA persistence from previous catch. Ongoing lab and data analysis are expected to demonstrate the feasibility of using eDNA metabarcoding for accurately documenting elasmobranch landings. Through Identifying opportunities and limitations, we will refine and make recommendations for a standardized eDNA monitoring protocol in artisanal fisheries contexts. Successful implementation would enhance elasmobranch monitoring, enforcement and biodiversity assessments, aiding in the management of poorly documented, conservationsensitive species in biodiverse regions.

1594: Review of the conservation status of Western Indian Ocean (WIO) Guitarfishes (Acroteriobatus, Rhinobatos) found that species occur in the region, with (29%) assessed as Vulnerable or higher, with additional species (50%) assessed as either Data Deficient (n = 5) or Not Evaluated (n = 4). 1595: Data on sevengill sharks (Notorhynchus cepedianus) in the southwestern Atlantic have historically relied on a limited number of fisheries records and ecological studies at specific aggregation sites. A recent habitat suitability study integrating these data proposed a theoretical migration model suggesting consistent seasonal north–south movements: sharks migrate south during warmer months (summer and autumn) for coastal feeding, then move north between late autumn and spring, coinciding with pupping off the coasts of Buenos Aires Province (Argentina) and Maldonado and Rocha Departments (Uruguay), with broader offshore dispersal during this phase. This study tests this hypothesis by integrating a decade of conventional tagging programs (2011–2025) and the first satellite tagging campaign, conducted in summer 2025 at the southernmost known aggregation site, Reserva Natural Ría Deseado (47.8°S), Santa Cruz, Argentina. From 1,066 tagged individuals, 38% by shark anglers from a citizen science program, recaptures were obtained showing liberty periods from to 1,488 days and movements of to >1,700 km. These findings, combined with satellite-tracked movements of two females from the southern tagging location into northern regions, confirm the theoretical large-scale migration model for this species in the southwestern Atlantic. Moreover, satellite data provide unprecedented insights into vertical movement patterns, thermal preferences, and seasonal timing across latitudes. Collectively, these results support the existence of a single, regionally connected stock spanning Uruguay and Argentina, highlighting the species’ vulnerability to extensive fishing pressure and underscoring the urgent need for coordinated regional conservation measures that protect key migratory corridors and aggregation habitats.

1598: Accurate identification of shark species is fundamental for biodiversity conservation, sustainable fisheries management, and the regulation of international trade under CITES frameworks. However, conventional mitochondrial markers such as cytochrome oxidase I (COI) and standard 16S rRNA often exhibit limited discriminatory power among closely related or cryptic shark taxa. This study presents a genomic and applied framework for developing a novel 16S rRNA marker optimized for shark species identification. Complete mitogenomes from diverse shark lineages available in the NCBI GenBank database were mined to locate variable regions suitable for primer design. Candidate loci were validated through in silico analysis and laboratory testing. Market-derived fish tissue samples were used for DNA extraction, and PCR conditions for the designed primers were optimized for general laboratory application. Amplification success was verified using 1.2% agarose gel electrophoresis, and PCR products were sequenced via Sanger sequencing in a cost-effective manner. The resulting sequences were analyzed for species identification using the NCBI BLAST tool, followed by phylogenetic reconstruction in MEGA 11. The results revealed that the 16S rRNA gene contains highly conserved regions suitable for universal primer binding, while specific variable domains enable clear interspecific resolution. Phylogenetic analyses demonstrated that the novel primers effectively discriminated among shark species, forming distinct clades with high bootstrap support consistent with established taxonomy. This newly developed 16S rRNA marker provides enhanced resolution, robust amplification from degraded DNA, and broad applicability in molecular taxonomy, forensic identification, and shark biodiversity monitoring.

1599: Genetic diversity is the foundation of life, underpinning the ability of species to adapt to changing environments and to maintain healthy, resilient populations. Enhancing and preserving this diversity is central to rewilding efforts, which aim to restore natural populations and ecological balance. In this study, we explore key genetic considerations for rewilding sharks and rays, emphasizing the risks and benefits associated with both outbreeding—such as genetic pollution and the disruption of local adaptations—and inbreeding, including the occurrence of parthenogenesis. Using case studies from the Stegostoma tigrinum Augmentation and Recovery (StAR) Project, we examine how genetic monitoring and management can inform effective reintroduction strategies. We also discuss how these insights can guide the establishment of new rewilding programs by identifying suitable source populations, minimizing genetic risks, and promoting long-term adaptability. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating genetic assessments into conservation planning from the outset in order to ensure population viability and evolutionary potential.

1601: The bigeye thresher shark (Alopias superciliosus) is a globally vulnerable pelagic species frequently caught as bycatch in longline fisheries, presenting fisheries management challenges and raising concern over population status. Pelagic longline observer records from Hawaiʻi were analyzed to identify spatial and temporal drivers of bigeye thresher shark interactions in the Pacific longline fishery (1994-2005, ~118,000 sets, ~250 million hooks). We quantified encounter rates by sector, characterized spatial distribution, bathymetric association, and temporal patterns, and evaluated haulback condition and ultimate fate. Across the study period, observers recorded 45,373 individuals, predominantly from tuna-targeted deep-set fisheries (deep-set: 44,289; shallow-set: 992; unknown: 92). As less than 20% of deep-set trips in the Pacific longline fishery have observer coverage, these values likely underestimate true captures. CPUE was substantially higher in the deep sector (0.197966 sharks·1,000 hooks⁻¹) than the shallow sector (shallow-set: 0.039389 sharks·1,000 hooks⁻¹), suggesting greater overlap with preferred habitat during deep tuna sets. Delta generalized additive models incorporating isobath distance, sea surface temperature, and geospatial coordinates as smooth effects revealed significant capture hotspots, most notably south of the Hawaiian archipelago, and a highly significant relationship with SST. Bigeye thresher encounters are heightened during winter months, peaking in March (40.136578 sharks·1,000 hooks⁻¹). Approximately threequarters of bigeye thresher sharks were reported alive at haulback and release. Results suggest that seasonal reductions in deep-set effort during winter months (especially in areas with the relatively lowest SST), and avoidance of spatial hotspots for bigeye thresher encounters, may be the most effective strategy for mitigating bycatch.

1602: Nutrition is a fundamental mediator of ecological processes, shaping foraging behaviour, performance, and population persistence across ecosystems. Traditional foraging theory has long centred on unitary measures of nutrition, such as energy maximisation, as the key driver of food selection. However, recent work has transformed our understanding of nutritional ecology in terrestrial systems by demonstrating the important role of nutrient balance in foraging and its consequences. This perspective is, however, underutilised in marine research and conservation generally, and in shark research specifically. A nutrient balance perspective could offer powerful insights into shark ecology and management, ranging from predicting habitat use and migration to understanding population declines or changes in diet in response to warming oceans. Nutrient balance is, however, a more complex nutritional paradigm than unitary measures such as energy maximisation and poses specific challenges in its application to marine predators, such as sharks. Here, we introduce the Nutritional Geometry Framework (NGF), a modelling approach that has been applied in terrestrial research for examining the role of nutrient balance in terrestrial systems. We illustrate its use by using select terrestrial examples, then present an example of its application in shark research. As ocean temperatures rise and prey communities shift under climate change, understanding the nutritional dimensions of predator–prey interactions are becoming increasingly pertinent. By framing shark foraging through the lens of nutrient balancing, we can better predict species responses to changing environments and improve the management of predators in dynamic marine ecosystems.

1603: Studying animal migrations is valuable in understanding survival and reproductive success in many species, especially large marine predators, such as sharks. Bull sharks have been extensively studied in the Pacific and Atlantic, however, there is still limited understanding about long-distance migrations, regional connectivity, and susceptibility to risk in the Western Indian Ocean (WIO). In this study, we investigated the movements and habitat use of female bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas) caught and tagged in the Amirantes, Republic of Seychelles, using V16 acoustic transmitters and Pop-up Satellite-linked Archival Transmitter (PSAT) tags. An array of acoustic receiver stations was used to monitor animal movement within the Amirantes and movements outside of the array were reconstructed using light-based geolocation from the PSATs. Between August 2014 and November 2017, ten gravid females left the Amirantes bank, where six individuals undertook large-scale, open ocean, return migrations trips (>1000km) to transitional waters in the south-east and western coast of Madagascar, remaining in very shallow depths (<5m) during their time there. Three others travelled north to the inner islands of Seychelles and only two individuals remained in the tagging area during this period. These transoceanic movements coincide with bull shark parturition months providing strong evidence of natal philopatry within the WIO population. Findings from this study provide important insight into bull shark migratory behavior, regional life cycles within Seychelles Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and additionally highlights important reproductive areas for bull sharks in the WIO.

1605: The scalloped hammerhead, Sphyrna lewini is widely distributed across tropical and temperate coastal waters worldwide, yet its population has declined in many regions due to fishing pressure, raising serious conservation concerns. To address the lack of ecological knowledge regarding the northwestern Pacific population of this species, this study aimed to fill critical gaps by analyzing long-term monitoring data (2006 – present) from southwestern Japan, particularly Ariake Bay, where both juveniles and adults are seasonally abundant. We conducted comprehensive analyses of S. lewini individuals incidentally caught in small-scale coastal fisheries (e.g., gillnets and set nets) and culling programs targeting rays and sharks. These analyses included size- and season-specific occurrence patterns, age determination, identification of neonates with unhealed umbilical scars, in situ measurements of water temperature and salinity, and assessment of the nutritional condition of age-0 individuals. Our findings confirm that Ariake Bay is currently the only known nursery habitat for S. lewini in the northwestern Pacific, meeting the criteria proposed by Heupel et al. (2007). Evaluations of diet and nutritional status further suggest that the bay has high functional value as a nursery ground. Given the potential connectivity between the Ariake population and other coastal regions across the northwestern Pacific, strengthening ongoing collaborations with other Asian countries is a key priority in elucidating the scale of population connectivity. Large-scale incidental catches of S. lewini have occurred in Ariake Bay. Comprehensive transboundary research is expected to serve as a scientific cornerstone for effective conservation and management strategies globally.

1606: To effectively and responsibly undertake any elasmobranch reintroduction effort, there are many important checks and balances. One key element is adequate consideration and active investigation into the species’ spatial ecology at all stages of the program, from planning through to pre- and post-release monitoring. Here we present examples of the required data to responsibly undertake an elasmobranch reintroduction program, strategies for obtaining these data including technological requirements, and real challenges experienced. Our case study for the planning phase is provided by the Shark Ray Spatial Ecology Working Group, currently collecting the first movement data of the critically endangered bowmouth guitarfish (Rhina ancylostomus), to inform the required parameters for suitable future release sites. We detail challenges with identifying tagging opportunities for these very rare animals, and present examples of relevant novel data on movement behaviour. Our case study for the post-release monitoring phase is provided by the StAR Research Steering Committee, who todate have released >50 tagged Indo-Pacific leopard sharks (Stegostoma tigrinum) in Indonesia and Thailand. Here we detail considerations taken in developing a post-release monitoring plan, successes, challenges and resultant adaptations in execution, and examples of how resultant data is informing practices and project progress.

1610: With over species of elasmobranch sighted between 2019-2024 through BRUV, UVC and small-scale fisheries surveys, Rote Ndao, the southernmost island of Indonesia, provides exceptional habitat for elasmobranchs, including cleaning stations, feeding grounds, and potential migratory channels. 1611: Amid declining global manta ray populations, their growing tourism industries offer substantial economic benefits and support conservation legislation. As charismatic flagship species, manta rays drive economic sustainability for island nations like the Maldives, necessitating economic evaluation to justify conservation amongst competing demands on public resources. Using tour operator surveys (n=106) and data mining, this study provides the first socioeconomic assessment of manta ray watching (MRW) tourism in the Maldives. In 2021, Maldivian MRW generated an estimated US$227.3 million (including US$39M from snorkelling/diving excursions and US$188.3M in related tourist expenditure), representing 4.8% of national Gross Domestic Product. Accounting for flow-on benefits (to staff, local businesses, and government), the total economic value exceeded US$311 million annually. Hanifaru Marine Protected Area (MPA) in the Baa Atoll Biosphere Reserve is a pivotal national case study, generating $252,800 in revenue in 2021, with the profit used for community education and research. This compelling value emphasises the critical role of innovative and equitable financing for robust, conservationfocused management that ensures future prosperity for threatened species and host communities alike.

1614: Four species of rhinorays; three wedgefish (Rhynchobatus australiae, R. springeri, and R. laevis) and one guitarfish (Glaucostegus typus), inhabit the waters of Karimunjawa National Park (KJNP). These species are part of the fishers’ catches in Karimunjawa, Kemujan (KJNP) and Demaan Village (Jepara mainland). This study aims to assess utilization and catch of these species based on market surveys across the villages from August 2023-October 2025. Catches were dominated by R. australiae, followed by R. springeri and G. typus. In 2024 and 2025, total catch in Demaan exceeded the Central Java annual quota (700 fish/year) by 66% and 74%. From total catch, immature individuals were predominant, 81,11% of females and 68,95% of males. Karimunjawa and Kemujan catches were 2.27% and 1.24% lower than Demaan in 2024-2025 respectively, and transported to Demaan for sale. In Demaan, meat is smoked and sold locally, while fins are dried and sent to Jakarta and Surabaya for export. Seasonal decreases in catch corresponded with reduced fishing effort during monsoon periods. Overall, catch trends increased in Demaan from 2023-2025 while remaining consistently low in Karimunjawa and Kemujan. The high exploitation of R. australiae may suggest overfishing, highlighting the need to review the current management, especially quota and the size catch recommendation, to ensure more effective protection of the species in its developmental grounds.

1615: Oceanic manta rays (Mobula birostris) occur along Myanmar’s extensive coastline, from Rakhine State bordering Bangladesh to Tanintharyi State bordering Thailand. However, little is known about their population, habitat use, or movement patterns, and no systematic monitoring program currently exists. In this context, community collaboration has been essential for generating baseline knowledge. Photo identifications collected through Manta Matcher, by recreational SCUBA divers in Myanmar’s south coast, the Myeik Archipelago, have so far identified manta individuals across encounters at six sites; Black Rock, South Twin, North Twin, Fan Forest, Western Rocky and Burma Banks. Among these dive sites, Black Rock, hosts the highest aggregation of manta rays, a finding that contributed directly to the designation of Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) in Myanmar; “Black Rock and The Twins”. These data also suggested connectivity of manta populations between Myanmar and Thailand, underscoring the need for transboundary conservation approaches. Local knowledge from fishers has expanded known occurrence ranges beyond sites known to recreational scuba divers, revealing manta presence in previously undocumented areas across Rakhine, Ayeyarwady, and Tanintharyi States. In a country with limited scientific infrastructure and restricted access to offshore sites, information gathered through community science has been pivotal in establishing a foundation for manta research and management. This work demonstrates how engaging fishers and divers fills critical data gaps and fosters local ownership of marine conservation, showcasing the transformative potential of citizen science in data-deficient regions.
1616: Reintroduction of elasmobranchs into natural habitats represents an emerging strategy for species recovery. In accordance with IUCN reintroduction guidelines, post-release monitoring to assess survivability of individuals is an essential component to the success of these programs. However, standardized, welfare-based tagging procedures particularly for juvenile individuals remain limited. This case study describes the development and assessment of an internal acoustic tagging procedure and pre-release healing process in juvenile Indo-Pacific leopard shark (Stegostoma tigrinum) as part of rewilding initiative in Raja Ampat, Indonesia. A total of juvenile sharks were surgically implanted with Vemco acoustic transmitters. The procedure initially employed smaller V13 transmitters (13 × 30.5 mm) for individuals averaging cm in total length, before transitioning to larger V16 tags (16 × mm) for individuals around cm to improve signal retention. Tags were inserted into the abdominal cavity through a - cm incision closed with non-absorbable sutures, which were removed after - days once visible healing was observed. Post-operative monitoring focused on wound healing, feeding activity, tag retention and swimming behavior to ensure full recovery prior to release. Complete wound closure and minimal scarring were observed by week four, and all individuals maintained consistent trend of behaviors and feeding responses throughout recovery, indicating good tolerance to the procedure when closely monitored. These findings demonstrate that internal acoustic tagging can be a suitable and welfare-compliant method for juvenile S. tigrinum, providing a practical reference for integrating telemetry into future elasmobranch rewilding monitoring programs.

1618: The rapid expansion of online marketplaces has transformed global wildlife trade, enabling the anonymous exchange of threatened marine species. This study investigates the diversity of shark and ray species traded on Shopee Indonesia, combining digital market surveys with genetic identification. Product listings were mined using keyword-based scraping (e.g., 'cucut', 'iwak pe'). Tissue samples randomly selected from random products and vendors will then be subjected to DNA barcoding (COI mini-DNA marker) to validate species identity. Data mining of product listings from unique vendors revealed an active and diverse online trade. Smoked meat (205 listings) and salted meat (197 listings) were identified as the dominant processed products derived from shark and ray, respectively. We also identified a substantial trade in non-food derivatives, including shark liver oil (79 listings) and ray leather or craft products (11 listings). Furthermore, listings for live ornamental fish (e.g., Bamboo shark, Motoro stingray) and specific body parts (e.g., shark fins, shark cartilage, ray tails) were documented. Jakarta, West Java, Central Java, East Java and West Kalimantan emerged as key provinces where many vendors operate. Genetic analyses are expected to reveal a high diversity of species, including CITES-listed taxa, highlighting discrepancies between declared and actual species. The findings demonstrate the persistence of unregulated trade in protected elasmobranchs. This study underscores the critical role of digital surveillance and molecular tools in enhancing trade transparency, monitoring, and enforcement. Strengthening collaboration between researchers, authorities, and e-commerce companies is essential to curbing this illicit trade.

1620: The Mascarene Archipelago hosts exceptional marine biodiversity, yet its elasmobranch populations remain poorly documented. Since 2021, the Mascarene Archipelago Elasmobranch Observatory (MAEO) has worked to fill this gap through a multidisciplinary program combining participatory science, in situ surveys, and educational outreach across La Réunion, Mauritius, and Rodrigues. Over four years, MAEO has compiled more than 1,600 validated sightings of species (23 sharks, rays), including one new to science. The sighting network now involves over contributors, complemented by field surveys using underwater visual census and remote video systems. This integration of citizen science and professional research provides a scalable model to strengthen baseline knowledge in data-deficient regions. Current analyses explore the relationships between species occurrences and environmental parameters. Preliminary spatial results reveal species-specific habitat preferences and potential aggregation areas of conservation concern. Beyond data collection, MAEO promotes strong public engagement through a dedicated online platform, awareness campaigns, and school programs that have reached more than 3,000 participants. This community involvement fosters ocean stewardship and long-term conservation support. As conservation priorities intensify across the Western Indian Ocean, MAEO offers a replicable regional framework for evidencebased management of threatened elasmobranchs. The next phase focuses on expanding spatial coverage, integrating tagging to study mobility and connectivity, and translating findings into actionable policy recommendations. MAEO thus enters a stage where data synthesis and advocacy become central to advancing collaborative elasmobranch conservation in the region.

1621: The high extinction risk for sharks and rays in Bangladesh is evident, with 77% of shark and 86% of ray species assessed as threatened by IUCN Red List. This risk is driven by overexploitation from targeted and non-targeted catches, requiring robust data to inform effective conservation management. The Wildlife Conservation Society addresses these gaps through citizen science programs involving gillnet fisher groups and community data collectors. Fishers, in exchange for safety equipment and mentorship, record georeferenced catch and bycatch data at sea, while data collectors record shark and ray landing data at nine coastal landing sites with modest incentives. Between 2014 and 2025, from 7,751 net sets, fishers documented 16,560 sharks from species and rays from species with safe release of many protected species, including guitarfishes and whale sharks. Between 2016 and 2025, over 14,702 days, community data collectors documented about million sharks (14,196 mt) from species and about million rays (1,613 mt) from species, including the country’s first confirmed sharptooth lemon shark, world’s largest largetooth sawfish, smalleye stingray and more than critically endangered Ganges sharks. These data have directly supported the establishment of three MPAs, uplisting of threatened species in the Wildlife Act, development of a National Plan of Action and Non-detriment Findings, and designation of an Important Shark and Ray Area in Bangladesh. This initiative proves that cost-effective, community-based monitoring can generate the necessary evidence for elasmobranch conservation and offer a scalable model for data-poor regions.

1622: Elasmobranchs play a critical role in maintaining the balance of aquatic ecosystems, Still, populations of many species are declining globally due to unsustainable fishing.In Cameroon, the overexploitation of sharks and rays has become a major conservation issue, with of the documented species listed as threatened on the IUCN Red List. However, information on the species exploited , their biology, and habitat use remains limited. Since 2015, the African Marine Conservation Organisation (AMCO) has been collecting data through fish-market surveys and the SIREN application, a citizen-science tool that enables fishers to report species sightings. Frequent captures of juveniles, including Critically Endangered species such as the Blackchin Guitarfish (Glaucostegus cemiculus) and the Scalloped Hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), suggest the presence of nursery and breeding grounds requiring urgent protection. A community-led conservation initiative was launched along the southern coast of Cameroon (Kribi) to reduce mortality in artisanal fisheries. Between June 2024 and December 2025, more than 2,000 individuals from species were recorded through landing-site monitoring. Eight local fishers were trained in safe-release techniques and in the use of GPS devices to document capture locations. During eight sea trips, two Daisy Whiprays (Fontitrygon margarita) were successfully released, and capture sites were mapped. This monitoring also documented, for the first time in Cameroon, the Atlantic Nurse Shark (Ginglymostoma cirratum) highlights the ecological importance of national waters. By working continuously in collaboration between communities and scientists, this project lays the foundation for sustainable fisheries management and longterm elasmobranch conservation in Cameroon.

1627: Silky sharks (Carcharhinus falciformis) are among the most frequently caught shark species globally, regularly interacting with commercial longline and coastal fisheries. Analysis of three decades of Hawaiʻi pelagic longline observer data (1994–2025; 117,649 sets, 248.9 million hooks) showed that silky shark bycatch was rare (3.8% of sets) and strongly structured by season, temperature, and space. Encounter probability and CPUE were higher during winter and exhibited pronounced non-linear responses to sea surface temperature and distance to the 200m isobath, with distinct geographic hotspots. These patterns suggest that silky sharks occupy a preferred thermal-bathymetric envelope whose spatial availability expands northeast of Hawaii in summer, concentrating bycatch risk in specific environmental contexts rather than reflecting broad latitudinal shifts. Most (~99%) interactions occurred in the tuna-targeting deep-set sector (south of 20°N, west of 150°W), where ~90% of fishing effort was concentrated. Although CPUE declined significantly over time, the proportion of sharks released alive increased in both sectors (35% to 79% shallow, 53% to 72% deep). I evaluated cost-benefits associated with hypothetical seasonal spatial closures targeting silky shark bycatch reduction. Together, these findings highlight key environmental and operational drivers of silky shark exposure to longline gear and can inform more precise, seasonally tuned bycatch-mitigation strategies.
Beyond the Net: Addressing the Impacts and Innovations in Shark & Ray Bycatch

1629: Rapid and accurate identification of sharks, which is an essential first step in both ecological and conservation research, remains a major challenge in the field and lab-based studies. Currently, scientists rely on paper-based identification keys, which are not easy to use in field or laboratory shark research, as the information remains confined to physical documents. Here, we present a user-friendly virtual shark dichotomous key that enables the rapid identification of sharks. This key is based on a scientific publication by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) on shark identification. Software guides the user through a questionnaire based on information about the morphological features of sharks and finally leads to their identification. A User Guide to the software that covers all the technical terms and morphological features was also incorporated into the software itself to improve the usability of the software for layman users. As a pilot-scale project, we tested the use of this key to identify sharks at various taxonomic levels: family, genus, and even species, and obtained promising, reliable, and accurate results. Further work is in progress to extend its application to include the existing 400+ Shark species globally. This virtual shark key has multiple potential applications beyond identification; it can also be used in ecological and conservation research, sustainable fisheries management and monitoring, as well as science education and training.

1630: South African waters exhibit some of the most diverse elasmobranch communities in the world. Situated on the northeast coast lies the country’s largest coastal marine protected area (MPA), the iSimangaliso Wetland Park, which is home to Africa’s southernmost coral reef system. The area is currently encompassed within the Thongaland Transboundary Corridor ISRA, designated primarily under sub-criterion C4 (Movement) due to migratory pathways and the presence of Critically Endangered species. As part of my PhD, I have deployed nearly baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVs) across the MPA to investigate how management zonation and submarine canyons affect elasmobranch community structure. Unexpectedly, the dataset revealed omnipresent neonates, juveniles, and substantial female bias in adults across all sampling sites. Together, these observations represent strong – albeit circumstantial – evidence that the MPA is utilised for reproduction by at least ten elasmobranch species, including several that are Critically Endangered. These findings effectively extend the recognised ecological importance of the area beyond movement corridors, highlighting its likely role as a multi-species nursery and reproductive hotspot. Despite this emerging evidence, elasmobranchs remain largely unmentioned in the MPA Management Plan and the area continues to experience persistent enforcement challenges of current regulations. The herein presented findings highlight the need to formally recognise the reproductive value of the area within both MPA policy and ISRA frameworks and to align management measures with emerging evidence of reproductive habitat use in the area.

1632: Indonesia is one of the world's leading shark and ray fishing, driven by high diversity combined with high demand for both international and domestic markets. Although known as a top exporter country, domestic demand is notably high, both for daily local consumption and/or for special occasions such as the Lunar New Year. Shark fin soup is a popular Chinese food and often served during the Lunar New Year. Despite existing national regulation, particularly for CITES Appendix species, through the Implementation of fish utilization permit (SIPJI), their use in restaurants remains unregulated. Market surveys were conducted at restaurants in Jakarta, Surabaya, and Bali in 2024. All restaurants estimated an average supply capacity of approximately kg/day of shark fin on a normal day, and this number increased to 242.5 kg/day on the Lunar New Year. During the one-week Lunar New Year period, an estimated 1,697 tons of shark fin, or 33,950 bowls/4,035 individual sharks, were consumed with a total value of billion Rupiah (450,000 USD). Unexpectedly, DNA analysis revealed that none of the shark fin soup dishes in the restaurants used shark species but instead contained critically endangered rhinorays species (R.australiae, R.springeri, R.palpebratus, Rhina ancylostoma, and Glaucostegus typus). The large number of stocks illustrates that shark-ray consumption is still quite high. All this information provides important insight for management authorities to improve and comply with local trade regulations and stock traceability, specifically for restaurants, and raise awareness for the public to reduce illegal trade and sustainable seafood consumption.
From Ocean to Plate: Unpacking the Shark & Ray Meat Market
1633: The blue-spotted ribbontail ray Taeniura lymma is broadly distributed throughout the coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific. Acoustic monitoring data from the Red Sea suggests that this species may exhibit high-residency in mature females, potentially limiting connectivity among populations to male-mediated gene flow. To test this hypothesis of sex-biased dispersal, we examined the genetic connectivity of T. lymma at three sites (Al Wajh lagoon, Thuwal, and the Farasan Banks) along the Saudi Arabian Red Sea coast and assessed the population structure using an analysis of the mitochondrial COI gene and 7088 single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers in the nuclear DNA. The results of this study revealed the opposite of what was expected, showing no significant structure in either the mitochondrial or nuclear DNA. The analysis of molecular variance (AMOVA) of the mitochondrial analysis reported only 3.2% variation among populations while showing 96.8% variance within populations. The AMOVA run on the SNPs data showed similar results, giving an among-population variance of 11% while within-population variance came in at 89%, exhibiting a notable level of genetic homogeneity between Red Sea populations. This suggests that there may be more biparental movement and gene-flow across the region in a species that is suspected to have limited female movement. These findings support expanding to a global analysis of T. lymma gene flow and population dynamics.

1634: Ninety-four per cent of Sri Lanka’s Exclusive Economic Zone is deep ocean. Despite this, little is known about this ecosystem, with existing knowledge being largely limited to fisheries catch data and historical scientific trawls, which often fail to provide important information such as depth, habitat, or species’ behaviours. In this study, we undertook the first-ever scientific exploration of Sri Lanka’s deep ocean using the National Geographic low-cost deep-sea camera system. During seven deployments on the island's northwest coast, between depths of and 1000m, we documented two species of rays and two shark species. Etmopterus sps) in Sri Lankan waters, and a first live sighting of a juvenile Roughskin dogfish (Centroscymnus owstonii). 1636: Port Phillip Bay (PPB) in southern Victoria, Australia is extensively used for commercial and recreational purposes, including fishing, shipping and ecotourism. Sharks and rays are abundant throughout PPB, holding high ecological, cultural, and economic importance. Despite this, our understanding of how sharks and rays use the bay is limited. Previous research has shown that Southern Fiddler Rays are common in Swan Bay, yet our understanding of their residency and movement patterns is limited. Here, we use acoustic telemetry to describe both fine-scale and larger-scale patterns of space use and activity of Southern Fiddler Rays across varying life stages, within both Swan Bay and wider PPB. Preliminary movement data suggests that Southern Fiddler Rays exhibit high residency within southern Swan Bay, some undertaking movements into wider Port Phillip Bay and the open coast. Notably, one individual was recorded over km from its tagging location along the Victorian coastline, highlighting occasional long-range movements. We will present our findings to date and outline how these results enhance understating of the spatial ecology and habitat use of Southern Fiddler Rays within PPB.

1637: Acoustic telemetry is used globally for passive monitoring of movement and behaviour of aquatic species like elasmobranchs, however, interpretation of movement data is heavily limited by array design. Range testing is an important process for optimising array configuration, as it provides insight into spatial and temporal variability in receiver detection range relating to environmental and anthropogenic influences. This process is often overlooked, with assumed or manufacturer-provided ranges, or ranges derived from unrelated locations, thus, reducing the accuracy of subsequent spatial analyses leading to the potential misinterpretation of results. Detection ranges of receivers are highly variable due to environmental factors including tides, time-of-day, biological and anthropogenic noise, and bathymetry. The aim of this study is to determine how array configuration can be optimised for location specific receiver ranges, which will increase efficiency in receiver placement and ensure the most effective coverage in a study area. Simulations were performed using multiple detection ranges in two contrasting environments. One array in a shallow, seagrass-dominated embayment (Swan Bay, Queenscliff), and one in a deep, high-current channel (Port Phillips Heads). We present preliminary results of empirical range tests and simulation models with the aim to develop best practice guidelines for calibrating and configuring acoustic arrays. Protocols produced from this study will improve planning, testing and configuring array designs to provide more reliable estimates of habitat use, connectivity and interpretation of animal movement data.

1638: Habitat homogenisation due to anthropogenic pressures is altering coral reefs at unprecedented rates with unknown consequences for reef-associated sharks. A lack of synergy between habitat assessment technologies and behavioural tracking has left uncertainty about how fine-scale habitat complexity shapes shark residency and habitat use. We combined 3D reef habitat structure-from-motion photogrammetry with acoustic telemetry data to investigate how reef structure influences the habitat use of grey reef (Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos), blacktip reef (Carcharhinus melanopterus), and sicklefin lemon (Negaprion acutidens) sharks in the Outer Islands of the Seychelles. In contrast, grey reef and lemon sharks showed no significant responses to the investigated habitat metrics, and models explained <12% of the variation in the habitat associations of these species. Our findings indicate that blacktip reef sharks are particularly at risk from climatedriven loss of coral complexity, while grey reef and lemon sharks may exhibit greater resilience due to broader habitat use. We highlight the urgent need for conservation strategies that consider species-specific habitat dependencies in a time of accelerating reef homogenisation.

1640: Using the Chagos Archipelago, one of the world’s largest no-take marine protected areas, as a case study, this research examines why traditional enforcement- and policy-led approaches often fail to deliver measurable reductions in shark mortality. Through a mixed-methods analysis combining fisher interviews with patrol vessel movement data and interception records, we show that patrol-based deterrence alone is insufficient to curb illegal shark fishing, even under conditions of near-continuous enforcement presence. While patrol strategy was shown to influence interception rates, no detectable general deterrence effect was observed, highlighting major limitations in conventional approaches that assume rational compliance with risk of detection. Instead, deterrence was found to be shaped more strongly by national-level regulatory reforms, vessel monitoring requirements, and socio-economic pressures affecting fisher decision-making. These findings demonstrate that science-driven recommendations must be embedded within the political and capacity contexts in which conservation occurs. Enhancing the effectiveness of shark conservation therefore requires greater consideration of strategies that strengthen national governance rather than reliance on punitive localised enforcement.

1641: Understanding trophic interactions in sharks and rays is crucial for assessing their ecological roles and conservation needs. Traditionally employed dietary methods are often invasive, requiring lethal sampling and presenting applicability limitations for threatened species. Recent advances in molecular ecology offer powerful, non-lethal alternatives. Although molecular scatology has been applied to a variety of taxa (mammals, birds, reptiles), the metabarcoding of fecal DNA (fDNA) has remained largely unvalidated in sharks and rays. This study aims to elucidate the accuracy of this innovative technique, offering the first direct validation of fDNA metabarcoding in elasmobranchs. Cloacal swabs were collected immediately after capture from individuals belonging to species of sharks and rays during the 2024 MEDITS survey in the central Mediterranean Sea. Corresponding stomach samples were subsequently obtained in the laboratory, where DNA was extracted from swabs and stomachs. The mitochondrial COI region was amplified, and sequencing was performed using Oxford Nanopore technology. Raw reads were quality-filtered, taxonomically assigned via reference databases, and analysed to compare prey composition across methods and against the backdrop of visual stomach content identification. fDNA metabarcoding successfully detected prey DNA. Prey richness and detection rates in fDNA samples were lower compared to stomachs, and exogenous DNA derived from species caught in the net was also detected. Despite these limitations, the technique effectively captured key trophic signatures, supporting its value in dietary reconstructions. Our findings highlight the promise and current limitations of fDNA metabarcoding for marine ecological studies, especially in fisheries contexts where individuals must be processed swiftly.

1643: This study investigated the feeding ecology and trophic position of four deep-sea cartilaginous fish species from the Strait of Sicily: Galeus melastomus, Scyliorhinus canicula, Raja clavata, and Chimaera monstrosa. The Shannon– Wiener index and trophic niche breadth indicated low trophic diversity across species, with S. canicula displaying the broadest feeding niche. Estimated trophic levels were highest in G. melastomus, consistent with its greater intake of fishes and cephalopods, while lower values in S. canicula, R. clavata, and C. monstrosa reflected their stronger dependence on crustaceans. Overall, all four species exhibited medium to high trophic levels, highlighting their key roles in maintaining deep-sea community structure. Low vacuity index values suggested good prey availability in the area. Schoener’s trophic overlap index and cluster analyses revealed limited dietary overlap among species, indicating effective resource partitioning. These findings enhance our understanding of trophic structure and energy pathways in Mediterranean deepsea ecosystems, which are increasingly exposed to anthropogenic pressures.

1645: The international trade in mobulid gill plates is a major driver in the global depletion of manta and devil ray populations. As this trade increasingly shifts to online markets, monitoring and enforcement have become more challenging. Tracing the geographic origin of devil ray derivatives offers a powerful means to uncover trade dynamics and support enforcement of conservation regulations. Based on these results, we developed a panel of diagnostic DNA markers to enable species identification and geographic tracing of illegally traded samples. The study will discuss the development of this molecular tool and discuss its potential applications for strengthening compliance with the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) in exporting countries, as well as for improving surveillance of the evolving gill plate trade network.

1646: Understanding reproductive strategies and behaviours is fundamental to the effective management and conservation of threatened rays. Key reproductive aspects such as the timing, location, and mechanisms of mating and parturition remain poorly understood, largely due to the difficulty and rarity of observing these events in the wild. Pregnant females were consistently observed over several weeks each year, with seven and eight females acoustically tagged in 2022 and 2024, respectively. High residency indices for three months post-tagging indicate that females remained within the estuary, suggesting parturition occurred locally and providing rare evidence for a pupping ground. This was supported by opportunistic sightings of a neonate in 2024 and an observed parturition event in 2025. Further, the first wild observation of mating in this species was documented within two hours of parturition, providing rare insights into polyandrous behaviour and potential multiple paternity. Our findings identify the Knysna Estuary as a critical pupping and mating habitat for blue stingrays, with significant implications for its conservation and management, and contribute valuable new knowledge to the globally understudied field of stingray reproductive ecology.

1647: The Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) project provides a tool to examine shortfalls in spatial planning for biodiversity conservation of sharks, rays, and chimaeras (chondrichthyans). ISRAs are three-dimensional portions of habitat that are important for one or more chondrichthyan species and have the potential to be managed for conservation. New Zealand and Pacific Islands is one of ISRA regions assessed, covering ~85,000,000 km² across jurisdictions, and hosting chondrichthyan species. A total of experts contributed to the delineation of ISRAs for species (47 sharks, rays, chimaeras). This includes over half (n = 48, 62.34%) of the threatened species and one third (n = 28, 26.84%) of range-restricted species in this region. Significant knowledge gaps were evident in potential high diversity areas and for pelagic and deepwater species. Most ISRAs were delineated for reproductive areas (n = instances) and undefined aggregations (n = instances). Although nearly half (42.18%) of the ISRA surface overlaps with marine protected areas (MPAs), only 1.25% (~39,000 km²) overlaps with no-take MPAs (~500,000 km², 0.58% of the region’s surface area). Protection of critical chondrichthyan habitat can be increased through locally-designed measures that are effectively implemented and enforced such as Locally Managed Marine Areas (LMMAs). By integrating ISRAs into marine spatial planning, conservation practitioners, policymakers, fisheries managers, and researchers can significantly enhance efforts to safeguard chondrichthyans while meeting global conservation targets.

1648: Shortfin mako sharks (Isurus oxyrinchus) are highly migratory pelagic predators found in temperate and tropical oceans. Listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List, this species is routinely caught as bycatch in longline fisheries, raising conservation concerns. We analyzed years (1994–2025) of Hawaii-based longline observer data from the deep-set tuna and shallowset swordfish fisheries to identify factors influencing shortfin mako bycatch. Using Generalized Additive Models and Generalized Linear Mixed Models, we assessed the effects of spatial location, distance from the 200-meter shelf edge, season, interannual variation, sea surface temperature (SST), and lunar cycle on bycatch rates. Bycatch in the shallow-set fishery is strongly structured by surface environmental conditions. SST (particularly during winter), lunar phase and clear spatial clustering, emerged as major predictors of mako occurrence. In contrast, bycatch in the deep-set fishery showed a weak but statistically significant response to winter SST, and its spatial hotspots were far less pronounced than those observed in the shallow sector. Seasonality and distance to the 200-meter contour influenced bycatch only in the shallow-set fishery. Together, these patterns suggest that shallow-water hotspots are shaped by dynamic surface processes well captured by our environmental covariates, whereas deep-set hotspots reflect drivers not explained by the present models. Notably, the shallow-set fishery accounts for 53% of all mako bycatch despite comprising only 10% of total hooks deployed, underscoring its disproportionate impact on the population. These insights support mitigation strategies that leverage the identified environmental predictors to reduce shortfin mako bycatch in longline fisheries.

1651: Zoos and aquariums are increasingly recognized as vital partners in global efforts to rewild sharks and rays which face steep population declines due to overfishing, habitat loss, and climate change. These zoological institutions serve as living laboratories, offering controlled environments to study elasmobranch biology, behavior, and reproduction. Advances in husbandry and veterinary care have enabled successful breeding and transport of several threatened species, laying the groundwork for future translocation programs. Aquariums also play a pivotal role in public engagement, fostering awareness and support for shark and ray conservation through immersive education and storytelling. Collaborative initiatives between aquarium professionals, field researchers, and conservation organizations are beginning to bridge the gap between ex situ care and in situ restoration, with numerous projects exploring habitat suitability criteria, post-release monitoring, and genetic management. Examples of the skillset that zoos and aquariums bring to rewilding success will draw on two ongoing projects: the StAR project which focuses on breeding, translocation, and wild release of Indo-Pacific leopard sharks (Stegostoma trigrinum) in Thailand and Indonesia and SharkRay360 which will focus on bowmouth guitarfish (Rhina ancylostomus) translocations across their native range. As the urgency to restore marine ecosystems grows, zoos and aquariums stand poised to contribute not only their technical expertise but also the social capital needed to drive meaningful change. The evolving role of zoos and aquariums towards increased investment in conservation action marks a paradigm shift in how we conserve and rewild some of the ocean’s most imperiled species.

1653: Mobulid rays are wide-ranging pelagic species that exhibit slow life histories compared to other elasmobranchs, making them highly vulnerable to overexploitation. In Sri Lanka, they are incidentally caught in drift gillnet fisheries targeting tuna and billfish. Although the export of mobulid gill plates is now prohibited, some fishers continue to retain and store them, anticipating potential future trade. This highlights the importance of understanding population trends and potential declines, as such knowledge provides a strong scientific basis for effective conservation measures and for reinforcing regulatory decisions. Our fisheries survey data recorded mobulid fishery landings across sites, totaling 9,220 individuals from 2011 to 2025. As surveys were irregular while landings occurred daily, we developed a machine learning framework to predict daily catches and assess long-term trends. A two-stage hurdle approach was applied: a Random Forest classifier estimated daily presence using predictors such as landing site, vessel type, monsoon season, lunar illumination, and rainfall, while a Negative Binomial Generalized Additive Model (GAM) predicted abundance on presence days, with Random Forest regressors used for comparison. The model achieved a mean area under the curve (AUC) of 0.76, indicating good discrimination between mobulid presence and absence, despite the sparse data. Predictions revealed clear spatial and seasonal patterns, with higher mobulid occurrence during the southwest monsoon and in multiday boat-dominated landing sites such as Negombo, Mirissa, and Valaichchenai. This framework bridges data gaps, identifies bycatch hotspots, and provides a scalable, data-driven tool to support management and enforcement of Sri Lanka’s mobulid trade ban.

1655: Shark deterrent technologies offer a promising non-lethal approach to reducing human–shark and shark–fisheries conflicts, yet real-world efficacy remains variable across species, environments, and devices. This study examines the behavioral responses of tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) to magnetic and electrical deterrents deployed across the Pacific. Using baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS), four deterrent devices—two magnetic (Sharkbanz and Brute Wildebeest Magnet) and two electrical (Ocean Guardian FREEDOM7 and the Tickler)—were tested in active and control trials around Hawai‘i (O‘ahu, Maui, Moloka‘i, and Lāna‘i) and Fiji (Kuata) between January 2023 and October 2025. To date, over BRUV deployments spanning 9–133 m depths have been completed and sharks have been tested. All behavioral data derive from isolated, single-shark encounters, verified through individual identification to eliminate pseudo-replication and potential competition effects. Behavioral metrics, including bait contact frequency, approach time, and nictitating-membrane activation, were quantified using EventMeasure and BORIS software. Preliminary analyses suggest variable avoidance behavior among individuals, potentially influenced by device type and field strength. Early trends indicate reduced bait contact and slower approach times during active Brute trials. Continued data collection through 2025 into 2026 will expand the sample size to ensure robust statistical comparison of deterrent efficacy and individual variability. The outcomes of this research aim to refine understanding of shark sensory ecology and provide data-driven recommendations for non-lethal shark management strategies worldwide. By advancing knowledge of deterrent performance under real-world marine conditions, this research supports ongoing efforts to balance human safety, fisheries sustainability, and shark conservation.

1656: There has been rising interest in shark physiology over the last decade, largely due to intensifying anthropogenic pressures on the marine environment. Haematology and blood chemistry parameters are important tools for assessing wildlife health, thus assisting management and conservation decisions. In protected areas such as the Galapagos Islands, these tools are particularly relevant as they help assess habitat change effects on resident species; however, physiological data remains limited in elasmobranchs. To help fill this gap, we described haematology and blood chemistry parameters in blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) from Santa Cruz Island, Galapagos. Blood samples were collected from adult females captured by handline under a protocol designed to minimize physiological stress. Lactate (4.9±2.3 mmol/L) and pH (7.2±0.1) indicated minimal physiological disturbance. Lactate was higher than values reported in juveniles of the same species (1.4±0.7 mmol/L). Total red (RBC, 0.42±0.1 106/µl) and white blood cell (WBC, 27.8±8.8 103/µl) counts, including differential leukocyte profiles, were consistent with values reported for different carcharhinid species, although RBC were higher (0.9±0.2 106/µl) for juvenile blacktips. This study provides the first description of blood cell morphology and baseline haematology data in adult blacktip sharks in the Galapagos, offering preliminary values for future health monitoring under scenarios of climate change and pollution that may affect the quality and suitability of habitats within the Marine Reserve. Standardized physiological assessments should be integrated into conservation monitoring to better track shark population health under increasing human pressures.

1657: The Galapagos Archipelago lies at the convergence of major oceanic current systems in the Tropical Eastern Pacific, creating two distinct marine seasons. While seasonal shifts in marine conditions influence reef fish community structure, such patterns in the Galapagos are not well understood. We assessed seasonal variation in reef fish assemblages at Darwin and Wolf using three stereo-video methods: Diver-Operated Video surveys (DOVs), benthic Baited Remote Underwater Video systems (BRUVs), and mid-water BRUVs. Sampling occurred during the warm (March) and cold (August) seasons of 2017 on the islands’ northwestern and southeastern coastlines. Total fish biomass was over three times larger in the cold season (25 t/ha) than in the warm season (7 t/ha). This increase was primarily driven by scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini), whose biomass rose from t/ha in the warm season to t/ha in the cold season, likely reflecting seasonal migration of adult females. Other benthopelagic teleosts and the schooling planktivore Cephalopholis colonus also showed reduced biomass during the warm season, consistent with lower productivity and prey availability. In contrast, demersal mesopredators and herbivores remained relatively stable across seasons. These findings highlight the value of multiple stereo-video methods for detecting seasonal patterns, particularly at oceanic islands where highly mobile species show pronounced temporal variability. Overall, results suggest seasonal oceanography drives substantial variability in northern Galapagos fish assemblages. The high biomass recorded across seasons underscores the global conservation significance of these ecosystems, especially as critical aggregation sites for critically endangered S. lewini.

1658: The Galapagos Marine Reserve is globally recognized as a world-class shark-diving destination, where the large abundance of sharks and the reliability of encounters with iconic species support a well-established shark tourism industry. This study quantified the socio-economic importance of sharks as a non-extractive asset in the Galapagos, estimating their economic value, the tax revenues generated, and the jobs supported by shark-watching tourism (i.e., diving and snorkeling). When accounting for economic multiplier effects, shark watching had an overall economic impact of US$76.4 million in 2023, representing approximately 15% of the gross revenues generated by the Galapagos economy. This industry alone generated US$1.7 million in National Park entry fees and directly supported approximately 1,900 jobs across the archipelago. The scalloped hammerhead was the most sought-after species, generating US$9.8 million through tourism—an amount times higher than the historical national fisheries landing revenues for this species. Whale sharks were also economically significant, generating US$3.5 million in tourism revenue during their six-month season. Our study shows that, beyond their ecological importance for marine ecosystems, healthy shark populations in the Galapagos are key to maintaining the socio-economic stability of the archipelago and the livelihoods of the local community. Given the importance of scalloped hammerheads and whale sharks, both migratory species threatened by fishing, this study provides a strong economic argument for strengthening conservation and fisheries regulations to reduce bycatch mortality of protected species in the region. Such measures are essential to safeguarding shark populations and the long-term socio-economic benefits they provide.

1659: The ecology and evolution of a species is shaped by the social environment, for example through disease spread, information transfer or group foraging. Our ability to analyse the social environment of animals has substantially advanced with technological developments. Acoustic telemetry is increasingly used as a method to gather aquatic animal behaviour data from the wild. However, the potential effects of different analysis methods on inferring social behaviours and reconstructing population structures from acoustic telemetry data in sharks have received relatively little attention. Here, we used an agent-based movement model to simulate acoustically tagged reef shark movements with a pre-existing social structure within an acoustic receiver array. We then compared multiple commonly used path reconstruction analyses for deriving aggregation events, positions and movement trajectories of fish, to infer associations among dyads from the simulated acoustic telemetry data. Namely, we used raw detections, centre of activity, and state-space-models (crawl and patter). For each methodology, associations networks are constructed from the acoustic telemetry dataset and compared to the ‘true’ network built from the exact trajectories of the simulated sharks. Preliminary results show distinct differences in network structure based on the various methods used. Our work is the first that quantifies the effect of different approaches on inferred social networks using acoustic telemetry and highlights that depending on the study design and objective, the choice of method can have impact on the conclusions drawn.

1660: Gili Matra, consisting of Gili Trawangan, Gili Air, and Gili Meno, is one of Indonesia’s premier marine tourism areas, where the diving community is distributed across the three islands. Sharks and rays are among the most attractive marine fauna encountered during dives, with whitetip reef sharks being the most commonly sighted shark species across dive sites. The first citizen science initiative in the region, Unite Gili, was launched in mid-2016. The reporting method has remained consistent throughout the program, with data submitted monthly by the diving community from 2017 to 2021, and weekly by individual dive centres from 2022 to 2025. A standardized data sheet was distributed to partner dive centers around Gili Air that included key parameters for long-term monitoring, such as date, dive site, time in, dive duration, current, visibility, temperature, species encountered, number of individuals, size estimate, sex, and sighting time. Our data shows that whitetip reef shark sightings increased noticeably after 2023, especially at two main sites known for resting juveniles (Shark Point and Halik Reef). Halik Reef recorded a steep rise in juvenile sightings, dominating overall observations by life stage. In contrast, Sunset Reef showed a more balanced distribution across age classes, but showed a decreased number of juveniles, suggesting it may function as a feeding or adult aggregation site. These patterns highlight how citizen science data is reliable to reveal habitat use and population trends of whitetip reef sharks within the Gili Matra Marine Park based on long-term monitoring.

1661: Sharks are one of the most important apex predators in the marine ecosystem. However, as of the latest available global assessment, approximately 25% of shark species are categorized as “threatened” according to the IUCN Red List criteria. Thus, conservation of sharks will ensure the stability of the marine food webs, maintain the population diversity in the ocean, and serve as an indicator of ocean health. In this context, rapid and accurate identification of shark species is an essential first step for their conservation and marine biodiversity monitoring. Accordingly, this research proposes a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model based on underwater images of shark species for their automated and accurate identification. This CNN model is helpful to track migration patterns, determine the habitat preferences, and calculate the species abundance, diversity in a specific area, and prevent bycatch. After categorizing pre-existing underwater images of sharks from the internet, we annotated 7000+ images of sharks and trained the model locally with that dataset. This model achieves an accuracy of 0.71 (mAP50) and 0.67 (mAP50–95), demonstrating promising performance for automated shark species identification with potential for further optimization to improve classification accuracy.

1662: Sri Lanka is home to more than species of sharks and rays. The shark and ray fishery plays a vital role in the fishing industry due to high local and international demand for shark and ray meat and other byproducts. The fishery can be divided into two sectors: the pelagic fishery and the coastal fishery. Although the pelagic fishery is partially regulated under national and international management frameworks, the coastal fishery remains unregulated, with largely unreported catch, despite contributing a considerable amount of shark and ray landings in the country. This study focuses on applying a semi-quantitative data-limited stock assessment method, Productivity Susceptibility Analysis (PSA), to assess the vulnerability of the most commonly landed sharks and rays in the coastal fishery of Sri Lanka in, bottom-set gillnets.In this study, eleven productivity and twelve susceptibility attributes were considered to assess vulnerability, and the results showed that nine species have high vulnerability, while eleven species showed very high vulnerability to the bottom-set gill net fishery. Glaucostegus granulatus was the most vulnerable species, followed by Himantura uarnak and Aetobatus ocellatus. Neotrygon indica was the most frequently recorded species and also the least vulnerable. Based on IUCN listings, all very highly vulnerable species are Threatened, including five Critically Endangered, three Endangered, and three Vulnerable species, yet none of these species are included in the national regulation or conservation frameworks. These results highlight the necessity of implementing fisheries management actions to help ensure sustainable exploitation of sharks and rays in Sri Lanka.

1663: The endemic walking shark Hemiscyllium halmahera inhabits shallow coral reefs and seagrass beds in North Maluku, Indonesia. This study investigates how ecological degradation influences its spatial distribution and conservation status. Field surveys combined with GIS analyses revealed that areas with greater coral and seagrass loss, high sedimentation, and anthropogenic pressures—such as mining and coastal reclamation—show reduced species occurrence [1], [2]. The species is mostly found in structurally complex habitats with live coral cover exceeding 30% and low sediment load [3]. Statistical analysis demonstrated significant positive correlations between live coral cover and H. halmahera presence (p < 0.05) [4]. These findings indicate that habitat degradation directly limits spatial distribution and population density, emphasizing the need for targeted habitat protection. As a unique and charismatic species, H. halmahera holds ecotourism potential as a flagship for community-based marine conservation [5]. Integrated management focusing on habitat restoration, sustainable tourism, and reef protection is essential to preserve the ecological resilience of North Maluku’s coastal ecosystems [6]–[8].

1664: Sharks are apex predators in the sea, play an important ecological role in maintaining the balance of the marine ecosystems. However, globally, shark populations are at risk of extinction due to natural and anthropogenic causes, including habitat loss. Therefore, identification and protection of their habitats are critical for ensuring their long-term survival, supporting ecosystem stability, and guiding effective conservation and management efforts. Shark habitat distribution prediction is an important establishing Marine Protection Areas (MPAs). We present a satellite-based approach that enables scientists to remotely identify sharks’ critical habitats, such as spawning, nursery areas, and feeding grounds. This satellite-based approach has modelled habitat distribution for shark species using multiple oceanographic parameters (sea surface temperature, Chlorophyll concentration, Sea Surface Salinity) acquired from NASA ocean observation platforms. We have confirmed the accuracy of the model output with available research findings. This application will provide resource managers, conservation practitioners, and researchers with an easily accessible, reliable, cost-effective monitoring platform, which updates every days, covering the entire ocean. This approach can be further expanded to other shark species, offering a scalable solution for global shark conservation efforts. This combination of remote sensing technologies with pre-gathered research data can produce dynamic habitat maps that support various applications, including optimizing marine protected areas, reducing human-shark conflict, reducing bycatch of sharks, and sustainable fisheries management. Also, it can easily be adopted to threatened marine species other than sharks by manipulating relevant data, providing a replicable framework for biodiversity monitoring and ocean conservation on a global scale.

1665: International wildlife trade poses substantial mortality risks to species worldwide, yet many traded species go unreported under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES), concealing the true scale of harvest and trade. We address this challenge for sharks and rays—the largest source of wildlife trade globally—by developing a hierarchical Bayesian compositional model that integrates genetic identification of fin products, customs data, fisheries landings, and other trade records to quantify hidden international trade through time. This compositional framework probabilistically allocates ambiguous trade categories (e.g., "shark meat unspecified") to specific species while propagating uncertainty through all estimates, revealing patterns invisible in any single data source. By linking meat and fin trade through a latent hierarchical structure, we demonstrate that the estimated million sharks killed annually are dwarfed by nearly million rays, tripling global elasmobranch mortality estimates. More than species are involved in this trade—predominantly from coastal fisheries —with substantial illegal trade components. The model reveals that fin trade patterns predict meat trade underreporting, suggesting coordinated concealment across product streams. Our hierarchical Bayesian approach demonstrates how integrating diverse data sources within a unified statistical framework can expose hidden wildlife trade, making demand, supply chains, and potential trade violations transparent for enforcement and conservation.
