1667: Buoyancy allows aquatic species to occupy three-dimensional habitats. Sharks regulate buoyancy through the accumulation of lipids in their livers, but trade-offs between buoyancy and movement efficiency have led to a spectrum of evolved strategies. Speed-focused pelagic species tend to be negatively buoyant, generating lift with their fins to maintain vertical position, while sluggish deep-sea species are typically neutrally buoyant, relying on fattier livers at the expense of a streamlined form. Measuring buoyancy in live animals is challenging, but biologging allows it to be inferred from swimming behaviour in species that exhibit frequent diving, since vertical movements in the buoyancy-aided direction require less effort than those in the opposite direction. Here, we present the first buoyancy assessment for one of the world’s slowest fish, the Greenland shark (Somniosus microcephalus). Using data from individuals tagged with acceleration biologgers in Canada and Norway, we compared the effort (overall dynamic body acceleration [ODBA] per speed) required for individuals to ascend vs. descend during dives. Results show that Greenland sharks support theoretical expectations and are on average neutrally buoyant. Significant differences in directional swimming effort (up to 234%) and occasional buoyancy-enabled gliding, however, provide evidence that individuals can be either negatively or positively buoyant to an extent as well. Biologger-derived buoyancy not only informs our understanding of the ecology, behaviour and energetics of vulnerable species such as Greenland sharks, but could provide a non-lethal means of assessing body condition in sharks through buoyancy’s fundamental links to the liver.

1668: As human-shark interactions increase worldwide, electromagnetic deterrent devices are increasingly promoted as tools to reduce shark depredation on fishing gear, yet empirical evaluations of their effectiveness remain scarce. Understanding species-specific behavioral responses to these stimuli is essential for evaluating their potential to mitigate shark depredation and bycatch. To assess their effectiveness, Baited Remote Underwater Video Systems (BRUVS) were deployed at more than sites in Hawaiian coastal habitats, testing four deterrent types (two electric and two magnetic) for their ability to reduce or delay elasmobranch contact with bait targets. Shark and ray interactions were quantified using SeaGIS EventMeasure and BORIS software, focusing on three common species: Carcharhinus galapagensis, Carcharhinus plumbeus, and Bathytoshia lata. To date, none of the devices significantly reduced or delayed bait contact. Power analyses indicated that the study was only sensitive to large effects (≥50 % reduction in bait contact), suggesting that smaller deterrent effects may have gone undetected. Further experiments will determine whether these devices can achieve smaller but statistically detectable responses. These results indicate that the performance of current deterrent technologies remains limited under natural field conditions. Additional testing in alternative contexts will help clarify how environmental and experimental factors influence outcomes. This research advances understanding of electromagnetic deterrents as potential depredation-mitigation tools and establishes a repeatable, evidencebased framework for evaluating and improving deterrent design and performance.

1669: Rising human use of coastal waters is driving more frequent elasmobranch encounters, intensifying depredation, increasing bycatch risk, and amplifying concerns about sharks biting ocean users. In response, magnetic and electromagnetic deterrent technologies designed to disrupt elasmobranch electrosensory systems are being promoted as potential mitigation tools. However, their effectiveness under natural field conditions remains insufficiently evaluated. To rigorously test the performance of these technologies, stereo Baited Remote Underwater Video System (BRUVS) deployments were conducted around the Yasawa Islands, Fiji, using a control–impact design in which BRUVS were fitted with either active deterrent devices or visually identical dummy controls. Four deterrent types (two magnetic, two electromagnetic) were tested to assess their ability to delay or prevent bait contact. Behavioral interactions were quantified using BORIS and SeaGIS EventMeasure across commonly encountered coastal species, with particular focus on Nebrius ferrugineus, Negaprion acutidens, Triaenodon obesus, and Carcharhinus melanopterus. With sampling ongoing, preliminary results show that roughly one quarter of deployments lead to elasmobranch interactions and about 15% of these interactions result in bait contact. These patterns will be refined as the dataset grows, providing increasing power to detect deterrent effects. These emerging results provide important context for evaluating the practical value of electrosensory deterrent devices and offer early insight into their potential roles in reducing depredation, lowering bycatch risk, and improving ocean-user safety.
1670: Mobulid rays (Family: Mobulidae) represent a group of large pelagic elasmobranchs occurring along the entire Indian coastline of the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. The Indian mobulid fishery is primarily incidental, contributing as bycatch averaging 3,338 t annually (2007–2024) and contributing 3–13% of total elasmobranch catches in multiple gear types including gillnetters, trawlers, hook-and-line units, longliners, and motorized gillnetters operating from landing centres on both coasts. The fishery composition is dominated by six species Mobula birostris, M. mobular, M. tarapacana, M. kuhlii, M. thurstoni and M. eregoodoo and with distinct regional variations. The maximum mobulid landing was recorded from Tamil Nadu, contributing more than 50% of the total landings, followed by Kerala. The dominant species was Mobula mobular, followed by M. birostris. Conservative life histories heighten vulnerability to multiday fishing, tuna gillnet/trawl bycatch, habitat loss, and weak species-level reporting; recent listings under India’s Wildlife (Protection) Act (1972, amended 2022) and CITES Appendix II have renewed conservation focus. Management options for Indian waters must emphasize enhanced bycatch documentation, species-level identification, fisher awareness on legal protection, and region-specific mitigation measures such as state-seasonal closures aligned to peak aggregations; observer/e-monitoring and species-level reporting; rapid-release protocols for gravid and neonate rays; enforcement aligned to CITES listings and national schedules; spatial measures around hotspots. Strengthening community-based monitoring through cooperative data-sharing with tuna fishers also can ensure sustainable management of mobulid populations in Indian seas.

1672: Intertidal zones support diverse assemblages of juvenile rays. However, limited knowledge of species’ diets, particularly during early life stages, translates to a poor understanding of how species coexistence is facilitated through resource partitioning mechanisms. This study investigated the trophic ecology of four juvenile ray species at an intertidal sand flat in Queensland, Australia using complementary approaches. Stomach contents were collected using gastric lavage (i.e. gut flushing) to describe dietary composition of each species, while trophic niche size and overlap were quantified using stable isotope analysis (δ13C and δ15N). Furthermore, benthic prey availability was surveyed to contextualise dietary preferences and fine-scale foraging patterns. Cowtail stingrays Pastinachus ater had the broadest isotopic niche and fed mostly on polychaetes, bivalves, and gastropods. Australian whiprays Himantura australis primarily fed on decapod crustaceans and had a smaller trophic niche size than P. ater. Critically endangered giant shovelnose ray Glaucostegus typus and brown whipray Maculabatis toshi both had narrow isotopic niches and specialised on penaeid prawns, suggesting direct competition during young-of-year life stages. Benthic invertebrates were abundant within the study area, albeit there was some patchiness across sites with different microhabitat features. This heterogeneity, combined with vertical distributions of prey throughout the sediment column, provide insights into how species-specific foraging strategies shape dietary variability. This study provides foundational knowledge on the diets of four understudied ray species during early life stages and how species’ morphologies and foraging strategies may facilitate the exploitation of different prey resources.

1673: Sri Lanka’s coastal waters support extensive one-day fibreglass-reinforced plastic (OFRP) fisheries that operate in nearshore habitats overlapping with all Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs). Despite their ecological importance, these fisheries remain poorly monitored due to the absence of formal vessel-monitoring systems. This study presents GPS-based monitoring of OFRP fleets across three focal ISRA: Pasikuda–Kalkudah(Eastern), Mathagal (Northern), Baththalangunduwa (Northwest), to examine spatial fishing effort, behavioural patterns, and temporal shifts in operational footprints since 2021. Handheld GPS units were deployed on selected vessels, complemented by elasmobranch landing surveys. Pasikuda–Kalkudah recorded frequent landings of Neotrygon indica, Maculabatis gerrardi, and Pateobatis jenkinsii, with fishers operating across wider and deeper habitats. Until last year, the site supported regular landings of the Critically Endangered Acroteriobatus variegatus (Stripenose Guitarfish), but recent surveys recorded only a few individuals, indicating a possible local decline. In Baththalangunduwa, Eusphyra blochii (Winghead Shark) remains the second most frequently caught species. Although the species is now mostly restricted to remnant populations in northern Australia and Papua New Guinea, its presence in Sri Lankan waters highlights the global conservation value of this region. Spatial mapping showed that most E. blochii capture sites and fishing activity occurred outside the designated ISRA boundary, indicating a gap in habitat coverage. Mathagal supported high diversity, including Glaucostegus granulatus, Brevitrygon imbricata, and Rhizoprionodon oligolinx, indicating a multi-species hotspot with fishing activity largely confined within ISRA boundaries. Collectively, these results show how GPS tracking can guide fisheries management by defining priority zones and protecting vulnerable elasmobranchs.
1674: Since 2017, Blue Resources Trust (BRT) has conducted surveys of fisheries across Sri Lanka, providing valuable data on the diversity and distribution of sharks and rays in the surrounding waters. Data from 2017 to 2025 were considered for this analysis, and during these eight years, the study identified over species of elasmobranchs, evenly divided between sharks and rays. This balanced distribution highlights the country's rich marine biodiversity and helps pinpoint areas of priority for conservation. Species abundances were standardised using rarefaction, and diversity was assessed with Shannon and Simpson indices to calculate an integrated hotspot score for each site. Three sites, Point Pedro (JPP), Valaichchenai Landing Site (VLS), and Valaichchenai Fishery Harbour (VFH), were identified as the most biodiverse landing locations. JPP had the highest hotspot score (8.19), dominated by benthic stingrays, such as Neotrygon indica and Brevitrygon imbricata. VLS (hotspot score = 7.75) was primarily dominated by large pelagic mobulids, notably Mobula mobular, Mobula tarapacana, and Mobula birostris, indicating its significance as a high-use area for pelagic rays. VFH (hotspot score = 7.74) supported a mixed assemblage of benthic and pelagic species, including N. indica, M. mobular, Carcharhinus falciformis, and M. tarapacana, marking it as a key multi-species hotspot. Differences in species assemblages across the top hotspots reveal the ecological diversity of Sri Lankan fisheries. Highlighting these high-diversity landing sites provides critical information for conservation planning, monitoring population trends, and directing management interventions for elasmobranchs.

1676: Understanding the ecological impacts of human activity on biodiversity is essential for conservation management. Quantifying the effect of human activity on highly mobile predators is difficult in areas with pre-established human pressure. The Covid-19 pandemic offered a unique opportunity to examine the effect of human activity on near-coastal shark populations in the Cayman Islands. This study used diver-based surveys from the citizen science programme, Sharklogger Network, to assess the spatial distribution and population structure of recorded shark species from 2019-2025. Volunteers reported 36,079 dives across three islands, noting shark abundance and absence with environmental variables. During the 6-year study period, 10,393 sharks of species were recorded. Covid-19 regulations considerably reduced human activity levels from 2020-2022. Overall relative abundance, defined by the number of shark sightings per dive, significantly increased during this anthropause with a number of species reoccupying near-coastal waters during the nation-wide ban of in-water and beach activities. The relative abundance of nurse sharks significantly increased from 2020-2021 whereas relative abundance of Caribbean reef sharks significantly increased throughout 20192021, suggesting species-specific tolerance thresholds for human activity. The reintroduction of human activities, followed by phased boarder reopening for stay-over tourism in 2021 and, subsequently, cruise ships in 2022, resulted in relatively quick changes to the relative abundance and spatial distribution of recorded sharks. These findings demonstrate that human activity, including the degree of tourism pressure, directly impacts the spatial distribution of near-coastal sharks in the Cayman Islands, providing valuable information to marine conservation management for nations with ample tourism.

1677: Fishing activities worldwide have driven severe declines in populations of many chondrichthyan (shark, ray, and chimaera) species, making them the second most threatened group of vertebrates. To halt and reverse these declines, effective area-based conservation and management strategies are urgently needed. While “Fully protected” Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) remain the gold standard for biodiversity recovery, their establishment is often unfeasible in areas where fisheries are of high socio-economic importance. Integrating fisheries management measures into spatial planning may offer a pragmatic and socially accepted pathway to balance conservation goals and local livelihoods. Although non-regulatory, the Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRA) process identifies critical habitats based on species’ vulnerability, life-history traits, and ecological and functional significance. We examined ISRAs across eight global regions to explore how a portfolio of fisheries management measures could be applied within these areas to enhance conservation outcomes. Options include restrictions on fishing gear (type, amount, configuration), catch or size limits and area or seasonal closures. When applied individually or in combination, particularly within ISRAs that overlap with existing zoned MPAs, these tools can help maintain key ecological functions such as reproduction or feeding in areas that are known to be demographically important, while sustaining fishing opportunities. Our findings demonstrate that ISRAs can serve as evidencebased spatial units for implementing diverse and flexible management actions that collectively contribute to the recovery and long-term conservation of chondrichthyan populations.

1679: Understanding how sharks use coastal waters with high human activity is essential for fostering coexistence with coastal communities. The dynamic nature of inshore waters and their proximity to human populations also present sharks with a range of advantages and disadvantages unique to the region. The Noosa Biosphere Reserve (NBR), Queensland, Australia represents a critical case study, as a UNESCO designated biodiversity hotspot supporting diverse shark assemblages, while sustaining strong tourism and recreational value. Using an array of acoustic receivers deployed throughout NBR’s inshore waters, this research investigates the spatial and temporal habitat use of large shark species including threatened species (Sphyrna mokarran, S. lewini, Carcharodon carcharias, Carcharias taurus), and other ecologically important species (Carcharhinus leucas, Galeocerdo cuvier). Diel and seasonal movement was assessed, including patterns in residency to identify transients, migrants and resident individuals for all focal species. Insights into population connectivity and migration patterns gathered through the acoustic array, was further investigated to identify environmental drivers influencing habitat selection. By comprehensively quantifying how different species of sharks navigate coastal waters, this research provides actionable insights for managing humanwildlife interactions in coastal tourism hotspots.

1680: In Venezuelan coastal communities, shark fishing including whale sharks (Rhincodon) and hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna) has long been common and culturally desired due to traditional dishes such as baby shark or cazón. Although legal, this practice made community level behavioural interventions essential to reduce shark mortality while improving community wellbeing. “100 % Life, 1000 % More Income” is a community based initiative that applies behaviour change science to support fishers in shifting from shark capture to sustainable livelihoods. The project integrates local ecological knowledge, identity building and pride centred conservation with practical economic alternatives. A major achievement has been the creation of a strong alliance between fishers and scuba divers. Previously these groups worked separately, but fishers are now trained in diver support, maritime safety, tank handling, risk prevention and site management. Their boats were upgraded with safer access and better operating conditions, allowing them to provide a professional service that dive operators depend on to reach pristine sites once known only to fishers. Additional livelihoods include reusable “grandma bags” made from ghost nets that reduce single use plastics in cities and a culinary initiative based on invasive lionfish. These activities benefit eighty households and have increased incomes by up to 1000 percent. Behavioural change is demonstrated by the voluntary abandonment of shark targeting gear, the rejection of illegal fin buyers and an increase in whale shark reports and wildlife monitoring. A whale shark mural at the port reinforces community identity and discourages fin traders. The model is replicable.

1681: Coastal reef shark populations across the Indo-Pacific are under growing pressure from habitat degradation, fisheries bycatch and increasing coastal activity. Despite their ecological importance, long-term data on juvenile blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus) remain limited in the Gulf of Thailand. This study examines temporal and spatial trends in juvenile shark occurrence around Koh Tao between 2015 and 2025 to identify key nursery habitats and assess emerging threats. Standardised surveys and citizen-science observations in earlier years were later combined with RUV’s to evaluate encounter frequency, size class distribution, and habitat use. Juveniles (< 60–90 cm TL) were primarily observed within shallow reef flats and sheltered bays, indicating the importance of these areas as nursery grounds. A marked decline in observations was recorded between 2015 and 2019, followed by a partial recovery in 2023 and 2025. Several mortality incidents were linked to fishing gear entanglement, including ghost nets and hook-and-line bycatch, suggesting that anthropogenic pressures continue to affect local populations even in these shallow ecosystems. These findings reinforce the ecological significance of Koh Tao as a critical nursery area for C. melanopterus and support its 2024 designation as an Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA). The study highlights the need for strengthened local management, targeted outreach to reduce bycatch, and continued long-term monitoring to inform regional conservation strategies for reef-associated sharks.

1682: Sharks, as ancient navigators of the ocean, have long turned their movements to the shifting rhythms of, temperature , ecological balance and prey availability. the migratory paths of sharks are redrawn in ways both subtle and profound. This study explores how climate-driven shifts in prey abundance alter shark movement patterns across costal and pelagic ecosystems, with an emphasis on species that rely heavily on predictable prey distributions. Using combination of satellite-tag data, remote sensing of sea surface temperature, and prey-biomass modeling investigated how multiple shark species adjust their seasonal movements in response to changing prey hotspots. Tracking data were analyzed across three ocean basins, and prey fields were reconstructed using chlorophyll-a productivity layers and fisheries-independent surveys. Spatial overlap between predators and prey was qualified to identify emerging or collapsing migratory corridors. Preliminary results suggest a consistent poleward displacement of both prey and shark, with several species extending their ranges by 200-600 Km in warmer years. Some predators exhibit delayed or accelerated migration timing as they followed shifting forage fish populations, while others showed reduced route fidelity and grater exploratory movement. These behavioral changes may increase energetic costs, alter predator-prey balance, and heighten interactions with coastal fisheries. As climate change continues to transform the oceans, traditional conservation tools may no longer align with movement of species. Our findings highlight the need for adaptive, climate-informed management strategies-such as dynamic marine protected areas and mobile monitoring networks-to protect sharks as they navigate a rapidly changing world beneath.

1683: Deep Norwegian fjords are undergoing rapid ecological change as warming surface layers, increased nutrient loading, and the progressive shallowing of oxygen minimum zones compress the vertical habitat available to deep-water fauna. The LOST project (Impact of Climate-driven habitat LOss in Norwegian fjords on ecosystem STructure and functional ecology of cartilaginous fishes) investigates how this habitat compression affects the ecology, behaviour, and population structure of data-deficient fjord sharks. Through replicated longline surveys, population genomics, and acoustic telemetry, we assess whether sharks form vulnerable local populations, how individuals adjust depth use and activity in response to warming and hypoxia, and how changing environmental conditions influence overlap with fisheries and aquaculture. By integrating movement data with oxygen and temperature profiles, we aim to quantify realized niches, energetic constraints, and emerging conflict zones under rapid environmental change. In this contribution, we will present results on longlining surveys, the effects of aquaculture, and the influence of climate on shark distribution and habitat use.

1686: Whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) form predictable seasonal aggregations within Al Shaheen oil field (ALS), off-shore Qatar, potentially overlapping with local and international merchant vessel fleets. Understanding fine-scale vertical habitat use, surface behaviour, and thermal exposure is important for informing management of this Endangered species at this critical site. Between April 2023 and September 2024 we used tri-axial accelerometer tags to quantify depth-use, surface presence, and cumulative temperature exposure of whale sharks. Sharks exhibited seasonal deepening, from ~0.7m in April to ~14m in June and ~40m in September, alongside greater short-term depth variability later in the season. Surface use (<10m), a proxy for potential vessel collision risk, was significantly seasonal, peaking in April (83%) and declining through June (61%) to September (19%), with patterns consistent across sex and size. Aggregatory behaviour (<5m) had temporally predictable peak-hour activity, shifting from early morning in April, mid-morning to early afternoon in June, and mid-morning in September, coinciding with daylight, increasing sea-surface temperature and elevated potential collision risk. Mean water temperatures increased from ~26°C in April to >34°C in September, potentially limiting surface-use activity and aggregatory behaviours, highlighting increased collision risk during cooler early-season months. Cumulative temperature exposure rose with month and depth, but depth and temperature were not directly correlated, indicating habitat-use reflects behavioural or ecological factors beyond thermal conditions (e.g. prey availability). These results highlight seasonal and diel periods of elevated collision risk to inform seasonally and temporally targeted management and adaptive planning to safeguard whale shark aggregations within ALS.

1690: As a 14-year-old underwater photographer from Thailand, I spent the past few years trying to capture sharks and other marine life to highlight the beauty and importance of them in the underwater ecosystem. My images have received international recognition, but more significantly, it has allowed me to share several photos with worldwide audiences. Although it may not be something that contributes to conservation directly, visually representing sharks as elegant creatures can change the perspective of those who see the image. Since protection starts with acknowledgement and a positive viewpoint, this is a vital part in a long journey to influential impact. By presenting sharks photos with explanations about behavior and ecology to the children from underprivileged schools in my country, I found that visual storytelling can quickly transform fear into curiosity. I will share samples of my shark images, describe the process of capturing pictures and explain how I create visual narratives that support understanding about marine animals. I also hope to encourage other youths to become ocean guardians because every voice can make an impact. The broader goal of my work is to demonstrate that meaningful contributions to conservation do not always require professionals. All people can inspire action by combining creativity, skill, and passion. Visual communication can become a bridge that brings people closer to sharks, to science, and to the heart of conservation. A photograph may not change the world, but it can remind us why it’s worth saving.

1694: Megachasma pelagios, commonly known as the megamouth shark, is the lone extant species from the family Megachasmidae and genus Megachasma. It was first discovered in 1978, with only about specimens recorded to date. Given its rarity and elusiveness, no gravid or neonate megamouth sharks have ever been documented. On November 2023, a freshly dead adult female shark carrying seven pups washed up on the shores of Barangay Ipil, Dipaculao, Aurora, Luzon Island, Philippines. In this study, we aimed to establish the identity of the specimens using morphological and molecular methods, identify morphometric differences through allometric analysis, and determine the paternity of the pups using Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) as markers generated by single-digest Restriction Site-Associated DNA sequencing (sdRAD-seq). Based on the results, morphological and molecular analysis confirmed the identity of the specimens as M. pelagios. Morphometric differences were observed in most traits, showing patterns of allometry, including those that have significant functional roles in feeding, stability, and propulsion, such as the head length and mouth width, anal fin, and caudal fin, respectively, implying that the offspring do not completely scale proportionally with the mother. Furthermore, genetic analysis revealed that the identity by descent (IBD) estimates between specimens were close to 0.50, indicating a first-degree relationship. Hence, the seven-pup litter was sired by a single father. Overall, this study provides a definitive identification of the specimens and offers new insights into their morphometric differences and reproductive strategy, which may serve as a baseline for species conservation and future studies.

1696: Elasmobranchs are heavily overexploited, with ~40% of the known species in the Western Indian Ocean (WIO) threatened with extinction. To support their improved conservation and management in this region, ecological surveys were conducted using stereo baited remote underwater video (stereo-BRUV), to provide data on elasmobranch distribution ranges, diversity, relative abundance, and habitat associations. The dataset comprised over 3,500 hourlong BRUV deployments conducted over reef and sand habitats (5–98 m deep) across Comoros, Kenya, Madagascar, Mozambique, South Africa and Tanzania, from 2016 to 2025. The surveys revealed inter alia a hotspot for the Critically Endangered whitespotted wedgefish Rhynchobatus djiddensis, a 2,000 km range extension of the Critically Endangered shorttail nurse shark Pseudoginglymostoma brevicaudatum, a 1,800 km transboundary movement of a white shark Carcharodon carcharias from South Africa to Mozambique, and the importance of sand habitats for elasmobranchs. South Africa and southern Mozambique displayed the highest frequency of occurrence (62% and 42% of samples with at least one elasmobranch recorded, respectively) and species richness (19 and species, respectively), supporting this area’s recognition as a global elasmobranch hotspot. However, frequency of occurrence overall was generally much lower than results from other regions globally. Notably, no sharks were recorded in deployments throughout Kenya and deployments in Antongil Bay in northeast Madagascar, the WIO’s only shark sanctuary. These findings highlight the severe impacts of coastal fisheries on regional elasmobranch populations and provide critical guidance to identify priority areas for focused conservation efforts for elasmobranchs in the WIO.

1699: Elasmobranchs in Saudi Arabia face significant threats from fisheries bycatch and illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing. Quantifying these threats along Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea and Arabian Gulf coastlines required a broad approach, including fish market surveys, genetic analyses, and electronic monitoring of trawl bycatch. Twice monthly market surveys were undertaken at landing sites from February 2024 through April 2025. Tissue samples were collected during these surveys to confirm species identification and assess population connectivity for commonly observed species. Electronic monitoring of vessels operating within the shrimp trawl fishery was undertaken to record instances of shark and ray bycatch. Fish market results revealed a stark contrast in elasmobranch landings between the two basins, with the Red Sea exhibiting higher occurrences likely driven by differences in enforcement on the two coasts. Genetic analysis confirmed most morphometric identifications but also revealed the previous cryptic presence of the Java cownose ray (Rhinoptera javanica), highlighting knowledge gaps. Camera-based monitoring of shrimp trawl vessels revealed substantial bycatch, with occasional mass captures of cownose ray schools as well as individual captures of several Critically Endangered species. These results, among others, will inform the development of a national Shark and Ray Conservation Action Plan for Saudi Arabia, contributing to evidence-based conservation regulations aimed at minimizing bycatch mortality, protecting critical habitats, and ensuring the long-term sustainability of these vulnerable species in Saudi waters.

1700: Understanding the distribution of elasmobranchs is critical for their conservation, yet data is often scarce. However, opportunistic sightings from ongoing survey efforts can begin to provide insights into their occurrence. Here, we present elasmobranch observations from coastal habitat surveys undertaken in the Saudi Arabian Red Sea and Arabian Gulf over a twoyear period (2023-2025). In the Arabian Gulf, elasmobranchs from species, including two vulnerable (Nebrius ferrugineus and Taeniurops meyeni) and four endangered (Aetobatus ocellatus, Carcharhinus leidon, Himantura uarnak, and Mobula mobular) species, were recorded with most sightings occurring in the northern region. The Red Sea was more diverse, with individuals from species observed. Once again, several species were within threatened categories including one critically endangered (Devil Ray, Mobula mobular) and six endangered species (Aetobatus narinari, Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos, Mobula birostris, Rhincodon typus, Torpedo panthera, and Urogymnus asperrimus). The Farasan Banks and Islands in the southern Red Sea emerged as key hotspots for sharks and rays. These results underscore elasmobranch species richness in Saudi waters and demonstrate the power of opportunistic data in understanding distribution patterns of sharks and rays. This approach provides a valuable, cost-effective tool for guiding targeted conservation strategies for threatened elasmobranch populations in these understudied regions.

1701: The Red Sea is a semi-enclosed basin in the northwest Indian Ocean exhibiting distinct circulation and thermal regimes. We investigated how elevated sea surface temperatures and deep-ocean mixing in the Red Sea influence the movements of two large-bodied, circumtropical shark species: the silky shark (Carcharhinus falciformis) and tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier). Using a combination of acoustic and satellite telemetry, we tracked horizontal and vertical shark movements along the eastern Red Sea of Saudi Arabia. Silky sharks largely remained within 100km of their tagging location and moved throughout the mixed layer during cooler winter months. However, when sea surface temperatures rose above ~30°C, silky sharks descended below the mixed layer, occupying a thermal refuge in an intermediate water mass (70-100m depth). Tiger sharks were relatively more dispersive, moving upwards of 1200km. During localized deep-ocean mixing events (when temperatures at the surface and seafloor vary by <1°C), tiger sharks repeatedly exhibited consecutive, oscillatory “yo-yo” dives to bathypelagic depths (>1000m) representing some of the deepest depth records for this species. Such dive profiles have previously been linked to foraging, leading us to suspect that tiger sharks exploit diminished thermal gradients to forage at bathypelagic depths. These findings offer new insights into the link between ocean stratification and movements of widespread shark species. If our results are consistent with projected climate-driven oceanographic changes, these novel patterns of shark depth use could have further implications for fisheries catchability relative to commercial longline set depths.

1702: Rays (batoids) are a key group of elasmobranchs, contributing significantly to India's elasmobranch fishery along both east and west coasts. They hold subsistence, economic, and cultural value for coastal communities; however, research and conservation efforts, particularly on socio-economic aspects, are limited. Understanding market structure, trade dynamics, and socio-economic aspects of rays is crucial for developing effective conservation and management policies that promote sustainable fishing and consumption practices. Palk Bay, an Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) in Tamil Nadu, supports a diverse array of ray species. Rays have historically been integral to the livelihoods and culture of local communities. Our study aimed to understand the actors, supply and value chain, and market dynamics of ray meat and products in the Palk Bay region, including gender participation and livelihood dependence. Seven to ten actors are involved in the supply and value chain in the Pamban landing centre, Palk Bay. Both small-scale and mechanised fishing sectors contribute, with fresh and dried ray meat forming the primary traded products. The species composition varies from large rays such as Mobula thurstoni and Aetobatus ocellatus, to small rays including Brevitrygon imbricata and Neotrygon indica. Fresh raw meat of big rays is sent to Kerala, while dried meat of big and small rays is distributed to various districts and states for consumption. The price of rays varies depending on their size and species. The insights from this study could facilitate timely, evidence-based management and livelihood support, leading to equitable and sustainable use and conservation.
1703: Family Rhinobatidae comprises an enigmatic group of elasmobranchs known as guitarfishes, considered to be the most vulnerable taxa after sawfishes (Pristidae). Our study aimed to investigate aspects of the biology and fishery of two critically endangered (CR) guitarfishes Acroteriobatus variegatus (Stripenose Guitarfish) and Rhinobatos annandalei (Bengal Guitarfish), along the southwest (SW) coast of India. The two species were historically abundant along the southern coasts of India but have experienced rapid declines in recent years. In the present study, a total of and individuals of A. variegatus and R. annandalei were examined from February 2023 to January 2024, with maximum observed total lengths (TL) of 79.5 cm and cm, and individuals carrying pups measured 65–77 cm TL and 70–90 cm TL, respectively. Reproductively active individuals were recorded primarily in May and August, characterised by lecithotrophic viviparity. Both species are not directly targeted by fishers but are regularly landed as bycatch, primarily in bottom trawls and to a lesser extent in bottom-set gillnets. Larger individuals (>1 kg) were retained for either local human consumption or transported to nearby districts and states. Smaller individuals (<1 kg) are typically discarded as trash and eventually used as poultry feed. Out of two species, A. variegatus is preferred by consumers and traders due to higher meat yield and lower wastage. Our study provides valuable insights into the biology, fisheries interactions, and trade dynamics of these two poorly known yet imperilled species and can form the basis for developing effective conservation and management strategies.

1705: Shark sanctuaries, established through retention and capture bans, have successfully protected sharks and rays within the national boundaries of multiple Central Pacific nations, including the Cook Islands and French Polynesia. However, highly migratory species, like the Oceanic Whitetip Shark (Carcharhinus longimanus), frequently move into adjacent unprotected waters, where they are exposed to high rates of commercial longline bycatch, targeted fishing pressure, and deep-sea extractive operations. To quantify long-term movements of this species in the Central Pacific, pop-up archival tags were deployed on individuals within the protected waters of the Cook Islands, in collaboration with local recreational fishers in Rarotonga. Tracking data was processed using movement models to identify migratory movement behaviors. The resulting migratory routes revealed highly consistent pathways utilized by both sexes and across multiple years, connecting the southern Cook Islands with the northern Austral Seamounts and Penrhyn Plateau. A critical finding was the consistent use of the unprotected high seas pocket, the international waters separating the protected Exclusive Economic Zones, as a primary migratory corridor. Dive data from archival tags also identified patterns of depth use in these unprotected areas, highlighting their vulnerability to fisheries operations in international waters. The regular reliance on these transboundary areas exposes the species to significant risks outside national protection. These findings highlight a critical gap in regional conservation, demonstrating that effective management is impossible without high-seas cooperation to protect these vital, unprotected routes.

1707: Deep-sea sharks’ genetic connectivity remains a challenge due to the limited knowledge of their ecological and biological traits followed by the complexity of deepwater environments. The aim of this study was to explore the genetic diversity of a common Mediterranean deep-sea shark, the small-spotted lanternshark Etmopterus spinax, through a multi-disciplinary approach combining biometric, parasitological, and genetic analyses. With the objective to investigate potential stock boundaries in the central-eastern Mediterranean Sea, we collected a total of specimens, from commercial trawls. Three analytical approaches showed high connectivity among regions and levels of genetic variability previously unreported for this species in the Mediterranean Sea. Analysis of sequences (Mitochondrial DNA Control Region) revealed a possible subdivision into two metapopulations, displaying low genetic differentiation with the partial isolation of the Ionian population. This may either reflect a recent colonization event or a limited gene flow influenced by hydrographic and geographical features. Parasitological data did not reinforce population structuring but provided insights for future research at finer spatial scales. Biometric variations supported the potential isolation of the Ionian population. Overall, E. spinax exhibits high connectivity and subtle population subdivision than previously reported for deep-sea sharks. The observed low genetic differentiation across broad spatial ranges suggested a shared pattern among deepwater species characterized by high dispersal potential. In the conservation field, the understanding of population dynamics is crucial for effective stock assessment and the novelty of this approach reveals key points from different prospectives for management strategies.

1708: Effective conservation action depends on translating legal frameworks and scientific knowledge into accessible tools for those managing, enforcing, and depending on marine resources. In India, the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 strengthened the conservation mandate for marine fauna, particularly sharks and rays, by expanding the list of protected species and aligning national legislation with international frameworks such as CITES. To support implementation at the ground level, ICAR–CMFRI developed the Illustrated Guide to Protected Elasmobranchs in Indian Waters, a visual knowledge product designed to facilitate accurate field identification and awareness of protection status. The guide features meticulously illustrated species, using primarily real photographs complemented by detailed drawings, each annotated with corresponding listings under the WPAA, CITES Appendices, IUCN Red List categories, and Non-Detriment Finding (NDF) assessments. Quick reference sections at the end of the guide explain these frameworks in simplified terms to enhance user comprehension. To maximize outreach, the guide was translated into ten regional languages and distributed to fisheries officials, enforcement agencies, and fishing communities across coastal states. Feedback from users highlighted its practical utility in species recognition, compliance monitoring, and awareness generation. By integrating visual communication, multilingual accessibility, and field validation, this initiative demonstrates how participatory knowledge tools can bridge the gap between policy and practice, thereby empowering conservation action and strengthening marine biodiversity management in India.

1710: Sharks are declining worldwide, largely due to overfishing and the international fin trade, yet effective monitoring remains constrained by difficulties in identifying species once products are processed. Here, we evaluate portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) spectroscopy as a rapid, non-destructive alternative for shark species identification. Fin tissues from six species including silky (Carcharhinus falciformis), blacktip (C. limbatus), gummy (Mustelus antarcticus), mako (Isurus oxyrinchus), roughskin dogfish (Centrophorus squamosus), and tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier), were analysed using an Olympus Vanta M-Series pXRF analyser. Elemental concentration and raw spectral datasets were examined using PERMANOVA, SIMPER, canonical analysis of principal coordinates (CAP), and random forest classification. Both concentration and spectral profiles differed significantly among species (PERMANOVA p < 0.001). Random forest classification success using concentration data achieved a mean accuracy of 92.5 ± 0.9%, while spectral models achieved 76.1 ± 2.3%. CAP cross-validation showed similarly high correct allocations (≈ 90%). These findings demonstrate that pXRF captures species-specific elemental fingerprints reflecting ecological and physiological differences among sharks. Its portability, speed (< min per sample), and non-destructive nature make pXRF a powerful complement to genetic methods, enabling rapid, portable screening of shark products in markets, ports, and enforcement contexts. Integrating pXRF into multi-method traceability frameworks could enhance the detection of illegal or mislabelled shark products and support compliance with CITES and fisheries management regulations.

1711: Marine shagreen is a material made from elasmobranch skins which peaked in popularity in northwestern Europe around the 18th century. This material was often used on cases for highvalue objects; also being incorporated into items such as sword handles and scientific instruments. Historical records indicate elasmobranch exploitation for shagreen occurred in a geographic range spanning the Indo-Pacific to the Atlantic, encompassing at least species from taxonomic families. Understanding which animals and seas were targeted remains understudied, leaving large gaps in our knowledge of how the demand for shagreen impacted historic elasmobranch species and may have contributed to their conservation status today. Utilising a combination of archival research and methodological approaches (dermal denticle analysis, proteomics), we are beginning to gain new insights into early modern period exploitation of elasmobranchs to meet demands for shagreen. This initial work encompasses ~140 objects from several museums: Winterthur Museum, M/S Maritime Museum of Denmark, Rijksmuseum, and Rijksmuseum Boerhaave. Historic preparations of the skins have left the dermal denticles, characteristic of many elasmobranchs, preserved to varying degrees on the objects. Preliminary analysis of dermal denticle patterns on these objects indicates that many of the objects were likely made from the skins of deep-sea species - a surprising, yet feasible finding when considered alongside the bottom trawling being practised, especially off the southern coasts of England at this time. Further refinement of identifications using proteomics will enhance our understanding of which species may have been historically abundant or readily available, thereby revising our historical ecological baselines.

1713: Deep-sea skates are among the most frequently bycaught species in Southern Ocean demersal fisheries. Their life history traits and strong overlap with fishing effort make them highly susceptible to fishing pressure, yet critical knowledge gaps remain regarding post-release survival and behavioural ecology. This presentation synthesizes three years of research on Kerguelen sandpaper skates (Bathyraja irrasa) to inform evidence-based management strategies for deep-sea demersal bycatch. Using popup satellite archival tags (PSAT) deployed on skates caught at 1200-1600 m depth during toothfish longline operations, we estimated a post-release survival rate of only 26% (95% CI 13-46%), substantially lower than estimates for other deep-sea skate species. Survival probability declined significantly with increasing capture depth. Complementary physiological analysis (n=100, including PSAT-tagged individuals) revealed that capture depth, soak time, and skate size significantly affected haematological stress markers, though these markers could not predict individual survival outcomes. This low survival rate indicates that current release practices may not effectively reduce fishery mortality, and extensive research would be needed to meaningfully improve post-release survival. Movement analysis from surviving PSAT tagged skates (n=6) and longterm mark-recapture data (n=291) revealed that B. irrasa typically remained within km of capture sites and undertook extensive vertical migrations following bathymetric contours at 800-1600 m depth. These movement patterns suggest bycatch avoidance through spatial closure measures are likely to reduce fisheries mortality more effectively than efforts to improve post-release survival. Collectively, these findings warrant an urgent review of current bycatch management protocols in Southern Ocean deep-set fisheries.

1715: Small-scale fisheries play a crucial role in developing countries, such as Sri Lanka, by providing food security, employment, and income to millions of people. However, these data-poor fisheries often lack effective management, placing their long-term sustainability at risk due to higher likelihood of overexploitation. The Spinetail Devil Ray (Mobula mobular) is a Critically Endangered, slow-growing species that is highly susceptible to overfishing. This study aimed to assess the stock status of M. mobular in Sri Lanka using a Length-based Bayesian Biomass model and examine the influence of asymptotic length (L∞) and bin width on the model’s results through a sensitivity analysis. Data were collected from landing sites across Sri Lanka between 2017 and 2024. The model was tested with L∞ values and seven bin widths, resulting in parameter combinations. Further, a multi-year and single-year analysis were conducted to compare the results between a larger dataset with variable data and a small dataset with representative data. The current levels of exploitation and estimated biomass indicate there is high fishing pressure and the stock is overfished, when modelled with larger L∞ and bin widths. Results demonstrate that the current maximum length of the M. mobular population in Sri Lanka is lower than the published asymptotic length. These findings, along with published literature, indicate that M. mobular populations in Sri Lanka are experiencing overfishing. Furthermore, this study highlights the importance of representative, high-quality data for reliable assessments using data-limited approaches.

1717: Scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini), listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN, are key apex predators whose presence influences the structure and resilience of marine ecosystems. Until the 2010s, Rasdhoo Atoll (Maldives) supported one of the most notable aggregations of S. lewini in the Indian Ocean, reportedly reaching up to individuals, which has since disappeared for reasons that remain unclear. This project aims to identify the environmental, ecological, and anthropogenic factors underlying this local decline through an integrated, community-driven research approach. The study combines conventional ecological surveys with local ecological knowledge interviews to generate long-term, site-specific data otherwise unavailable through traditional research methods. At each location, structured interviews with a minimum of divers and fishers will document historical and current shark observations, fishing activity, and ecosystem changes. These data will be complemented by standardized dive surveys and environmental parameter collections per site, targeting shark abundance, reef condition, and oceanographic characteristics. Local partners across two atolls will support sampling and data interpretation, while researchers collect complementary datasets on sea temperature, productivity, and reef health using in-situ and remotely sensed methods. Comparisons between Rasdhoo, where hammerhead aggregations have disappeared, and Fuvahmulah, where they persist, will elucidate the key drivers shaping these contrasting population trends. This collaborative framework contributes one of the first multi-scale assessments of S. lewini ecology and habitat decline in the central Indian Ocean.

1718: Offshore wind energy expansion has significantly increased the prevalence of subsea power cables, which emit electromagnetic fields (EMFs). Elasmobranchs depend on their perception of the earth's magnetic field and biologically induced electric fields, for orientation, navigation, locating conspecifics and detecting prey. EMF levels from subsea power cables will add to natural signals potentially disrupting elasmobranch perception, but the effects are not fully understood. Within the Elasmopower project the risk of EMFs was investigated with two benthic species e.g. the small-spotted catshark (Scyliorhinus canicula) and the thornback ray (Raja clavata) across three life stages (embryo, juvenile, adult). We present a comprehensive overview of the collected data concluding years of laboratory and field studies. These include multi-year EMF field measurements to learn about EMF patterns, followed by five laboratory experiments with all life stages, using realistic EMF exposure levels to monitor development and behaviour. Subsequent eDNA fieldwork revealed the presence of elasmobranchs in offshore wind farms. The results of these studies enabled a Species-Specific Risk Assessment resulting in species ecology and life-stage dependant risk levels, focussing follow-up research. Further research should focus on field-scale predator–prey interactions, impacts on migration under DC exposure, long-term adaptation or habituation processes, and cumulative stressor effects in offshore multi-use environments including other (OWF related) stressors. Results will support decisions-making about potential mitigation strategies (e.g., cable bundling, increasing burial depth, micro-routing) and help guide responsible offshore wind development compatible with elasmobranch conservation.

1719: Global ocean warming, exacerbated by anthropogenic activities, is dramatically altering marine ecosystems, with consequences for threatened species. The reef manta ray (Mobula alfredi), a large charismatic zooplanktivore, faces intense pressure from overfishing, which has contributed to significant global population declines. It has long been suspected that the species is further threatened by the effects of climate change through altered prey availability and, disruption to feeding and cleaning activities that are vital for their survival. This study examines the impacts of the 2024 acute warming event at one of the largest aggregation sites in Seychelles. Long-term data from boat-based surveys, coral reef and fine-scale temperature records show that the 2024 warming event coincided with changes in presence/absence, surface feeding and cleaning behavior of M. alfredi. We investigated the drivers behind these changes, including shifts in plankton biomass and coral cover at cleaning stations. Findings show that acute warming events do affect how manta rays use aggregation sites and influence their essential behaviors. This work provides some of the first evidence of how acute warming impacts Mobulid rays and highlights the urgent need for global action.

1720: Incidental capture, or bycatch, in fisheries is the primary threat to sharks, rays and chimaeras (Class Chondrichthyes). Chondrichthyan bycatch is often discarded, unrecorded, or reported under broad taxonomic categories, leading to major uncertainty in total mortality estimates for this threatened and sensitive taxon. Bottom-trawl fisheries typically generate high levels of bycatch and require careful monitoring to ensure sustainable management. The Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) uses evidence-based assessments to certify fisheries which achieve this management. Using observer and logbook data from South Africa’s bottom-trawl hake fishery, we evaluated how sparse and aggregated chondrichthyan bycatch data was assessed through years of MSC certification. Observers reported on catches of chondrichthyan species, including threatened species. Observers also documented sharks in 20–40% of trawls and rays in 12–40% of trawls, four to times more frequently than logbook records depending on sector and taxon. We standardized observer-based catch per unit effort (CPUE) using generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) to generate fishery-wide catch estimates. Annual shark catches in the offshore sector were estimated at 180–760 tonnes, four to fifteen times higher than logbook landings of 20–50 tonnes. Importantly, we identified systematic shortcomings in logbook reporting and observer protocols, which prevent accurate sustainability assessment. MSC assessments of chondrichthyan bycatch should consider IUCN Red List assessments of threatened species, require trawl-level records, reporting on discards of retained chondrichthyans and targeted observer sampling. We conclude that data requirements in MSC-certified trawl fisheries require improvements to ensure sustainable management of threatened shark and ray bycatch.

1721: Foraging and feeding are fundamental tenets of animal behaviour, providing critical insight for targeted conservation efforts. Observing foraging behaviour in natural environments, however, can be challenging, especially for aquatic animals. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have become an increasingly popular tool to help overcome a number of traditional limitations in ecological research. In this study, custom-designed, high-resolution GPS logging units were combined with commercial UAVs to construct short-term, active tracks for reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi; n = 30) using an important aggregation site in the Seychelles. Continuous time movement models were generated to estimate activity-specific home ranges for 1) surface feeding and 2) cruising/foraging. Tracks revealed highly area restricted space use during surface feeding (x̄ = 0.08 km2 ± 0.07) and found tidal influences on feeding periodicity. Findings showed that the no-take marine protected area (MPA) around D’Arros is effective in protecting these important feeding areas and offer valuable information for defining management measures, such as speed restriction zones within the MPA. This research highlights the importance of aggregation sites such as D’Arros for feeding and fitness in this threatened species and demonstrates the potential for UAV tracking as a tool to passively track aquatic animals at high-resolution, without requiring capture or impacting behaviour.

1722: Rhincodon typus (whale sharks) form the world’s largest feeding aggregation in the Al Shaheen oilfield, Qatar, where they feed on the Euthynnus affinis (kawakawa tuna) spawn. While this aggregation is well described, little is known about the broader fish assemblages associated with this phenomenon and the potential ecological role of offshore platforms. Here, we used environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding to characterise seasonal and spatial variation in fish communities across three permanent sampling sites and R. typus feeding aggregations, spanning more than a year and two aggregation seasons. Community analyses revealed significant seasonal shifts in assemblage composition, largely driven by the spawning of E. affinis, which was identified as a significant indicator species across all sites during the R. typus aggregation season. Rhincodon typus eDNA was detected almost exclusively during this period, coinciding with peaks in E. affinis eDNA. Aggregation sites were characterised by distinct assemblages compared with surrounding open-water sites, with several associated taxa identified as indicators. Although feeding aggregations were occasionally observed outside Al Shaheen, R. typus eDNA was detected far more frequently within the oilfield. Our findings suggest that offshore platforms may directly or indirectly influence the aggregations, potentially by shaping E. affinis spawning dynamics and associated fish communities. The likely role of platforms should therefore be considered in future management and decommissioning strategies, where Rigs-to-Reefs approaches may provide an ecologically beneficial alternative.
1723: Eusphyra blochii (Winghead Shark) is the most divergent species in the hammerhead family (Sphyrnidae), currently listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List. While recent studies confirm remaining populations in northern Australia and Papua New Guinea, baseline data from the Indo-Pacific range are absent due to severe population declines. Monitoring over sites across Sri Lanka since 2017, Blue Resources Trust (BRT) provides refined biological and spatial evidence showing that winghead sharks are restricted to Baththalangunduwa Island on the northwest coast. There are no targeted fisheries for winghead sharks; however, they are frequently landed as bycatch in gillnet fisheries (mesh sizes and inches). At Baththalangunduwa, bamboo sharks (Chiloscyllium sp.) dominate shark landings (84%), while E. blochii contribute 13%, making them the second most abundant. Analysis of sex and maturity revealed a predominance of immature individuals (84%) with a nearly balanced sex ratio. Among the recorded E. blochii specimens, 26% were neonates (37.5–43 cm TL), all within the known size-at-birth range for the species. Through a BRT community-based GPS tracking program, fishers’ vessel movements were recorded during incidental winghead captures, revealing more precise habitat use, requiring an expansion of the ISRA for E. blochii. Next steps include using this knowledge to develop management recommendations to alleviate fishing pressure on this threatened species. Simultaneously, running an awareness campaign for local communities, highlighting the value and uniqueness of this species to encourage proactive community-led conservation action to supplement the slower, national-level conservation actions.

1724: Rays of the family Rhinopteridae Jordan & Evermann, 1896 are highly migratory species, distributed in warm waters of tropical and temperate seas. Due to their coastal habits and the formation of large schools, they are frequently caught as bycatch in trawling fisheries, especially those targeting marine shrimp. Along the Brazilian coast, the species exhibit similar external morphology, being primarily differentiated by the conformation of the teeth in their oral plates. The mitochondrial genome of Rhinoptera lalandii was obtained by next-generation sequencing, yielding 16,217 base pairs (bp), comprising protein-coding genes (PCGs), two ribosomal RNA (rRNA) genes, transfer RNA (tRNA) genes, and one non-coding control region (D-loop). All PCGs initiated with the ATG codon, except for COX1, which started with GTG, and the majority terminated with complete stop codons (TAA/TAG). Genomic models that support conservation measures are essential given the accelerating loss of marine biodiversity caused by anthropic actions. The phylogenetic analysis showed that R. lalandii was recovered as the sister species of R. bonasus from the US. Currently, there are only four mitochondrial genomes available for the genus Rhinoptera, making it necessary to expand this number to enhance the understanding of the evolution and systematic position of the group. These data can contribute to phylogenetic analyses, population studies, and the comprehension of the molecular evolution of the family Rhinopteridae.

1725: Understanding mechanisms enabling coexistence of ecologically similar elasmobranchs in coastal environments is essential for species-specific management and conservation. Scyliorhinus canicula (small-spotted catshark) and Scyliorhinus stellaris (nursehound) are sympatric, benthic mesopredators inhabiting temperate coastal waters in the Northeast Atlantic. Both species play key ecological roles as coastal mesopredators but are exposed to multiple anthropogenic stressors. Despite extensive overlap in distribution, diet, and habitat, competitive exclusion theory predicts these congeners must partition resources to facilitate coexistence. While previous studies have documented seasonal and trophic partitioning, spatial and temporal patterns of habitat-use remain poorly understood. This study investigates the niche partioning of these two ecologically similar species in the same coastal environment through analysis of spatial and temporal movement. Initial baited remote underwater video (BRUV) surveys within Plymouth Sound, the UK’s first National Marine Park, revealed overlap in distribution of the two species. Acoustic telemetry was employed to quantify movement patterns and space use in individuals of each species to test the hypothesis that these species exhibit distinct movement strategies within the same coastal waters. Analyses of spatial distribution, habitat preferences, and activity patterns will determine whether spatial and temporal partitioning occurs, potentially reducing interspecific competition. These findings will provide the first direct examination of movement-based niche partitioning in these Scyliorhinidae species. These insights into fine-scale habitat use and niche partitioning are critical for developing effective, species-specific conservation strategies and marine protected area planning in urbanised coastal environments.
1726: Rhino rays (Rhinopristiformes), a group of shark-like batoids, are among the world’s most threatened elasmobranchs, largely due to their vulnerability to fishing and the high demand for their fins. Conservation efforts are often constrained by limited ecological and physiological data, particularly in the understudied Red Sea, with little in-situ ecological information. The critically endangered Halavi guitarfish (Glaucostegus halavi), is locally abundant in the Al Wajh Lagoon, a northern Red Sea location recently designated as an Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA), which may serve as a nursery and refuge for the species. However, the region is undergoing rapid coastal development and experiences extreme seasonal temperature variation (12–38 °C), exposing resident populations to environmental and anthropogenic stressors. To investigate how these factors may influence the species’ physiology and life history, we collected and analyzed blood plasma metabolite profiles from Halavi guitarfish individuals across life stages, sexes, and seasons. Preliminary analyses suggest ontogenetic shifts in fatty acid signatures, with smaller individuals exhibiting slightly higher MUFAs and significantly lower proportions of ARA, compared to larger conspecifics. This study presents the first physiological dataset for this species and establishes a framework for interpreting fatty acid patterns in the context of changing environments. These findings will support longterm physiological monitoring and help predict the resilience of rhino rays in response to rapid coastal change.

1727: In Sri Lanka, approximately 14% of all harvested fish is processed as dried fish through traditional salting and sun drying, helping meet 65% of national demand for dry fish. Sharks and rays form a major component of this dry fish. At this heavily processed stage, morphological identification is often impossible, and conventional cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) barcoding (655bp) becomes challenging when DNA is degraded, complicating species identification. This study developed a DNA mini-barcoding protocol targeting a ~150 bp gene region of the COI gene for species identification of salted dried sharks. Sampling was conducted over six months and dried shark products were randomly collected (N>30) from public markets across the country. Tissue samples were soaked in nuclease-free water and incubated at °C as a pre-treatment to reduce the salt level. DNA was extracted using the QIAGEN DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit and the results indicated low DNA concentrations and high salt contamination (1>260/230). Two mini-barcode primer combinations were tested, using one forward (VF2) with two shark-specific reverse primers (Shark 150R & Shark COI-MINIR), and the best-performing pair was selected for sequencing based on the amplification success. The developed protocol successfully amplified degraded DNA from salted dried sharks, and multiple shark species were revealed including Carcharhinus falciformis, Prionace glauca, Sphyrna lewini and Isurus oxyrinchus demonstrating its reliability for species identification. This molecular tool will provide essential baseline data for monitoring and regulating the dry fish industry and the shark fin trade in Sri Lanka.

1728: Due to targeted and bycatch fisheries triggered by demand for shark, ray, and chimaera (sharks) products, one-third of all species are threatened with extinction. Global dynamics and extent of the shark fin trade are relatively well-understood, but for shark meat remains significantly under-investigated, preventing the assessment of its impact on populations and the accountability of nations trading CITES-listed species. Within the Global Shark Meat Project, this study examines the scale, scope, and market dynamics of the shark meat trade in Mexico, the world´s fourth-largest shark producer. Surveys and interviews with fishers and supply chain actors were conducted at key ports, landing sites, and markets to investigate catches, local consumption patterns, and the shark meat value chain. Internal consumption of shark meat accounts for most of the sharks caught in Mexico, with a small part exported, mostly to the USA and Taiwan. National production is insufficient to supply the national demand, as ~2,000 t of meat is imported yearly, mostly from Costa Rica. While sometimes mislabeled, the greatest proportion is bought as shark meat. Demand for shark meat exists year-round peaking during Lent, and Christmas season. Most consumed meat comes from threatened species, juveniles, and small sharks. These findings highlight the complexity of Mexico's shark trade, driven by high consumer demand and localized distribution networks rather than solely international trade. Understanding domestic market forces is fundamental to develop effective fishery management strategies, improving species-specific conservation efforts, and strengthening the application of CITES-regulations in this important shark fishing nation.

1731: Many extant sharks (Neoselachii) are facing a significant threat of extinction. Worryingly, all shark species are expected to face some level of climate change threat over the next century. However, their long generation times and the confounding influence of other anthropogenic factors, such as overfishing and habitat degradation, make it challenging to assess the realtime effects of current climate and environmental change on shark ecology and biodiversity. Neoselachii, a monophyletic group including all extant sharks, have survived every mass extinction and extreme climate change event in their 200-million-year evolutionary history. The Neoselachian fossil record, therefore, offers a valuable ‘natural experiment’ for understanding how their ecology and biodiversity are affected by unprecedented environmental change. This project aims to investigate how mid-Cretaceous (113.2 ± 0.3 to 93.9 ± 0.2 million years ago) Neoselachian ecology and biodiversity responded to environmental change during a period marked by drastic increases in sea surface temperature and sea level, as well as an ocean anoxic event. This will involve collating a large dataset of fossilised teeth to document midCretaceous Neoselachian taxa and apply morphometrics to infer functional traits and ecology. These will then be compared with proxies that infer palaeoenvironmental factors such as sea surface temperature, sea level, primary productivity, sea level and anoxia to understand the relationship between Neoselachian ecology and biodiversity and past environmental change. By providing a long-term perspective without the influence of anthropogenic confounding factors, this research may help predict the vulnerability, or resilience, of extant sharks to current climate and environmental change.

1732: Rays play key ecological roles as mesopredators in marine ecosystems, yet they remain among the least studied and most threatened elasmobranchs globally. In Brazil, data scarcity hampers the development of effective conservation and management strategies. This study investigates the relative abundance and population structure of rays across protected insular systems along the coast of São Paulo, southeastern Brazil (Laje de Santos, Alcatrazes Archipelago, Queimada Grande, Queimada Pequena, and adjacent reefs), using baited remote underwater stereo-video systems (stereo-BRUVs) between 2017 and 2025. A total of deployments recorded individuals representing species from families, with Dasyatis hypostigma and Myliobatis freminvillei being the most frequent. Species richness and abundance were highest in fully protected areas (Laje de Santos and Alcatrazes), whereas multiple-use MPAs exhibited reduced species richness and dominance by a few taxa. A marked female bias was observed in most species, notably in D. hypostigma (up to 1M : 16F), suggesting sexual segregation and preferential use of these insular environments by females for feeding or reproduction. Eight species recorded are listed as threatened under Brazil’s official conservation system. Our findings highlight the critical role of marine protected areas in sustaining diverse and reproductively relevant ray populations, emphasizing the need for continued monitoring and adaptive management. This study provides one of the first multi-site assessments of ray assemblages using stereo-BRUVs in the Southwestern Atlantic, offering essential insights to guide conservation policies for threatened batoids in subtropical island ecosystems.

1733: Scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini; IUCN Red List: Critically Endangered) form iconic seasonal aggregations in the northern Galápagos Islands, Ecuador. Although these sharks are protected within the Galápagos Marine Reserve (GMR), their highly migratory nature exposes them to intense fishing pressure throughout the Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP). To conduct the first genomic assessment of these aggregations, we collected biopsy tissue samples from free-swimming, adult aggregating sharks in the GMR and genotyped them (n = 354) alongside samples obtained from young-of-year S. lewini from putative nursery areas along the Pacific coasts of Central and South America. We leveraged the resulting high-resolution single nucleotide polymorphism data to estimate genomic diversity metrics and investigate genetic connectivity throughout the ETP. Furthermore, we compared the genomic diversity of the Galápagos S. lewini aggregations with non-aggregating adults caught near Seychelles (W. Indian Ocean) and Florida (W. Atlantic Ocean). Our results revealed high genetic connectivity throughout the ETP, suggesting the Galápagos adult shark aggregations are part of a large, interconnected ETP population and underscoring the need for comprehensive conservation measures beyond the GMR borders. Estimates of species-wide autosomal heterozygosity (HO) were low, particularly for Florida sharks (Florida: 0.0009, Galapagos 0.0015, Seychelles: 0.0017), further emphasizing the risk that scalloped hammerheads face from a changing environment. Contemporary effective population size (Ne) estimated from Galápagos aggregation samples was estimated to be >11,340 sharks, suggesting the breeding population is large and/or connected enough to avoid losing genomic diversity due to natural population dynamic processes alone.

1734: Collaborations that lead to high-impact output are considered a major benchmark in elasmobranch research. A strong collaboration, authorship, and citation record reflect expertise, productivity, and leadership ability, and is often paramount in the establishment of a career in elasmobranch research, especially for early-career researchers (ECRs). Identifying the ecological facets that are being studied and how that work is being taken up by research communities and policymakers also highlights important themes that are shaping our contemporary understanding of elasmobranchs. In this introspective study, we examine how acoustic tracking research has shaped knowledge of elasmobranch ecology and characterise associated collaboration and authorship trends that help affirm the career trajectories of ECRs. Specifically, we explore how different types of collaborations and study metadata (e.g., journal ranking, species, conservation status, geographic area) influence citations (in peer-reviewed literation and policy documents) by drawing on a comprehensive database of >3,000 acoustic telemetry articles published by >6,000 unique authors since 2001 (trackdat.org). Furthermore, we explore how leaders in the field set themselves apart in terms of their role facilitating collaborations and student success. Our aim for this presentation is to provide a unique perspective of how elasmobranch ecology research is being translated into empirically based metrics that influence both career and scientific advancement. Our target audience is ECRs to provide guidance on navigating a highly competitive career path, but the patterns extracted are pertinent to elasmobranch researchers independent of career stage or field of expertise.

1735: Climate change is reshaping marine environments, with rising temperatures imposing significant physiological challenges on ocean life. While heat stress is known to disrupt immunity and inflammatory status in teleost fishes, little is known about this response in sharks. The epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium ocellatum) is a small tropical shark inhabiting reef flats of the Great Barrier Reef (GBR) with documented resilience against environmental stress. However, it is unknown if their thermal tolerance extends to immunity under future warming conditions. We collected sharks from Heron Island (Southern GBR) and transported them to the National Sea Simulator at the Australian Institute of Marine Science. For eight weeks, individuals were exposed to end-of-century temperature conditions across three groups: winter (23–28°C) and summer (28–33°C) treatments incorporating daily 5°C fluctuations to mimic natural reef-flat variability, and a static control (28°C) to assess the physiological costs of thermal fluctuations. Cellular and humoral immunity were evaluated through blood cell counts, leukocyte differentials, quantification of antibody and inflammatory markers. Initially, sharks exposed to the summer and control treatments exhibited elevated blood cell production compared to winter, indicative of inflammation and metabolic strain. If cell counts declined after eight weeks, persistent shifts in leukocyte profiles suggest potential long-term impairment of immune competence. This study provides the first experimental evidence of immune disruption in a reef shark under prolonged warming. By identifying physiological markers of stress and immune function, these findings advance our understanding of shark resilience and inform conservation strategies in an era of rapid climate change.
