1835: Great hammerhead sharks in the Mexican Caribbean remain poorly documented, and the lack of ecological data limits effective conservation planning. Former shark fishermen hold extensive local ecological knowledge (LEK) built over decades of targeted and incidental catch. Their observations include captures of mature, pregnant females, with higher occurrence in winter months when white-spotted eagle rays—an important prey species—arrive in the region. Nursery areas for sphyrnid sharks have been reported across the Caribbean, suggesting possible overlap between historical fishing grounds and key developmental habitats. Understanding these spatial links is essential to evaluate how past fishing pressure has affected early life stages and the reproductive output of mature females. This study will: (1) establish the first integrated baseline for great hammerhead ecology in the Mexican Caribbean; (2) identify priority conservation areas, such as nursery grounds and seasonal aggregation sites; (3) strengthen community participation by integrating LEK into scientific assessments; (4) inform management strategies, including potential spatial or temporal protections; and (5) offer a model for LEK-based shark research in other data-poor regions. Semi-structured interviews and participatory mapping will be conducted in collaboration with the Kab Xok Cooperative. LEK will be systematically analysed and compared with ecological data generated through BRUV deployments, stable isotope analysis and fisheries-independent datasets. Expected outputs include identifying seasonal hotspots, habitat preferences, pregnancy patterns and behaviours linked to eagle ray presence, as well as long-term trends in abundance and catch composition. Integrating traditional knowledge with ecological methods will provide a comprehensive baseline to support evidence-based conservation and community-driven stewardship.

1837: There is a growing need to monitor rhinopristiform rays (“rhino rays”) given their high extinction risk and recently enacted international trade regulations. The Global FinPrint project is the world’s largest survey of sharks and rays on coral reefs, having deployed over 25,000 baited remote underwater video stations (BRUVS) in jurisdictions from 2015-2025. Of these, are range states of rhino rays, offering an opportunity to assess the utility of BRUVS for monitoring populations. Rhino rays were detected during sampling in range states (42% of the sampled range states), but detections generally occurred on fewer than 2% of the total deployments, which could be due to low abundance and/or coral reefs being secondary habitat. We identified hotspot reef locations where rhino ray sighting frequency was greater than 10% of all sightings including Ashmore Reef, Kimberley, and Pilbara (all in Australia’s Indian Ocean), the Southern Great Barrier reef in Australia’s Pacific, Ponta de Ouro in Mozambique, and iSimangaliso in South Africa. Nearly all these hot spots are within Marine Protected Areas, highlighting the conservation potential of spatial management. We will also explore temporal changes in rhino ray sightings at a subset of locations to better understand population trends over time. Rhino rays nearly always actively oriented to deployed BRUVS, which further suggests that BRUVS surveys could be a useful sampling approach for detecting these species where they are rare and developing abundance time-series in hot spots.

1838: Pollution is one of the most pervasive threats to marine biodiversity, yet assessing its ecological impact remains costly and complex. The SHARKSense project introduces an unconventional research approach by investigating shark skin pigmentation as a bioindicator of pollution exposure. Building on the pigment melanin’s ability to bind and sequester toxic compounds, we integrate computer vision pipelines, biochemical assays, evolutionary modeling, and collaborative field surveys to uncover correlations between integument darkness and pollutant accumulation. This methodological framework spans taxa, geography, and time, offering a scalable, non-invasive tool for ecological monitoring. In this talk, I will share preliminary findings and highlight the technological innovations behind SHARKSense, including automated image analysis for pigmentation quantification, biochemical assays linking coloration to pollutant binding, and data modeling frameworks that connect pigmentation patterns to environmental stressors. I will also share lessons learned from managing a consortium of NGOs, universities, and institutes across seven countries, illustrating how collaborative protocols can strengthen data collection and reproducibility. By bridging molecular mechanisms with conservation strategy, SHARKSense demonstrates how pigmentation analysis can complement existing monitoring tools, fill critical data gaps, and advance innovative approaches to shark and ray conservation.

1839: Various countries have moved away from extractive uses of sharks, such as fishing, and are instead aiming to benefit from healthy shark populations through tourism. While shark tourism can occur without using food rewards, many operations in countries like The Bahamas utilize provisioning. The impacts of provisioning on the behavioural ecology of several shark species have been investigated, yet few studies have used stable isotope analysis to assess its potential effects on trophic ecology. Across behavioural, spatial, and health-focused research, reported impacts range from negligible to severe, highlighting the need to evaluate the practice across a broad range of species and ecological contexts. Here we examine the impacts of low-level provisioning of Ginglymostoma cirratum, the Atlantic nurse shark, by comparing individuals from one feeding site and two non-provisioning sites in South Eleuthera, The Bahamas. We used stable isotope analysis of serum, skin, and cartilage to determine whether provisioning influences trophic niche, and assessed serological health markers to evaluate whether dietary shifts affect physiological condition. We documented significant differences in stable isotope values between provisioned and unprovisioned individuals across tissues, with the provisioned sharks exhibiting a narrower trophic niche and feeding on more pelagic, higher trophic-level prey. These dietary shifts were not accompanied by changes in health status, suggesting that controlled provisioning may represent a sustainable touristic alternative to G. cirratum fisheries, especially when incorporating natural food items. To our knowledge, this is the first assessment of the effects of provisioning on both diet and health in this demersal mesopredator.

1840: Marine biodiversity loss is an escalating global crisis, exemplified by rhino rays (Rhinopristiformes), which include some of the most threatened vertebrates on Earth. Endemic to Indonesia, the Critically Endangered Clown Wedgefish (Rhynchobatus cooki) was considered possibly extinct after two decades without confirmed records. Its rediscovery in 2019 from a specimen in a Singapore fish market, followed by social media reports of landings in Indonesia’s Lingga and Singkep Islands, renewed hope for its persistence by providing the first insights into its potential range. However, its contemporary distribution and habitat use remains poorly understood. Targeted environmental DNA (eDNA) techniques offer a highly sensitive, noninvasive approach for assessing the presence of rare and elusive species, such as R. cooki. In June 2023, one-liter water samples were collected from shallow coastal habitats surrounding Singkep Island, Indonesia, including coral reefs, seagrass beds, mangroves, and sandy bottoms. A species-specific droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) assay was developed to amplify a small portion of the R. cooki mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I gene from environmental samples. Capable of detecting a single copy of target DNA, this study provides the first quantitative insights into the species’ real-time occurrence across nearshore habitats. This eDNA assay offers a robust tool that can be used in additional locations where R. cooki is suspected to occur to comprehensively define its distribution. The results of eDNA surveys inform conservation priorities by identifying potential critical habitats where R. cooki occurs and establishing a baseline needed for monitoring this species.

1843: The Tropical Eastern Pacific (TEP) hosts Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) that support globally significant shark biodiversity. However, fishing pressure exacerbated by ineffective enforcement threatens population health, particularly in continental MPAs near human populations, while oceanic island MPAs benefit from remoteness. We deployed Baited Remote Underwater Video (BRUV) following standardized procedures to compare shark assemblages among three continental and four oceanic island MPAs in the TEP. Oceanic MPAs supported high shark relative abundances (3.8 ± 4.3 MaxN hour⁻¹), among the highest globally. These abundances are likely driven by oceanographic processes enhancing productivity and trophic diversity and sustained by reduced anthropogenic disturbances associated with remoteness and protection. Galapagos sharks (Carcharhinus galapagensis; ± 1.8 MaxN hour⁻¹) and whitetip reef sharks (Triaenodon obesus; 0.5 ± 0.9 MaxN hour⁻¹) occurred across sites. While silvertip sharks (Carcharhinus albimarginatus) were detected only at northern oceanic MPAs (Revillagigedo and Clipperton; 0.82 ± 0.9 MaxN hour⁻¹), and critically endangered, scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna lewini) dominated in equatorial MPAs (Galapagos and Malpelo; ± 5.1 MaxN hour⁻¹ vs. Revillagigedo; 0.2 ± 0.6 MaxN hour⁻¹). In contrast, four sharks were detected across continental MPAs (0.06 ± 0.2 MaxN hour⁻¹), supporting that fishing has depleted communities. These results highlight oceanic MPAs as refuges for sharks, including threatened and migratory species. Regional conservation requires strengthened enforcement to combat illegal fishing, priority protection of essential habitats in depleted continental MPAs, evidencebased fisheries regulations in and around MPAs, and coordinated transboundary management addressing connectivity of migratory populations across jurisdictions.

1847: Paramount Seamount is the only shallow seamount along the Cocos Ridge that lies in Ecuadorian waters. For many years, it was suspected to be a “stepping stone” along a migratory corridor that connects the Galapagos and Cocos Marine Reserves. Despite this, it was left just km outside the Hermandad Reserve, created in 2022, which protects Ecuador’s part of this corridor. However, Paramount’s designation in 2023 as an ISRA, based on observed aggregations of Critically Endangered scalloped hammerhead sharks, leveraged new research. Although highly mobile, to date no migratory route for scalloped hammerheads has ever been described. We tracked nine individuals (37-300 days) from Paramount in January 2025, finding a clear migratory route and differences between sexes. Six males resided within a radius of km from the peak of Paramount for their entire tracks. In contrast, all three females left Paramount in March, traveled east past Colombia’s Malpelo Island to the coastal Punta Chame and Panama Bay ISRA, which has been identified as a hammerhead shark nursery site. After 3-10 days, they returned to Paramount along a similar route, then two individuals moved into the Galapagos Marine Reserve while the third continued west for over 6900 km, making this the longest track on record for this species. Paramount thus plays dual roles for hammerhead sharks: as an area of high residency for males, and a regional node for migratory females. Based on these new findings, there is growing momentum to expand the Hermandad Reserve to protect the Paramount ISRA.

1849: Accelerometers have been widely applied now to evaluate elasmobranchs in the wild including recovery from capture events, sociality, and fine-scale behaviour classification. However, accelerometer loggers are challenging because they must be recovered from animals and the battery life can be limited, obviating observations throughout the full year. Accelerometer transmitters integrated into acoustic tags offer a solution for accessing long-term data about activity patterns of sharks and rays as long as the animals remain within an area covered by acoustic receivers. Using acoustic accelerometer transmitters in the Osterfjord system of western Norway, we investigated the full-year biological rhythms of spiny dogfish and thornback rays. Using a novel generalised additive model parameterisation, we identified interactions between season and diel period to reveal activity peaks for both species across an entire year. Results yield exciting insights into the ecology of sharks and rays using remote tracking tools, and offer a promising template for future research to investigate biological rhythms that reveal eco-evolutionary dynamics of species that are otherwise challenging to observe in the wild.

1850: This study aimed to assess how Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) are affected by fishing activity from a three-dimensional perspective. The results can assist decision-making for advancing area-based management for elasmobranchs. The next steps involve matching the results by area with the life habits of elasmobranch species to achieve a better understanding of how fishing pressure overlaps conservation-relevant habitats. Fishing activity from Global Fishing Watch (GFW) was used as a proxy for pressure, expressed as apparent fishing hours km1. Each fishing cell was classified according to gear type into benthic, demersal or pelagic, plus an “unknown” category (when fishing activity could be detected, but the gear type could not be identified). This approach provided a categorical vertical resolution to represent the depth domain of fishing activity. The study involves analyzing global datasets, with the preliminary results concerning the Brazilian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). Fishing activity within ISRAs accounted for 27.9% of all activity in the Brazilian EEZ. Benthic fisheries represented 56.68% of activity within ISRAs, demersal fisheries 32.71%, pelagic fisheries 2.63% and the unknown category 7.98%. The main gear types operating within ISRAs were trawlers, set longlines and drifting longlines. Limitations in the GFW dataset resulted in an underestimation of fishing effort, particularly for coastal zones and artisanal fisheries. The lack of detailed, species-level and gear-specific information may be critical for minimising fishing impacts in already delineated ISRAs and may obscure areas that could qualify as ISRAs but remain undetected due to insufficient data.
1852: Understanding the habitat use and movement patterns of critically endangered chondrichthyan species is essential for informing spatial management, protection, and conservation efforts. Sawfish are among some of the most endangered shark and ray species, and aspects of their movement and habitat ecology remain poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, we deployed towed satellite tags on seven sawfish in north Queensland between 2019 and 2025, resulting in three tracks longer than days: one dwarf (Pristis clavata, cm total length (TL); days transmitting) and two green (Pristis zijsron, and cm TL; and days transmitting). Generalised Additive Mixed Models (GAMMs) were then used to assess how environmental variables, including bathymetry, tide phase, rainfall, and time of day influenced sawfish movement and behaviour. Tide phase emerged as one of the most significant drivers, suggesting that individuals may use tidal cycles to optimise access to feeding or resting areas or to navigate between habitats. Additionally, all tracked sawfish used small, localised areas including estuarine, riverine, and marine habitats. Seasonal shifts in core use were evident in the longer-tracked green sawfish, highlighting potential seasonal changes to habitat use. Restricted spatial use and reliance on localised habitats for all three sawfish highlight the vulnerability of this species to anthropogenic activities such as habitat degradation, fishing pressure, and waterway modification. These findings emphasise the importance of identifying important habitats to directly inform the spatial planning of protected areas supporting the recovery of these critically endangered species.

1854: The endangered whitespotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari)(Dulvy et al. 2021), is a charismatic elasmobranch vital to the Mexican Caribbean ecosystems and dive tourism industry. These magnificent rays are a major ecotourism draw, but face severe threats from habitat destruction and fisheries. Our photo-identification study (Cerutti-Pereyra et all.2017), commencing in 2015, established the first regional catalog by analyzing over a thousand photographs from citizen scientists. In the baseline study, citizen science photos dating back to 2003 were incorporated, identifying individuals, our database currently holds individuals and counting. With the upcoming integration of 2025 data, we anticipate reviewing the initial 14.9% re-sight percentage, refining our understanding of their movements. This work evolved into a decadelong citizen science endeavor, fundamentally revolutionizing our understanding. Through continuous collaboration with a strong community of divers, snorkelers, and open water swimmers who provide invaluable data, our findings now suggests that a small proportion of individuals exhibit year-round residency in key habitats (coastal shallow reefs and the ship wrecks). This powerful collective effort has been instrumental in both unveiling new locations where eagle rays remain year round and to provide continuous monitoring in these key locations. These findings indicate a stronger, year-round site fidelity than previously understood, presenting a compelling case for targeted, year-round conservation and management strategies to safeguard A. narinari populations. We are actively working with the local community and Marine Protected Area (MPA) managers to enhance conservation and monitoring efforts for the species, demonstrating the effectiveness of community-driven conservation in high-tourism marine environments.

1857: Rhinopristiformes (i.e., rhino rays) are among the least studied species and are simultaneously facing high extinction risk. Illegal fishing and harvesting of their meat and fins pose the greatest threats, yet a lack of basic understanding of population demographics precludes the implementation of effective management measures. The White-spotted Wedgefish (Rhynchobatus djiddensis) is a Critically Endangered rhino ray found within South Africa’s iSimangaliso Wetland Park (IWP), a World Heritage Site listed for its natural attributes that support rich chondrichthyan diversity. The study goals were to 1) identify patterns in distribution, relative abundance, and demographic structure of the White-spotted Wedgefish and 2) investigate potential environmental variables influencing these population dynamics in the IWP. A total of Baited Remote Underwater Video Systems (BRUVS) were deployed across shallow (<15 m), medium (15-25 m) and deep (26-35 m) depth zones over a three-year period, in collaboration with iSimangaliso Wetland Park Authority and Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife. In total, White-spotted Wedgefish were documented, ranging from 94–301 cm total length and a female to male ratio of 4.5:1. Generalised additive models were used to explore relationships between MaxN and predictor variables (e.g., photoperiod, sea temperature, depth). Depth, bottom-sea temperature, lunar illumination, and Julian Day were significant (p <0.001); however, predictive power was low (deviance explained = 10.4%). Given recent declines, this research provides key insights into White-spotted Wedgefish ecology and highlights the importance of the IWP for future conservation.

1858: In 2011, Honduras declared its EEZ a Shark Sanctuary. This was a top-down approach with no previous consultation from fishers. In 2016, incidental captures of sharks were allowed to be commercialized specifically in the Moskitia Region, an indigenous region. Given the ambiguity of the legislation, artisanal fisheries continue unrestricted. We used a mixed-methods approach including using landings, fisher surveys and market surveys to understand the implications of the Shark Sanctuary legislation and its amendment. Findings indicate that despite the legislation, shark fishing continues driven by demand for salted-dry fillets known locally as “Cecina”. Although landings were dominated by small carcharhinids, critically endangered scalloped and great hammerhead young of the year and juveniles were frequently landed, underscoring significant conservation concerns. In terms of perceptions, fishers know that the shark sanctuary is in place, but they are not aware of why it was put in place or the importance of sharks. Market surveys determined that most sellers obtain their Cecina from the Moskitia region and noted some transboundary with Nicaragua. Sellers surveyed reported declining demand (48%), largely attributed to generational shifts away from Lent-related consumption. Traceability gaps were evident, as 59% of vendors did not know their products came from incidental captures revealing significant challenges in enforcing the Shark Sanctuary and its 2016 amendment. Our work highlights the importance of stakeholder involvement at every stage of management and demonstrates that shark sanctuaries are most effective in contexts where shark fishing is minimal or non-existent and where viable livelihood alternatives exist.

1860: Magnets are widely promoted as shark deterrents intended to reduce depredation, bycatch, and human-shark interactions. However, studies report mixed and sometimes conflicting results regarding their efficacy, potentially due to confounding factors such as bait, visual cues, and conspecific competition. To isolate sharks’ innate responses to magnetic fields, we ran controlled captive experiments with scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), sandbar (Carcharhinus plumbeus), and tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier). We constructed a non-visual magnetic “fence” bisecting an m × m tank using twenty-four neodymium magnets (4.5-kg mass; ~1928-kg pull force; ~1400 Gauss) positioned beneath and along the outer tank walls. This design exposed sharks crossing the tank's midline to a strong magnetic field absent of bait or visual cues. Thirty-minute active (magnets present) and control (magnets removed) trials were recorded from an overhead camera to quantify fence crossings and behavioral reactions. Repeated trials conducted at intervals over several days allowed us to assess potential habituation. Preliminary results show a pronounced initial avoidance response across species, although most individuals ultimately crossed the magnetic fence within the 30-minute period. Avoidance behaviors weakened with repeated exposure, indicating a habituation effect to the magnetic stimulus. By evaluating shark behavior in a controlled, non-baited setting, this study provides an upper-limit benchmark for the deterrent potential of solid-state magnets and highlights the likelihood of habituation. These findings offer important context for interpreting the performance of smaller portable magnets used in commercial deterrents and their practical value for fisheries and human safety applications.

1862: The Stegostoma tigrinum Augmentation and Recovery (StAR) Project Thailand is a collaborative, multi-stakeholder initiative supporting the recovery of declining Indo-Pacific leopard shark populations in Thai waters. Building upon the framework established by StAR Indonesia and informed by a citizen science initiative (Spot the Leopard Shark), the Thai program was launched in early 2025 to augment the western subpopulation of leopard sharks in the Andaman Sea. The roadmap and release protocol were nationally adapted to emphasize inter-agency coordination, local partnerships, and the integration of citizen science. Although guided by a shared conservation framework, Thailand and Indonesia operate in contrasting ecological and management contexts which shape the conservation strategies required in each country. StAR Thailand features NGO WildAid, Ocean Blue Tree, and strong government leadership through the Department of Marine and Coastal Resources (DMCR) and Department of National Parks (DNP) alongside private partners Aquaria Phuket and Maiton Island Resort. Juveniles for release are captive-bred in-country, acclimatized to local conditions, and tagged before release into acoustic array in Phang Nga Bay. A population viability analysis (PVA), conducted with the IUCN Conservation Planning Specialist Group, indicated that a 10-year release program combined with habitat protection should substantially increase long-term abundance and genetic diversity. The first release of three juveniles in late 2025 demonstrated two months survival and independent foraging. These early results highlight the feasibility of a fully domestic rewilding program, supported by strong institutional collaboration and adaptive management, and demonstrate the value of ReShark’s protocols as a flexible, scalable model for future initiatives.

1863: Essential habitats are critical to a species’ survival. However, essential habitat use is often dependent on environmental context and can change across ontogeny. While essential habitat use by tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) in subadult and adult life-stages is well-studied, our understanding of essential habitat use by juveniles, especially young-of-the-year (YOY), remains poorly resolved. This study characterized essential habitat use by juvenile tiger sharks along Australia’s east coast, using catch rates and acoustic telemetry to assess changes in movement across ontogeny (YOY to sub-adults) and latitude. Long-term tracking data from >400 tiger sharks aged from one to thirteen years old, revealed complex movement patterns and high mobility across ontogeny, especially for sharks in subtropical/temperate regions. Small juvenile sharks, especially YOY-3 years old, had high displacement (>100 km) and low residency. In the warmer, tropical regions, juvenile sharks tended to exhibit higher residency and lower movement, indicating stronger site fidelity when not constrained by temperature fluctuations. Taken together, these findings highlight that across ontogeny, tiger shark movement and residency patterns are shaped by both age and environmental context. Small juvenile tiger sharks, especially YOY-3 years old, are highly mobile and appear not to rely on discrete nursery habitats. These findings suggest a unique strategy of essential habitat use, where young juvenile tiger sharks demonstrate exploratory movements in lieu of nursery use.

1864: Over the past three decades, tropical stingrays (Batoidea) have shifted from low-value incidental catch to high-value commodities, with growing demand for their meat and, especially, for tanned skins known as shagreen or galuchat. We synthesize historical trends in utilization and examine opportunistic data collected from trader interviews as well as market and landing site surveys in Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia, Myanmar, Singapore, and Sri Lanka. We characterize the scale, species composition, and routes of the ray-skin trade. We document a transition from largely localized uses as abrasives, in traditional armory or small goods, to regionally integrated supply chains centered in Southeast Asia. Skins are sourced mainly from the Indo-West Pacific and processed primarily in Thailand and neighbouring hubs before entering luxury fashion and interiors markets in Asia and Europe. We identify a watchlist of ray species contributing to this trade—predominantly dasyatids—selected based on recurring appearance in markets, trader preference for large, patterned “pearl” skins, and overlap with intensive coastal fisheries. While some skins are likely by-products of meat fisheries, rising prices and targeted gears indicate increasing retention. Traceability is poor: products are frequently aggregated or mislabeled, obscuring species and volumes. Given widespread population declines of rays and limited monitoring at the species level, we outline immediate actions including strengthening port-of-landing documentation; developing rapid identification guides for processed leather; and Harmonized Systems codes for ray skins. Understanding this trade is essential to align utilization with conservation outcomes and to prevent market incentives from accelerating depletion of ray populations.

1867: Understanding the movement ecology of threatened species is essential for developing effective conservation strategies. The Raja Ampat epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium freycineti), listed as Vulnerable to extinction by IUCN and fully protected in Indonesian waters, occupies fragmented shallow coastal habitats across Raja Ampat. However, despite its protected status, detailed information on its residency and fine-scale movements remains limited, hindering targeted management efforts. This study examined the residency patterns, movement dynamics, and potential drivers of movements of H. freycineti around Arborek Island, a key habitat in central Raja Ampat. Passive acoustic telemetry was used to monitor individuals over an 18-month period (October 2023–April 2025). Forty-two sharks were surgically implanted with V13 Innovasea acoustic transmitters during two tagging periods (October–November 2023 and March 2024), and detections were collected from receiver arrays deployed in three configurations, totalling receivers encircling Arborek and covering an area of approximately 0.625 km2. Sharks exhibited high residency, with movements largely restricted to reef flat, seagrass beds, and mangroves on Arborek. Notably, none crossed to adjacent shallow patch reefs separated by only ~200 m of deeper (~25 m) water, indicating strong site attachment and apparent avoidance of movement across deeper channels. Detections and movement activity were concentrated on the eastern side of the island around reef flat near human settlements, suggesting possible anthropogenic influences on spatial behavior. These findings highlight the species’ limited dispersal capacity and strong site fidelity, underscoring the importance of localized conservation measures that protect critical shallow habitats and reduce human impacts.

1868: Indonesian waters is known to host populations of whale shark, the world’s largest fish. Despite this, little is known about the movements of this globally endangered species. Here, we described the horizontal movements, habitat uses, and residency of adolescence whale shark using satellite telemetry. We equipped sharks with dorsal fin-mounted satellite tags in four regions: Cenderawasih Bay (n=35), Kaimana (n=8), Raja Ampat (n=1), and Saleh Bay (n=24). The sharks were satellite-tracked from June 2015 to August 2023 spanning from to 1,286 days (~3.5 years) with an average of days (1.2 years). Spatially, the tagged sharks showed various degree of movements from locally restricted movements within the tagging regions to wide ranging movements to regional and international waters. Temporally, tagged individuals showed long-term residency from weeks to months and year-round occupancy in tagging regions. Moreover, they exhibited seasonal use and strong fidelity to aggregation areas. State space models suggested area restricted search (ARS) movements around tagging regions, likely indicating foraging behaviours. The 95% home range of tagged individuals showed segregated and preferred habitats with some degree of overlaps around the Banda Sea. Overall, our study using satellite telemetry provided evidence of Indonesian waters as important habitats for this species

1870: Kenya lacks robust data on the diversity, distribution, and abundance of sharks and rays. Existing information is derived primarily from NGO-led catch landing surveys that provide snapshots of fisheries captures, while dedicated underwater survey methods have so far proven ineffective. The global FinPrint BRUVS survey (2020) recorded no sharks in Kenya, prompting suggestions that reef sharks may be “functionally extinct” locally. A second FinPrint survey in 2025, comprising BRUVS deployments, again detected none. Yet sharks continue to be landed by artisanal fishers, indicating they persist, but may occur in habitats or depths not sampled by conventional BRUVS approaches. To address this disconnect, we conducted interviews with artisanal fishers to document local ecological knowledge (LEK) relating to shark fishing grounds, seasonal variation, and habitat use. Frequently cited sites were mapped collaboratively with fishers at sea, and BRUVS were deployed at these locations to evaluate whether LEK-guided sampling improves survey efficiency and increases the likelihood of detecting sharks and rays. This approach provides an opportunity to refine survey strategies, examine how LEK aligns with existing sampling tools, and assess whether fishers’ knowledge can enhance spatial targeting of shark research in data-poor regions. More broadly, integrating LEK with standardized monitoring offers a cost-effective and participatory framework for designing future surveys, while strengthening collaboration between fishers, researchers, and managers. By bridging local experience with scientific methods, this work aims to improve understanding of shark occurrence and habitat use, ultimately supporting informed and locally grounded fisheries management in Kenya.

1871: Grey reef sharks (Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos) are among the most frequently observed reef sharks in the Maldives, yet their aggregation dynamics and ecology remain poorly understood. This study provides preliminary insights into the aggregation observed in Rasdhoo-Madivaru Marine Protected Area and ISRA (Alif Alif Atoll). Through dives in Spring 2025, photo-ID of sharks highlighted a female-biased, mostly mature population. The majority of these individuals showed marked site fidelity, with many recorded for over days. Evidence of reproductive activity was frequent: females displayed mating scars, while showed features consistent with potential pregnancy, suggesting that the site may support reproductive behaviours. Sharks formed aggregations of varying size and function throughout the channel, ranging from small non-social resting groups to structured social subgroups and coordinated hunting formations, linked to hydrodynamic environmental conditions and reef morphology, that play a key role in how the aggregations form and persist. However, injury prevalence was high (53.8%). Individuals frequently displayed natural scars, mating marks, and a range of fisheries-related wounds: embedded hooks, trailing lines, constriction marks, jaw deformities, amputations of dorsal/caudal fins. Taken together, these findings highlight that the Rasdhoo-Madivaru MPA is an important aggregation site for grey reef sharks, exhibiting most of the characteristics consistent with a potential super-habitat. However, despite its protected status, its limited extension does not appear to provide full protection for resident sharks from anthropogenic threats. Strengthened enforcement, improved buffer-zone management, and long-term monitoring are urgently needed to protect and ensure the resilience of this population.

1874: Sabah’s coastal waters, located within the Coral Triangle, support high marine biodiversity, including diverse shark and ray assemblages. Most marine protected areas (MPAs) in Sabah, except Tun Mustapha Park (TMP), completely prohibit fishing activities and may act as de facto shark sanctuaries. Between 2015 and 2017, the Global FinPrint project surveyed coral reef sites along Sabah’s east and west coasts using baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS). Building on this baseline, WWF-Malaysia conducted additional surveys from 2017 to 2021, expanding coverage to a total of five reef sites and BRUVS deployments. Analyses from these combined efforts revealed that only Sipadan island exhibited relatively high shark abundance and diversity, while rays dominated assemblages in reefs lacking management or formal protection. In 2025, we resurveyed three of the five reefs; Sipadan and Mabul–Kapalai, nearly a decade after the initial Global FinPrint surveys, alongside additional surveys in TMP to assess current shark and ray assemblages under different management regimes. This coordinated effort provides an opportunity to evaluate long-term changes in fully protected (Sipadan), unprotected (Mabul–Kapalai), and multi-use (TMP) reefs, offering comparative insights into the effectiveness of various spatial management measures in supporting shark and ray populations. By comparing outcomes across protected, multi-use, and unprotected reefs, this study explores how existing MPAs can be enhanced or expanded to strengthen shark and ray conservation, and how other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs) and spatial fisheries management can complement formal MPAs in Sabah.

1877: The Gulf of Gabès, Tunisia is home to the Guitarfish Rhinobatos rhinobatos and the Giant Guitarfish Glaucostegus cemiculus. Both species are frequently bycaught by most types of fishing gear and G. cemiculus is targeted yearly during summer. As a result, both species have suffered steep population declines and are now listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN. Both are protected by various binding and non-binding agreements. We present findings from the project “Guitarfishes in the Gulf of Gabès: Conservation Strategy”, a collaborative project between the Shark Trust and ASCOB Syrtis in Tunisia. In total, landings were monitored and visits to fish markets were completed between July 2024 and June 2025 aiming to better understand species occurrence and gear interactions in the region. Investigations showed that both species appear in landings and fish markets throughout the year. All life stages of G. cemiculus, whilst only juvenile and adult R. rhinobatos were encountered in the study area. Initial findings suggest that the two species may occupy distinct spatial niches: G. cemiculus more common in south of the Gulf of Gabès, and R. rhinobatos more common in the north. Bottom longlines emerged as the most impactful gear on guitarfishes, followed by trawlers. Additionally, gillnets targeting G. cemiculus represent a considerable source of mortality for adult guitarfishes in the region. Working with project partners to improve our understanding of these dynamics, we can better deliver on legislative protection, whilst remaining conscious of local socio-economic needs.

1878: Recovery of endangered shark and fish populations requires compliance with fisheries and conservation policy. The global shock caused by the C19 pandemic had severe consequences for coastal communities, with downstream effects on protected ecosystems, providing an opportunity to identify social and ecological circumstances leading to different compliance decisions and conservation outcomes. During the pandemic, the Chagos Marine Protected Area (CMPA) saw a 20-fold spike in fisheries violation by Indian flagged-vessels, marking a departure from pre-pandemic baseline primarily of Sri-Lankan origin- to which levels have since returned. Here, we combine comprehensive ecological and social surveys with fishers, spanning before and after the pandemic, with estimates of violation from remote sensing and enforcement records, to investigate the drivers and consequences of this temporary shift in social ecological regime. We find that future compliance outcomes can be predicted from national socioeconomic trajectories and nearshore fisheries states. Further, analysis of ecological timeseries in CMPA, from underwater visual surveys and stereo baited remote underwater systems, suggest that return to pre-pandemic regime was motivated by a combination of ecosystemlevel attrition in shark and fish levels and increased deterrence, initiated by transnational enforcement collaborations. Human behaviour is multifaceted and adaptable, and our analysis reveals that complex trade-off – that include perceived risk and rewards – determines compliance decisions and can shape conservation successes. A better understanding of socialecological regime shifts, which can be triggered by different drivers individually or in combination, is key to improve mechanisms for compliance.

1880: Baited Remote Underwater Video Systems (BRUVS) were deployed in two distinct areas of the eastern Mediterranean in Greece: Amvrakikos Gulf, delineated as an Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA), and Northeast Lemnos Island, part of the Truva Shelf and designated as an Area of Interest (AoI). A total of deployments were conducted (87 in Amvrakikos, in Lemnos) between June 2024 and October 2025, at depths from 2.5 to 32.4 meters. Each deployment used grams of bait, varying from small pelagic fish, cuttlefish, and mussels. In Amvrakikos, deployments were successful, resulting in positive recordings of elasmobranchs (67.7%), representing eight of the ten species identified in the region. A total of individuals were observed, resulting in sightings over h min of analyzed footage. The genus Dasyatis dominated observations (76 individuals and sightings). Dasyatis spp., Gymnura altavela, and Mustelus mustelus recorded both during day and night. Deployments using small pelagic fish recorded highest elasmobranch numbers and diversity, while no significant differences related to depth were observed (Wilcoxon, p=0.1157). In contrast, no elasmobranchs were observed in Lemnos, despite fisheries-dependent data recorded individuals from species over two consecutive years (2024–2025). Among Lemnos’ species, five are listed as Vulnerable, four as Endangered, and three as Critically Endangered according to their IUCN global status. The results highlight the effectiveness of BRUVS in semi-enclosed areas like Amvrakikos, while suggesting possible limiting factors that might restrict elasmobranch detection in open-water habitats such as Northeast Lemnos.

1882: Tun Mustapha Park (TMP), Sabah’s second-largest Marine Protected Area, supports over 80,000 coastal residents who rely heavily on small-scale fisheries. Bycatch of sharks and rays is a major conservation concern, as these species are often retained for subsistence and income. Market surveys show a high proportion of Threatened species catches, and fisher interviews indicate declining catch frequencies compared to historical levels. These highlight the need for effective bycatch mitigation aligned with TMP’s management objectives to reduce impacts on endangered species. This study assesses the feasibility and effectiveness of community-based juvenile live-release practices as a potential mitigation strategy. A pilot program was conducted in two villages in 2024, engaging experienced fishers who voluntarily integrated live release of juvenile sharks and rays into their routine fishing activities. Local enumerators systematically recorded shark and ray captures, noting whether individuals were released alive or retained. Data collection used standardized sheets and video documentation of live releases where possible. Results indicate that 61% of individuals were landed alive, with nearly all released successfully. Evaluation suggests that voluntary live release is feasible and has minimal livelihood impacts. However, sustaining long-term adoption presents challenges, including variable fisher incentives and the need for robust monitoring to assess effectiveness. Based on pilot learning, adaptive measures were identified, including strengthening data recording and improving incentive mechanisms. Preliminary results will show the outcomes of these adjustments when implementation starts in 2026 and inform strategies for scaling up, ultimately formalizing juvenile live release as a sustainable fisheries management approach in TMP.

1883: Globally, sawfish (Pristis pristis and P. pectinata) have experienced severe population declines driven by the use of unsustainable fishing gear, the loss of critical habitats and illegal trade. In Central America, Honduras is considered a Priority I country within the Global Strategy for Sawfish Conservation, given the urgent need for research, conservation, and protection of these species. Despite this conservation priority, information on the abundance and distribution of these species in the country remains nonexistent. To address this urgent need, we established a baseline of local knowledge, historical and recent captures of these species in the country using fisher surveys. A total of surveys were conducted in seven communities in northeastern part of Honduras during the first half of 2025. The survey combined open and closed questions, allowing the collection of traditional ecological knowledge, historical captures, and cultural uses associated with sawfish, as well as insights into their decline over time. The results show that the Moskitia region contains the most recent records of captures and sightings, suggesting the persistence of remnant populations in this remote area. Additionally, rostra collected through the years were documented, providing evidence of a historical movement route of sawfish rostra, along with references to their relevance in Miskito religious ceremonies. These findings underscore the urgent need for more in-depth research to assess the population status in the region and guide effective conservation strategies. The study highlights the role of a local NGO in the conservation and protection of chondrichthyans in Honduras.

1885: The pelagic thresher shark (Alopias pelagicus) remains poorly understood in the Indo-Pacific, including the Philippines where it is nationally protected. In Puerto Galera, long-term diver and fisher observations exist, yet quantitative data on its seasonal occurrence and habitat use remain limited. Bridging this knowledge gap, we conducted a year-long Baited Remote Underwater Video (BRUV) survey, deploying units from March 2024 to February 2025 across 20–90 m depth in the Puerto Galera marine protected area, and examined how habitat, temperature, depth, and boat activity shaped cumulative shark time, time-to-first sighting (TFS), and abundance (MaxN), while also documenting their behaviour. Despite seasonal variation in biophysical conditions, the environmental drivers of occurrence were highly consistent. Sharks spent twice as much cumulative time in deeper habitats, and bare reef supported eight times more shark time than sand- or soft-coral-dominated substrates. Cooler temperatures increased cumulative time by 27%, while warmer conditions halved abundance. Boat activity exerted strong disturbance effects, reducing cumulative time by 46% and increasing TFS by 61%. Behavioural patterns were dominated by steady swimming, with only rare circling, a single cleaning interaction, and two tail-slap strikes. All individuals were adults, with a female-biased sex ratio but no spatial segregation. Our findings suggest that thresher shark occurrence responds predictably to a narrow set of environmental and human-driven gradients, highlighting Puerto Galera as a movement-oriented corridor rather than a multifunctional habitat. Importantly, management should prioritise minimising vessel activity and protecting the depth and habitat zones that consistently support thresher shark presence.
1886: White sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) occur sporadically but consistently in the Mediterranean Sea, yet their ecology and population structure remain poorly understood. Jaw morphology is widely used for shark identification, but morphometric data for Mediterranean white sharks are scarce. Because jaw dimensions scale with body size, they provide an opportunity to estimate total length and improve knowledge of population characteristics. Tunisia records the highest elasmobranch landings in the Mediterranean, with sharks captured both as targeted species and as bycatch. Following reports from local fishers, a systematic landing-monitoring program was initiated in January 2023 to document the occurrences and biological traits of white sharks. Among the individuals recorded, jaws were recovered from specimens, for which six morphometric measurements: Right Upper Jaw (RUJ), Left Upper Jaw (LUJ), Right Lower Jaw (RLJ), Left Lower Jaw (LLJ), Lower Jaw (LJ), and Total Upper Jaw (UJ) were collected. Total length data were available for of these specimens. A strong relationship was found between jaw dimensions and total length. The total upper jaw length showed the highest correlation (r = 0.974), with similarly high correlations for other measurements (TLJ: 0.962; RUJ: 0.969; RLJ: 0.956; LUJ: 0.972; LLJ: 0.964). These results demonstrate that jaw morphometry is a reliable tool for estimating shark size when complete specimens are unavailable. This approach enhances our ability to evaluate size-class distribution and supports the development of targeted conservation measures for this critically endangered species in Tunisian and Mediterranean waters.

1887: Releasing aquarium-raised sharks can be inspiring and challenging. Many captive-born or longterm aquarium individuals lack the natural skills needed for survival, especially locating and handling live prey. This project helped transition-phase leopard sharks (Stegostoma tigrinum) regain those instincts through behavior-based training. After transfer from the aquarium to an ex-situ conditioning pond, sharks were fasted for hours to reduce relocation stress and increase feeding motivation. Training began with live mollusks offered in an easier form: cracked shells releasing stronger odor cues to help sharks recognize them as food. As feeding responses improved, other live prey such as polychaetes and oval moon snails were introduced. Environmental complexity was increased by burying prey in sand, attaching prey to rocks, or allowing prey to float, encouraging natural foraging behavior and sensory engagement. After four months in the conditioning pond, sharks were moved to a sea pen and exposed to native prey, including polychaetes, oval moon snails, dog conch, and crabs to broaden familiarity with natural food sources. Throughout the process we documented behavioral changes: sharks became more active, responded to prey movement, and investigated buried items. In September 2025, after four months in the sea pen, three leopard sharks were tagged with acoustic transmitters and released. Tracking indicated all individuals remained active for nearly two months, suggesting positive short-term adaptation. This hands-on experience highlights how behavioral reconditioning can support smoother transitions from captivity to the wild. It also demonstrates that even small, carefully designed can meaningful improve the survival of reintroduced elasmobranchs.

1889: Reef-associated elasmobranchs are declining globally, yet large regions of the Red Sea lack critical baseline data needed for effective spatial management. This gap is increasingly vital in Saudi Arabia, where rapid coastal development is outpacing ecological assessment. To address this, we present an integrated, multi-platform assessment to quantify species diversity, relative abundance, and spatial patterns of elasmobranch occurrence in the Al Wajh lagoon. Survey effort comprised hours of baited remote underwater video (BRUV) deployments, benthic longline soak hours, and over validated incidental sightings. Collectively, these records document elasmobranch species (16 sharks, myliobatiform rays, and three rhinopristiformes), of which 83% are classified as threatened under the IUCN Red List (CR, EN, or VU). Key findings revealed structured habitat use with high conservation value. The interior lagoon supported disproportionately high batoid representation relative to regional baselines, with threatened species dominating nearshore and island assemblages. For example, neonate sicklefin lemon (Negaprion acutidens; EN) and blacktip reef sharks (Carcharhinus melanopterus; VU) were consistently recorded in shallow mangrove-adjacent habitats on the edge of the lagoon, indicating localised shark pupping and nursery function within an otherwise raydominated community. Outer reef-adjacent waters were characterised by wider-ranging taxa, such as mobulids and large carcharhinid sharks, including seasonal tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier; NT) aggregations. Together, these results highlight the substantial elasmobranch conservation potential of the Al Wajh lagoon, and demonstrate that integrated survey methods provide an effective evidence base for spatial protection planning in this rapidly developing region.

1890: The pelagic thresher shark (Alopias pelagicus) population declines are driven mainly by targeted fishing and bycatch in both small-scale and industrial fisheries. As the largest shark-fishing nation, Indonesia represents a critical priority for pelagic thresher conservation. Recent research has identified the Sunda Banda Seascape in eastern Indonesia as an important migratory corridor for this species. However, despite high fishing intensity in the region, limited information exists on interactions between fishers and pelagic threshers, hindering effective conservation and bycatch mitigation efforts. This study addresses these gaps by drawing on local ecological knowledge from fishers in Banda, Central Maluku, Indonesia. Employing a mixed-methods approach that combined surveys (N = 52) and focus group discussions (N = 25), we examined fishers’ socio-economic conditions, experiences, and perceptions regarding pelagic thresher sharks and their conservation. Fishers identified locations where threshers were caught or observed, all overlapping with the Ay-Rhun and Banda Sea marine protected areas. Nearly all respondents depended primarily on fishing for their livelihoods. Although some had previously participated in shark fishing and trade, threshers are no longer a target species due to their low market value. They are incidentally caught in small-scale handline and purse seine fisheries, often near fish aggregating devices. The meat is occasionally sold or consumed locally as an affordable protein source. Fishers also reported financial losses associated with bycatch, such as torn nets. Incentive-based strategies encouraging the safe release of bycaught sharks may therefore offer practical, mutually beneficial outcomes for both conservation and livelihoods.

1893: Effective science communication is critical for conservation. A one-size-fits-all approach often fails to engage diverse communities. In the Philippines, where shark and ray conservation is urgently needed, top-down messaging can be ineffective. “Pating Patrol” (pating is shark in Filipino) is a science communication initiative designed to overcome these barriers by building the capacity of community leaders in Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs). "Pating Patrol" was designed to be a one-day interactive workshop delivered in local language. Topics covered include shark and ray biology, national and local laws, species identification, and the value of ISRAs. Each short talk is followed by a game. The core sci-comm strategy was to frame conservation not as a restriction but as a shared responsibility and source of local pride, promoting a “soft enforcement” approach through education and community engagement. Preand post-workshop surveys conducted during the three workshops demonstrated the model’s success: positive words associated with sharks increased from 10% to 22%, and knowledgebased associations rose from 14% to 32%. All participants showed improved knowledge on species identification and understanding of regulatory frameworks. The true measure of the project's impact is in community action. Twenty local organizations and government offices made concrete pledges, including launching awareness campaigns, drafting supportive ordinances, and strengthening citizen science data collection via the Shark Spotted PH Facebook page. By centering local relevance and participatory dialogue, Pating Patrol shows how strategic communication can empower community members to become active advocates.

1895: The global trade in shark and ray meat presents intertwined challenges related to sustainability, legality, and traceability, and involves a large and diverse set of trading nations. Here we analyse two decades of international shark and ray meat trade data, updated to 2024, using network analysis to assess the role of key trading countries. Our results highlight the European Union (notably Spain, Portugal, and Italy) and South American nations (such as Uruguay and Brazil) as major actors in this trade, often functioning as intercontinental hubs for transfer and redistribution. These structural positions confer a central responsibility to a limited group of trade partners to ensure that shark and ray meat supply chains are sustainable, legal, and traceable. Beyond improved management at national level, our findings support policy measures that include strengthening and expanding CITES listings for shark and ray species, improving traceability mechanisms, and enforcing science-based catch limits. To support decision-makers, researchers, and conservation practitioners, we present a freely accessible Shiny web application that offers an intuitive, visually rich interface to explore shark and ray meat trade data by country, region, and product category, while retaining analytical precision and detail. Achieving a more sustainable global shark and ray meat trade will require coordinated international action and open collaboration, underpinned by strong leadership from key trading nations to reinforce implementation and enforcement of existing regulations.

1896: Coastal Bangladesh is home to million people, with roughly half relying on fisheries for their livelihoods. The artisanal fishers, contributing to over 80% of the annual marine catch, are vital for national food security. Their fishing grounds are habitats for over a hundred shark and ray species, of which more than two-thirds are threatened with extinction. Targeted fishing and bycatch, driven by high market demand, pose direct threats to these slow-growing animals. Overexploitation is exacerbated by non-compliance with regulations, lack of conservation knowledge, and absence of safe release practices, leading to the mortality of protected species. To address this, WCS Bangladesh initiated an interactive, mobile educational outreach program to foster marine conservation stewardship. This enabled connection among conservation professionals, fishers, and government officials. Between 2021-25, WCS Bangladesh program organized eight “Ocean Guardians” and thirty-eight “Healthy OceanHealthy People” mobile exhibitions across fifteen key sites, engaging over 60,000 fishers, processors, traders, community members, and government officials. Results from pre- and post-visit interviews indicated a significant positive shift, including over 40% increase in general knowledge, 68% improvement in identifying protected sharks and rays, and 30% better understanding of the threats they face. This collaborative effort successfully improved knowledge of national and international legislation. While short-term assessment confirms a positive shift in knowledge and increased reporting of safe releases over the years, these efforts underscore the critical importance of theory-of-change-guided outreach to counter human-driven wildlife declines. This outreach model offers a scalable, cost-effective strategy for achieving conservation compliance in high-pressure coastal fisheries.

1901: The whitespotted eagle ray (Aetobatus narinari) is a cosmopolitan elasmobranch species that has experienced substantial population declines over the last years and is endangered throughout most of its range. Efforts to quantify the scale of these declines and monitor recovery have been hindered because estimates of stock structure, abundance, and mortality rate are lacking in many regions. We addressed these key data gaps in the Western Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico (GoM) by applying genome-wide SNP data, population genetics frameworks, and close-kin mark-recapture (CKMR) models to whitespotted eagle rays sampled between 2009-2023. Our data reveal clear genetic differentiation between samples taken from Belize and all other sites, as well as subtle patterns of differentiation between the eastern and western GoM and between the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of Florida. We then used individualbased simulations to develop and hone a CKMR model, which we applied to over genetic samples taken from eagle rays off the coast of Sarasota, Florida, where rays aggregate annually between April and October. Estimates of population abundance suggest that between 7,000 – 35,000 reproductive adults contribute to the Sarasota aggregation site with annual mortality rates of 30% or lower. Overall, this study offers new insights into the evolutionary and population dynamics of whitespotted eagle rays in the GoM and Western Atlantic Ocean. In addition, this study offers valuable genomic and computational resources that can help facilitate conservation genomics research of eagle rays and other elasmobranch populations around the world.

1902: There are few examples of shark fisheries management leading to conservation outside of high- capacity nations. Here we present a case study from Belize, Central America, a mediumcapacity nation in which the management authority, shark fishers, and scientists collaborated to implement a shark fisheries management plan after international trade regulations were imposed on some exported species in 2013. This presentation will include perspectives from a representative of all three stakeholder groups involved in this process. From 2013-2025 shark fisheries management advanced from simple permitting and a seasonal closure to a more comprehensive system where there is also detailed catch monitoring and verification, high compliance with the obligations of international trade regulations, fishing gear restrictions, and large spatial closures specific to shark fishing. Standardized fishery independent monitoring of sharks executed jointly by scientists and fishers helped to reduce fishing effort by providing alternative fisher livelihoods. These data also provide evidence of shark recovery over time. We will discuss the lessons learned from this experience, some of which may be transferable to the management of other small-scale shark fisheries that are generally poorly managed around the world.

1903: Photo identification (photo-ID) enables individual-based monitoring when natural markings are unique, and recent machine-learning approaches promise gains in matching accuracy and workflow efficiency. We evaluated three commonly used tools for precision, accuracy and efficiency for whitespotted eagle rays (Aetobatus narinari): the semi-automated I3S Spot and two MantaMatcher (Wildbook) algorithms, Hotspotter and Miew-ID, using a curated dataset of images representing resighted individuals. Images were processed through all three methods and we recorded correct match suggestions, the rank of the correct match, and time taken to find the correct match. I3S Spot achieved the highest precision (91.9%), significantly exceeding both Hotspotter (67.6%) and Miew-ID (59.5%; all p < 0.001). I3S also produced the best mean rank of correct matches; this was not significantly better than Hotspotter, but both outperformed Miew-ID (p < 0.001). In contrast, the MantaMatcher methods were >2 times faster than I3S from upload to confirmed match, yielding significantly greater time-cost efficiency (p < 0.001). We provide a detailed protocol for implementing MantaMatcher with eagle rays and outline user-experience improvements for developers. Overall, while MantaMatcher (Hotspotter/Miew-ID) offers clear speed advantages, its current reduction in precision has practical implications for error rates in re-sighting datasets. Until MantaMatcher algorithms are further trained/optimized for A. narinari, we recommend I3S Spot as the primary photo-ID tool, with MantaMatcher used to accelerate triage where subsequent expert verification is feasible. This comparison highlights trade-offs between automation speed and identification precision and accuracy that should guide tool selection and future algorithm development.

1905: An individual Blacktip reef shark (Carcharhinus melanopterus) was first reported at Coco Island National Park in the Eastern Tropical Pacific in 2012, but it was unknown whether this observation represented an isolated event or if additional individuals were present. Through mark–capture–recapture monitoring conducted across dry and wet seasons in 2022 in two bays of the park (Wafer and Chatham), we documented a complete size population structure including neonates (<50 cm), juveniles, and adults, providing the first evidence of an established and functionally reproducing population in this remote oceanic Marine Protected Area. Multiple reproductive indicators were observed, including gravid females, neonates, and seasonal shifts in the abundance of adults and juveniles that suggest a biannual reproductive cycle. Also, photo-identification and recaptures showed site fidelity and residency within individual bays over multi-month periods, consistent with patterns described for the Indo-Pacific populations. The presence of neonates and small juveniles in shallow, turbid inshore habitats indicates the existence of nursery areas, while adults were more abundant during the wet season. These findings provide the first comprehensive population data for C. melanopterus in the Tropical Eastern Pacific.

1906: Drone surveys were conducted in the Marine National Parks of Baie Ternay and Port Launay in the Seychelles, during the shark pupping season of 2024 and 2025, with additional flights carried out throughout other months of the year for comparison. October and November consistently showed an increase in abundance of juvenile sharks, confirming that this period is the peak of the pupping season in the region. Multiple shark species were observed, with the most common ones being: Carcharinus melanopterus, Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos and Negaprion acutidens. Most individuals were approximately meter long. Juveniles were consistently observed in shallow areas around seagrass, sand banks and coral reef, suggesting these areas are important nursery grounds. Shark pups were often seen in groups (up to individuals). Their movements were localised, with individuals repeatedly swimming around the same small areas rather than dispersing to other parts of the marine park. Abundance was highest during sunset, indicating a potential diel pattern in habitat use. Moreover, several instances of active hunting were documented, with juvenile sharks targeting bait ball of schooling fish. Larger sharks were occasionally observed in these areas, however they quickly swam back to deeper areas of the reef. It’s unclear whether their presence in shallow waters was related to pupping activity or random movements. These observations highlight the potential of non-invasive drone surveys to identify species composition, foraging behaviour, seasonal reproductive periods, as well as, identify critical nursery grounds and support local conservation measures for coastal shark populations in the Seychelles.
1908: Global trade in elasmobranchs requires precise reporting across supply chains to assess impacts on species and the effectiveness of conservation measures, yet fisheries and trade records often lack this resolution. In Belize’s export-driven shark fishery—where more than 60% of landed species are now CITES-listed—this gap has prompted the country to strengthen transparency across the shark meat supply chain. This talk presents an innovative approach to enhancing species-specific monitoring in Belize’s shark fishery. Using anal fins and conversion factors, the method disaggregates shark catch and meat exports for species in the Mesoamerican Caribbean without requiring species separation during processing. A central outcome is the ability to convert live catch weights (LCW) at landing into species-specific salted fillet weights (SFW) at export, directly addressing a major barrier to reliable international trade reporting. Linear mixed-effects models converted LCW to fresh (FFW) and salted fillet weights (SFW) with high precision (R² = 0.79–0.98), while anal fins provided total lengths (TL) and LCW estimates that independently verified fisher-submitted government logbooks. Beyond improving trade transparency, this protocol also generates critical fishery data by enabling validation of species counts and estimation of size-frequency distributions for landed sharks. Overall, this work strengthens CITES reporting—particularly crucial given current listings—and offers an approach that could be replicated in other fisheries with comparable geographic and socio-economic contexts.

1909: Wildlife tourism offers opportunities for participants to connect with nature and engage with animals in their natural habitats. Yet, when not managed responsibly, wildlife tourism can be exploitative, posing risks to both wildlife and humans. Marine wildlife tourism is a major and rapidly growing global sector, providing close encounters with charismatic species such as elasmobranchs (sharks, skates and rays). Here, we analysed a total of 7,794 Tripadvisor reviews to examine global patterns in elasmobranch tourism and understand the main components of the tourism participant experience. Reports of elasmobranch tourism in participant reviews were concentrated in Hawaii (37.11%), Australia (13.10%), and Mexico (11.64%), with most interactions being purposeful and targeting species such as whale sharks (Rhincodon typus), manta rays (Mobula spp.), and reef sharks. Sentiment analysis revealed overwhelmingly positive review responses (96.8%), especially when activities included educational elements (n=1856; 98.87% positive; n=6; 0.32% negative). However, concerns were raised by participants about the sustainability of species-specific tourism, particularly for vulnerable species. Our analysis suggests that implementing strategies such as prioritising educational messaging, fostering environmental stewardship, regulating group sizes, and minimising provisioning practices could help align elasmobranch tourism with ethical and sustainable guidelines. By embedding species-specific conservation information into tours, operators have the potential to cultivate lasting pro-conservation attitudes among visitors, supporting responsible wildlife interactions while inspiring and educating the public.

1912: When searching "shark stories" online, the top results overwhelmingly focus on shark attacks. The Shark Stories Hub is an online and social media platform designed to challenge this limited narrative by celebrating the diversity, ecology, and individuality of sharks through creative storytelling. Rather than spotlighting people who work with sharks, the Hub tells stories about the sharks themselves: their roles in ecosystems, their unique behaviors, and their real-life antics. Through mixed-media carousels that combine illustration, photography, storytelling, science, and advocacy, the Hub shares stories that help people see sharks as the complex and diverse animals they truly are. Stories are developed around three main pillars that are clearly labelled and identifiable on the posts: (1) true stories drawn from research and real events, (2) biologically accurate fiction, and (3) storytelling-based introductions to lesser known shark species that don't usually come to mind when people think of sharks. Presenting the Shark Stories Hub at Sharks International aims not only to showcase the project as a model of artistic science communication, but also to invite collaboration with the global shark science community. By contributing their findings and experiences, researchers can help expand the library of shark stories and collectively reshape how the public perceives these amazing animals.

1916: Since the onset of industrialised fishing activities in the 1950s, elasmobranch populations have declined dramatically. However, changes in fisheries management from the start of this century have led to increases in the abundance several commercial skate species in the Northeast Atlantic. 1917: Recent biodiversity research has been shaped by a push toward greater geographic representation, open-science, and the diversification of data sources. Global biodiversity data appear not to reflect latitudinal gradients of biodiversity, but more closely trace macroeconomic patterns of income, political regimes, and colonisation. We seek to explore this hypothesis using a content analysis of published literature. A total of 30,000 chondrichthyan studies were published between 1950 and 2025 [SharkReferences.com]. Preliminary findings show that 35% were led by institutions in the USA (n=2,137), 14% in Australia (n=849), and 12% in the UK (n=708). Eighty-nine percent of studies were led by institutions in the Global North (highincome countries in North America, Europe, and Australia/New Zealand), with only 11% originating from the Global South. Chondrichthyans generally have higher species richness in countries with middle to lower per-capita income. Key biodiversity hotspots, including the Eastern Tropical Pacific and southeast Africa, remain underrepresented in the literature, and given the high overlap with fisheries these gaps represent a significant blind spot for chondrichthyan research. Forty-eight percent of studies were not conducted in the same country as the authors’ institutions. Madagascar, the Seychelles, and Mexico exhibited the largest disparities between study location and author institution, whereas Greece, Sweden, and Israel were the largest sources of researchers. The proportion of studies led by Global North institutions in Global South locations increased from 47% in the 1990s to 61% by 2024, indicating that geographic imbalances in research leadership are not only persistent but have increased substantially in recent years.

1918: Elasmobranchs exhibit varied population distribution drivers, making informed management plans key to mitigating environmental pressures and anthropogenic threats. Sexual segregation is an ecological behaviour observed in certain species, such as Scyliorhinus canicula, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood especially in regions like the Bristol Channel and Irish Sea. This study investigates the environmental and biological factors driving spatial and temporal patterns of sexual segregation in S. canicula. Using trawl survey data spanning 1993–2021, 3281 hauls were analysed, of which 1273 were single sex (female: 626, max. individuals; male: 647, max. individuals). Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) were used to analyse the impact of depth, sea surface temperature, substrate type, and spatial and temporal variables on male and female distributions. Significant sexual segregation was revealed, with females aggregating near the North Wales coastline. Whilst females favoured warmer habitats, environmental factors presented a weak effect on sexual segregation suggesting social factors may be behavioural drivers, such as female avoidance of male harassment. This is supported by the finding that sexual segregation was more prominent in larger individuals, and hauls were more likely to be significantly sexually segregated when mature individuals were present (all individuals 23.5%, mature individuals 63.9%; n>20). Identified hotspots of mature female aggregations could be at risk of localised overexploitation. These findings highlight the importance of better understanding sexual and ontogenetic differences in spatial distribution, which could be used to identify relevant management measures (e.g. spatial management), to protect important reproductive elements of the population.

1921: As shark management has started to yield conservation gains in some jurisdictions, fishers are reporting increased incidence of shark depredation (i.e., removal or damage of catch). There is growing pressure for shark population control by removing or culling the more common depredating shark species, reversing the successes from decades of management efforts. The use of deterrents could be a viable alternative and non-lethal solution to reduce shark depredation. An Electronic Pulse Device (EPD) deterrent was tested as a depredation mitigation tool for anglers by conducting controlled trials on bonnetheads (Sphyrna tiburo; adults) and sandbars (Carcharhinus plumbeus; adults/ juveniles) in captivity. EPDs were affixed to angling gear ~ cm from bait and active (functional) or inactive (non-functional) EPDs were exposed to the sharks individually, in pairs, or small groups. A total of trials conducted with all groups showed the EPD can be an effective tool for depredation mitigation. Bonnethead trials showed the bait was consumed significantly less often (51% of the trials) using the active EPD compared to the inactive EPD (93%). When bait was consumed, feeding was significantly delayed using the active EPD (~ 3x longer). Juvenile and adult sandbar trials showed the active EPD doubled the time to consume the bait. Sharks exhibited significantly more rapid withdrawals from the bait (1 to 43) with an active EPD compared to the inactive EPD (0). Electrical shark repellents delay and deter shark feeding and likely to help mitigate shark depredation in recreational fisheries.

1922: This study examines the historical and projected exploitation patterns of chondrichthyans (sharks, chimaeras, and rays) across five Large Marine Ecosystems (LMEs) of East and Southeast Asia: the Bay of Bengal, Gulf of Thailand, South China Sea, East China Sea, and Yellow Sea. Reconstructed catch data from the Sea Around Us database (1950–2019) were used to address gaps in official statistics, and ARIMA time-series models were applied to project catches to 2029. Results show a sustained increase in chondrichthyan catches from 1950 until the early 2000s, followed by a generalized decline across all five LMEs. Regionally, the South China Sea and Bay of Bengal accounted for the highest catch volumes, while the Yellow Sea and East China Sea displayed early and persistent collapses. End-use analysis indicated that approximately 85% of catches were directed to human consumption, showing an almost perfect correlation with total catches and highlighting the strong influence of market demand on fishing pressure. ARIMA projections reveal contrasting future scenarios among thae five LMEs: moderate increases in the South China Sea, stagnation in the Bay of Bengal, and continued declines in the Gulf of Thailand, East China Sea, and Yellow Sea. These results confirm that overfishing remains the primary driver of chondrichthyan depletion and suggest that recovery in Asian waters is unlikely in the near term without effective interventions. Strengthened regional governance, improved data reporting, and the implementation of strict conservation and fisheries management measures are urgently needed to ensure long-term sustainability.
