1923: Forty percent of the shark and ray species known from the Western Indian Ocean (WIO) are threatened with extinction, primarily due to overfishing. This is considerably worse than the global threat level (33%). Despite many high-quality scientific outputs on sharks and rays in the WIO, there remain major data gaps (e.g. species distribution ranges; reproductive areas; species-level fishery impacts; and sparse ecological and biological data on the less charismatic shark and ray species), which impede effective management and conservation. We collect basic (yet fundamental) biological, ecological and fishery information on sharks and rays, primarily though coastal fishery surveys, baited remote underwater video, and genetics, to inform management. This provides information such as species present, population demographics, habitat preferences, hotspots, fishery landings (species and size structure), impactful fishing gears, and species traded (including illegally traded products). From this information (and building on previous work by others), we also developed comprehensive national species checklists (a fundamental but perhaps overlooked tool), providing the basis for policy support work. Species checklists are cross-referenced against IUCN Red List statuses and national and international measures for shark and ray fisheries and trade, to identify gaps in both species-level data and domestic policy. This information is used to inform improved species-level management and conservation measures in each country. Over the past decade, the fishery, trade and ecological data collected have been used to support policy reform, strengthen fishery measures, trade controls, and the implementation of multilateral agreements, for shark and ray species in numerous WIO countries.

1924: Rhinopristiformes rays are among the most threatened elasmobranchs. Yet, species-specific biological data remain scarce globally, hindering the development of species-specific management strategies and conservation frameworks. The Critically Endangered Widenose guitarfish (Glaucostegus obtusus) from the family Glaucostegidae is regularly caught as both target and bycatch along the Bay of Bengal coast. However, no prior age- and growth information exists for this region. Of the specimens collected, provided estimated ages ranged from 2–16 years, with females attaining larger maximum sizes than males (TL = 110.5 cm, 96.6 cm). Both sexes matured at ~6 years, but females at a larger size (L50 = 69.9 cm, 62.2 cm). A multi-model assessment identified the VBGF as the model that describes its growth best under both frequentist and Bayesian analyses. The point estimates from the frequentist growth models (L∞ = 169.76, k = 0.055 yr⁻¹ and t0 = -2.97 years) were contained within the 95% credible intervals of the Bayesian analysis. This study provides the first baseline biological data for G. obtusus in this region, examining population dynamics using a cost-effective vertebral cartilage method. Age-length data construct growth trajectories while revealing reproductive seasonality and behavior. Like other elasmobranchs, their life-history traits indicate low population resilience and high vulnerability to overexploitation. These findings establish a critical foundation for stock assessments, conservation measures, and policy frameworks to prevent population decline and ensure species persistence. This research will inform future investigations of movement patterns and habitat utilization, supporting Marine Spatial Planning initiatives.

1927: Rhino rays represent one of the most threatened groups of vertebrates globally due to overexploitation for their fins and meat. The Maldives is one of the only countries in the Indian Ocean where these elasmobranchs are not targeted by fisheries, serving as a critical refuge. Long-term photo-identification offers a non-invasive approach that allows individuals to be tracked over time while providing essential data on population demographics, spatial use, and reproductive activity. Here, we present the first photo-ID database for Bowmouth Guitarfish (Rhina ancylostoma) and Bottlenose Wedgefish (Rhynchobatus australiae) across atolls in the Maldives. Through dive surveys, citizen science contributions from local dive guides, and the review of available archival videos from visiting divers dating back to 2016, individuals have been catalogued (n = R. ancylostoma, n = R. australiae) to date, identified by their distinctive spot patterns on the left flanks and pectoral fins. Resighting rates varied among atolls (15 - 42%), indicating spatial variation in site fidelity, with a pronounced female bias (91%). One seasonal aggregation hotspot hosting up to R. australiae, and the first mating observation for this species in Maldivian waters were also documented. Most encounters occurred in shallow reef and lagoon habitats, ecosystems increasingly threatened by coastal development and land reclamation. As a foundational tool for long-term monitoring, this database will be integrated with complementary methods such as laser photogrammetry and satellite telemetry to generate comprehensive ecological insights and inform evidence-based conservation measures for these elasmobranchs.

1930: The identification and safeguarding of critical habitats for sharks and rays requires spatial tools that integrate diverse data sources to reveal the ecological and environmental patterns underpinning species distributions. In this study, we use a multispecies joint Species Distribution Modelling (jSDM) framework to project elasmobranch distributions and hotspots in the Northeast Atlantic, and compare how jSDM-based predictions correspond to and differ from existing area-based conservation designations such as Important Shark & Ray Areas (ISRAs). To strengthen predictions for rare and data-poor elasmobranchs, we modelled fish species from the region, allowing information to be shared through co-occurrences and joint environmental responses. While ISRAs are grounded in direct observational data, jSDMs offer a complementary predictive, data-driven alternative that can reveal high-suitability habitats for rare or data-poor species by modelling environmental predictors and species co-occurrences. Our model predicted high habitat suitability for a range of species and identified potential elasmobranch hotspots, including areas corresponding with existing ISRAs as well as additional areas not currently recognised. Evaluating how jSDM projections align with ISRAs highlights how combining multiple approaches can provide a holistic understanding of elasmobranch spatial ecology, reveal how different data sources and spatial scales influence conservation priorities, and guide the design of area-based measures such as MPAs and OECMs, as well as spatial fisheries management. Integrating jSDMs with empirical observations in marine spatial planning can strengthen area-based decision-making and support the strategic, equitable conservation of sharks and rays in line with global biodiversity targets such as 30×30.

1932: Current understanding of the ecology, distribution, and conservation status of deep-sea sharks in the Maldives is highly limited. Seasonal artisanal fisheries targeting deep-sea species frequently result in sharks being caught as bycatch; although these incidental captures present conservation challenges, they also offer a unique opportunity to study deep-sea elasmobranchs. We established a citizen science program to engage artisanal and sport fishers in documenting deep-sea shark encounters. Participants record species, location, depth, size, and condition, and provide photographic evidence when available. To further expand coverage, researchers also systematically monitor fishing-related group chats for additional observations. This dual approach enables spatial and temporal data collection across six Maldivian atolls. The program has so far documented deep-sea shark sightings, including two records of Sharpnose Sevengill sharks (Heptranchias perlo), last reported in the Maldives in 1983, two records of the Bluntnose Sixgill Shark (Hexancheus griseus), and six records of gulper sharks (Centrophorus spp., species verification pending). These rare observations underscore the value of citizen science in collecting data on deep-sea elasmobranchs. Integration of local knowledge with structured data collection has produced the first citizen science dataset on deep-sea sharks in the Maldives, capturing occurrences that would otherwise remain undocumented. These observations provide essential baseline information for mapping species distributions, identifying key habitats, and informing bycatch mitigation and conservation strategies. The initiative further demonstrates that partnerships with fishing communities can convert routine fishing activities into a practical and scalable approach for monitoring deep-sea elasmobranchs in remote marine environments.

1933: Studies of the feeding ecology and gut microbiome of tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) have historically depended on invasive methods, including stomach content analysis and tissue biopsies, due to the difficulty of obtaining fecal material from wild individuals in sufficient quantities and intervals. The island of Fuvahmulah in the Maldives hosts the only confirmed tiger shark gestation ground in the Indian Ocean and supports a resident population of over individuals at a baited site. This unique setting enables continuous, non-invasive fecal sampling to investigate diet, seasonal foraging patterns, and the long-term ecological consequences of provisioning. In November 2025, local dive guides were trained to collect tiger shark fecal samples using standardized protocols and record photo-ID, depth, location, and environmental data. Within the first four weeks, seven samples (approximately mL each) were collected, transferred to sterile tubes, and immediately frozen to preserve genetic and biochemical integrity. Incorporating sample collection into routine tourism activities is intended to establish a long-term fecal sample repository. Laboratory analyses scheduled for February 2026 include DNA metabarcoding of stomach contents to identify prey species, microscopy to quantify and classify ingested material, and rRNA sequencing to characterize gut microbiomes. These analyses are anticipated to provide insights into seasonal foraging behavior and potential dietary changes during gestation.This project demonstrates the value of citizen science in enabling non-invasive dietary and microbiome research. It also establishes a foundation for assessing the ecological impacts of provisioning and informing evidence-based conservation strategies for these apex predators.

1934: Despite major biologging advances, fine-scale studies of juvenile shark ecology remain constrained by a lack of small, cost-effective and species-agnostic tagging systems. Here, we present a new low-cost, minimally invasive and customizable fin clamp tag platform designed for short-term deployments on juvenile sharks. The system can be easily scaled to fit different fin sizes and a wide variety of sensor payloads. A spring-loaded galvanic time release enables quick, non-invasive clip-on deployments on restrained and free-swimming animals. We evaluated the tag performance through eight deployments on fished and restrained juvenile smooth hammerhead sharks (97 to cm TL) using a mounted high-resolution accelerometer, depth, temperature, video logger and radio transmitter for recovery. Tag retention times ranged between to hours (2.5 weeks), with a single premature release on the smallest individual (<100 cm TL). Minor tag shifts on the fin occurred more frequently on smaller individuals but tail beat frequency data consistently matched video-based estimations. Tail beat dynamics indicated a post-release recovery period between 3–6 hours. Hydrodynamic effects of the finclamp tag were quantified using computational fluid dynamics for two juvenile hammerhead shark sizes, showing only a 4–6% increase in drag relative to untagged sharks. These results demonstrate the suitability of the tag platform as a practical, low-cost and scalable biologging tool for juvenile sharks in coastal environments. By enabling reliable, short-term deployments with minimal hydrodynamic impact, this tag design opens new opportunities for high resolution behavior studies previously limited by tag size, cost and impact.

1936: In the Northeast Atlantic, out of elasmobranch species are classified as threatened in the latest IUCN Red List assessment, primarily due to overfishing. Bycatch, in particular, represents the major threat to their long-term sustainability, and the extent of its impact on these iconic species is likely underestimated and poorly monitored. Accurate fish stock assessments are critical for sustainable fisheries management. Interest in the use of environmental DNA (eDNA) to improve catch composition information is increasing, highlighting its potential to supplement traditional methods like fisheries observers or logbooks. eDNA has proven powerful for detecting species presence, and more recently, studies have shown strong correlations between eDNA concentrations and species abundance. Quantifying bycatch biomass of multiple species simultaneously would bring eDNA applications closer to its pinnacle, but this remains particularly challenging. This project aims to develop innovative eDNA protocols to quantify elasmobranch bycatch across multiple types of fishing gear. Passive eDNA sampling, using “metaprobes” or derivatives, was employed to sample water aboard gillnet, tangle net and bottom trawl vessels in Irish and Icelandic waters. Using DNA metabarcoding and species-specific quantitative PCR (qPCR) assays, the eDNA reads obtained will be verified against data collected from visual identification of the catch. These results will evaluate how effectively eDNA can be used to quantify bycatch in commercial fisheries and improve our understanding of the scale of elasmobranch bycatch. Furthermore, this will contribute to the development of a bigger, multi-tool bycatch monitoring programme being established under the EU Horizon project MarineBeacon.

1938: Juvenile bonnethead sharks (Sphyrna tiburo) inhabit shallow estuarine nurseries that vary widely in environmental quality, yet the ecological and physiological consequences of coastal urbanization on this species remain poorly resolved. As Florida’s estuaries experience rapid seagrass loss, altered salinity regimes, and increasing anthropogenic disturbance, assessing how these changes impact early-life shark health is essential for informed nursery habitat management. This research integrates GIS-based habitat classification, environmental measurements, and non-lethal physiological assessment to compare juvenile bonnetheads from urbanized estuaries (Biscayne Bay, Tampa Bay) with those from relatively undisturbed nursery systems (Cedar Key, Ten Thousand Islands). Morphometric data were used to calculate Fulton’s Condition Factor, while in-situ water quality measurements (temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen) provided environmental context. Preliminary analyses revealed no statistically significant differences in condition factor between habitat types (p = 0.314), although spatial patterns suggest that sharks in more developed estuaries may experience environmental conditions associated with subtle physiological constraints. By combining habitat context, geospatial data, and indicators of body condition, this work establishes a baseline framework for detecting early physiological responses to habitat degradation in estuarine-dependent sharks. Continued sampling will incorporate blood-based biomarkers (glucose, lactate, hematocrit) to refine assessments of stress and improve sensitivity to habitat-driven differences. These findings highlight the bonnethead shark as a sentinel species for estuarine ecosystem health and underscore the importance of ongoing monitoring as coastal habitats undergo rapid change. This research provides actionable ecological insight for managing nursery habitats, informing seagrass restoration, and supporting conservation strategies relevant to early-life stages of coastal sharks.

1939: The global shark trade plays a major role in the exploitation of shark populations. Multiple studies have uncovered fraud in European shark meat markets, including sales of prohibited and threatened species, and high levels of mislabelling. However, to date, few have assessed large-scale patterns across multiple countries. Combining samples collected by citizen science projects and NGOs with data from a systematic meta-analysis, this study investigated a total of shark meat products identified using DNA barcoding, across ten countries: Greece, Italy, UK, Spain, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Austria and Iceland; and five retailer types: fish markets, fishmongers, restaurants/takeaways, supermarkets and online retailers. The blue shark (Prionace glauca), listed as critically endangered in the Mediterranean, was the most identified species in the study, especially among Mediterranean countries. The results indicate significant differences in species utilisation across countries, likely influenced by traditional patterns of consumption. Worryingly, threatened species were found on sale in all countries and retailer types in the study. Mislabelling rates were relatively high (32.4%), although likely causes of mislabelling were varied and context dependent. Overall, the study highlights the need for improved implementation of management and labelling legislation to enable more informed consumer choices and to reduce the overexploitation of shark populations.

1940: Manta rays (Mobula yarae) are ecologically significant species in the Mexican Caribbean, yet their populations face pressures from human activities and environmental change. This study combines long-term scientific research with active involvement of local communities to enhance conservation efforts. Data was collected through underwater surveys, photoidentification, and interviews with local stakeholders, enabling the documentation of manta ray movements, behavior, and critical habitats. Results identify seasonal aggregation sites essential for feeding, cleaning, courtship, breaching behaviors and highlight areas requiring targeted protection within and surrounding MPA's. By integrating scientific knowledge with local stewardship, communities are involved and participate in evidence-based management strategies, ensuring the long-term conservation of manta rays and their habitats.

1941: Strandings are well documented worldwide for some marine taxonomic groups such as cetaceans and marine turtles. Despite elasmobranchs being among the most threatened vertebrates, little information on strandings can be found throughout scientific literature. This study presents records of strandings and results of necropsies from years of work in the Strandings Network of the Valencia Region (western Mediterranean, Spain), from February 2012 to October 2025. A total of reports, including species (7 sharks, batoids), were obtained. The most stranded species was the blue shark (Prionace glauca, n=19), followed by bluntnose sixgill sharks (Hexanchus griseus, n=14) and spinetail devil ray (Mobula mobular, n=12). A sizeable portion of the stranding events (52.9%) occurred in the southern part of the region (province of Alicante), which could be explained due to the currents and oceanic orography of the region. Further attention should be dedicated to these events given the amount of biological information that they provide. The existing stranding networks dedicated to other species could easily include elasmobranchs. Further dedication, resources and training are needed to properly document and standardize protocols, to better understand these events. 1947: Overfishing remains the primary driver of global chondrichthyan population declines, with many species facing a high risk of extinction. In response to this crisis, the Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) initiative was launched to delineate critical habitats encompassing biological and ecological traits of these species. Despite their ecological importance, most ISRAs currently lack spatial protection and remain exposed to varying degrees of fishing pressure. To explore which ISRAs are most susceptible to fisheries impacts, we evaluate the overlap of fishing activity derived from Global Fishing Watch (GFW) AIS Apparent Fishing Effort. We assessed ISRAs across jurisdictions in three ISRA regions: Western Indian Ocean, Asia, and the Central and South American Pacific, including areas beyond national jurisdiction. Fishing pressure inside ISRAS was quantified as the proportion of the area of each ISRA exposed to fishing, and as total hours of fishing effort (2012–2024) within each area, with activity classified into ten fishing gear types (e.g. trawl). To assess gear-specific vulnerability for shark, ray, and four chimaera species occurring within these ISRAs, we adapted a semi-quantitative Productivity–Susceptibility Analysis (PSA) that integrates biological productivity traits with attributes related to susceptibility to fishing. By combining GFW effort data with PSA speciesgear vulnerability assessments, we were able to identify which species, ISRAs, and jurisdictions face the highest risk of compromising ISRA ecological integrity. Our findings provide an evidence-based foundation with recommendations intended to guide governance and policy frameworks needed for the effective conservation of chondrichthyan populations.

1948: Seamounts are increasingly recognized as key habitats for threatened pelagic sharks, yet standardized multi-year datasets from oceanic ecosystems remain rare. Between 2021 and 2024, we conducted a pelagic monitoring program at West Cocos and Las Gemelas, the two shallowest seamounts within Cocos Island National Park (Eastern Tropical Pacific), using drifting stereo-BRUVS paired with CTD profiles. For the first time in the region, we included paired open-ocean control sites located km from each seamount, allowing us to directly test whether seamounts generate localized predator aggregations. Across four expeditions, we deployed BRUVS and recorded pelagic species, including six elasmobranchs of high conservation concern. Shark abundance was consistently higher at seamount summits than at control sites. Scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini) and pelagic thresher (Alopias pelagicus) showed the strongest associations with seamount habitats, emerging as key indicator species in multivariate analyses. Community structure differed between habitats, with temperature, chlorophyll-a, and the depth of the thermocline and oxycline acting as important environmental drivers. Seamounts were characterized by cooler waters, higher productivity, and enhanced vertical mixing, conditions that appear to promote shark aggregation. These results highlight the ecological importance of shallow seamounts as predator hotspots within the Cocos– Galápagos migratory corridor and provide a baseline for evaluating the effectiveness of Costa Rica’s expanded marine protected area network. This work also contributes to a regional effort led by MigraMar to standardize seamount monitoring in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, strengthening the scientific basis for conserving highly mobile and threatened shark species.

1949: The Gulf of Fonseca, located in the Pacific coast of Honduras is classified as an Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) due to its ecological importance to several species of rays. Although 36% of ray species are threatened globally, information on their status in Honduras remains scarce. The lack of legal protection makes them vulnerable to unregulated exploitation. Beyond their ecological value, they represent a fundamental resource for the livelihoods of fishing families, particularly during Lent season, when demand for their meat increases.To better understand this activity and its impact, a study was conducted between January and July 2024 in three fishing communities through landings monitoring and semi-structured interviews. A total of rays were landed belonging to six species, two caught as bycatch. The most common species were Pacific Cownose Ray (Rhinoptera steindachneri, 55%), Longtail Stingray (Hypanus longus, 24%) and Pacific Eagle Ray (Aetobatus laticeps, 8%). Most captures occurred using gillnets (77%), with females representing 57% of individuals. Based on interviews, 90% of respondents depend directly on fishing as their main source of income. Rays represent 3.4% of fishing targets, with Hypanus longus (74%) preferred for its market value and ease of capture. Findings provide an initial insight into artisanal ray fisheries. The results document active artisanal ray fisheries for four species of conservation concern, providing the first evidence base needed to guide management. This work lays the groundwork to develop conservation strategies that support vulnerable ray populations and coastal communities that depend on them.
1950: Elasmobranch fisheries represent a complex system shaped by dynamic interactions between ecological and social components. Despite their importance, integrative understanding of these coupled dimensions remains limited. This study examines the social–ecological structure of shark and ray fisheries in Tuban and Lamongan Regencies (Java Sea) using network analysis based on degree, betweenness, eigenvector centrality, hub score, and authority score. The results show clear structural differences between the two locations. In Tuban, the system is ecology-driven, with Elasmobranch serving as the most influential node (degree = 8; betweenness = 32.47; eigenvector = 1.00), supported by Fishing Practice and Fishery Commodities as core connectors. This ecological dominance is strengthened by the availability index, which indicates high availability (>7) of several Least Concern–Near Threatened species— such as Chiloscyllium punctatum, C. plagiosum, and Neotrygon orientalis—alongside the presence of high-risk species including Sphyrna lewini, Rhina ancylostoma, Glaucostegus typus, Rhynchobatus leavis, and Rhynchobatus australiae. In contrast, Lamongan shows a market- and institution-driven structure, where the Fishing Hub (betweenness = 32.0; eigenvector = 1.0) and Auction Rules act as central nodes governing information flow and commodity distribution. Cross-metric patterns show that betweenness and degree are positively related in both sites, but with different slopes. This reflects different drivers of network centrality: ecological factors in Tuban and institutional–market influences in Lamongan. The same trend in betweenness– eigenvector correlations reinforces these structural contrasts. Overall, the findings highlight that elasmobranch fisheries are shaped by distinct social–ecological linkages across space— from landing sites to commodity flows—and provide quantitative support for more integrated, adaptive, and system-oriented management.

1951: Sharks have been victims of a distorted image that presents them as dangerous and aggressive creatures. This perception, fueled by sensationalist representations in media and cinema, hinders the understanding of their ecological role. In the last decade, conservation approaches have adopted a holistic vision that transcends the biological and fisheries aspects, incorporating social and economic variables to better understand the reduction of marine resources, considering several factors, among them local perceptions. The lack of knowledge and negative perceptions limit community participation in conservation. To analyze the perceptions of the communities of Margarita Island, a survey was applied that allowed for the description of socio-demographic factors and perception by means of a word association system. Word clouds were used to interpret the data. 1000 citizens were interviewed, resulting in 81.02% recognizing the presence of sharks on the island and 76.70% having consumed it. The majority (25.68%) have seen sharks through television. The words associated with sharks were mostly negative (46.20%) related to feelings of fear and danger, followed by neutral (34.50%) where the sea is recognized as their habitat, and positive (19.50%) which was linked to commerce recognizing the shark as a food resource. However, a large percentage (67.90%) expressed respect and ecological awareness towards these animals. The results show that, despite the negative image created by the media, there is a growing environmental awareness that can be leveraged to promote conservation through education and local knowledge.

1953: Baited Remote Underwater Video (BRUV) systems generate vast amounts of high-quality imagery of sharks and rays, but extracting ecological information from these data remains slow and labor-intensive. This analytical bottleneck limits the timely delivery of insights needed for effective management and conservation. Using a rigorously curated stereo-video dataset of five shark species from the Hawaiian Archipelago, we developed and validated an automated system for shark detection, species identification, and spatial measurement. Each shark in the dataset was annotated with a bounding box and species label to train a YOLOv5-based model for object detection, species classification, and snout localisation. The classifier achieved an F1 score of 0.94 at a confidence threshold of 0.49 across the five target species, meaning that when the model was at least ~50% confident, species identity was correct in nearly all cases. In parallel, template matching was used to detect a fixed bait-bag marker, and snout-localization outputs were referenced to this point to reconstruct 3D trajectories and minimum approach distances, providing a scalable method for quantifying shark–bait interactions. This automated workflow dramatically reduces processing time relative to manual annotation, enabling largerscale BRUV deployments and allowing analytical effort to shift from data processing to ecological interpretation. By integrating species recognition with spatial behaviour metrics, this system provides a robust foundation for accelerating BRUV-based assessments of shark communities and improving the responsiveness of conservation and management strategies.

1954: Manta and devil rays (mobulids) are inherently vulnerable to overexploitation due to their conservative life-history traits, yet they face serious threats from fisheries in Indonesia, particularly as bycatch in small-scale operations. This study quantifies the interaction between mobulids and small-scale fisheries in Muncar, a major fishing hub in the Bali Strait, to identify conservation priorities. We conducted landing site monitoring from 2015–2025, establishing standardized daily surveys in 2019 to assess this interaction. Data on catch trends, species morphometrics, and fisheries socio-economics were integrated to determine key threats and management opportunities. Five mobulid species were recorded (Mobula mobular, M. thurstoni, M. tarapacana, M. birostris, and M. alfredi), with a predominance of juveniles in landings (>60%). Catches peaked between August and October, coinciding with seasonal observations of pregnant M. mobular and M. thurstoni. Mobulid populations in this location are primarily threatened by incidental capture (bycatch) in multi-gear net fisheries, with landings driven by local consumption. Concurrently, a community development initiative, the Sustainable Seafood Network, is laying the groundwork to reduce mobulid bycatch by fostering fisher participation in conservation and market-based incentive schemes. This network promotes sustainable fishing practices (i.e., live-release of threatened elasmobranchs) through capacity-building and optimising the value of more sustainable teleost fish caught by local fishers through supplychain networking. This study demonstrates that integrating long-term fisheries monitoring with direct community engagement is essential for developing effective mobulid conservation strategies within Indonesia’s complex small-scale fisheries.

1955: Predator–prey interactions are a key driver of collective behaviour in animals, yet they are challenging to study in the wild. Among marine predators, sharks play an essential role in ocean ecology, but large within- and between-species variability makes their behaviour difficult to characterise. Drones have become increasingly popular for studying marine wildlife, and recent advances in computer vision and machine-learning–based video analysis are opening new opportunities for quantifying animal behavior. In our work, we use drone-based video to investigate interactions between blacktip reef sharks and fish schools on shallow sand flats in the Maldives. We combine aerial imagery with state-of-the-art multi-animal detection (YOLObased) and an open-source tracking framework that we developed, making these approaches broadly accessible to the community. On the predator side, we study how sharks associate with one another, how they hunt, and how they interact with other predator species. On the prey side, we segment fish schools to analyse how their shape reflects different collective states in the presence and absence of predators. To quantify fine-scale escape responses of prey, we use Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) to extract movement statistics in the area adjacent to the shark’s head as a function of the shark’s behavioural state. Together, these approaches allow us to characterise complex, predator–prey dynamics in a natural ecosystem, advancing our understanding of shark–prey behavioural ecology while providing open tools that can be used for field research, environmental monitoring, and conservation.

1957: Northern Australia represents a global stronghold for sawfishes, estuarine predators facing severe worldwide declines as a result of bycatch and trophy-keeping. Without historical baselines however, the true magnitude of population declines remains obscured, limiting effective conservation planning. Through extensive archival research, we compiled records from (n = 847) newspaper articles, (n = 189) museum specimens, and (n = 188) citizen scientist reports to reconstruct historical sawfish distributions (1875 – 1990) along Australia’s east coast. Records revealed previously unpublished hotspots for P. zijsron and extended the historic ranges for both P. clavata and A. cuspidata. Generalised additive models showed an increase and subsequent crash in sawfish catches, as well as a fragmented shift northward beginning in 1930 and intensifying in the late 1940’s. Extinction timelines suggest that following the introduction of netting, sawfishes were removed from their southern extent in under years. Meanwhile, text analyses documented both ‘monster’ and ‘pest’ narratives, with positive associations limited to trophy value. These findings establish critical historical baselines for future distribution modelling in Australia, while demonstrating the many dimensions and rapid pace of bycatch-induced population collapse for coastal megafauna.

1959: The scalloped hammerhead shark Sphyrna lewini, listed as Critically Endangered, has undergone severe global declines and an estimated 80% reduction in the southwestern Gulf of California. Understanding how juveniles use coastal, insular, and pelagic habitats is essential to determine whether key developmental stages are being disrupted and limiting population recovery. Between 2017 and 2025 we integrated acoustic telemetry, satellite tagging, and stereo-BRUVS to examine residency, distribution, abundance, and demographic structure of S. lewini across key sites in the region. All detected individuals (67–174 cm TL) were below published size-at-maturity thresholds, and neither telemetry nor BRUVS recorded adults, indicating that the area is used exclusively by juveniles and subadults. The tagged sharks showed continuous detections over weeks to months, with fidelity to insular habitats and seamounts, particularly El Bajo Espíritu Santo and Las Ánimas. BRUVS data revealed an ontogenetic gradient, larger juveniles (>100 cm TL) occurred mainly in insular–oceanic environments, whereas smaller individuals (<100 cm TL) remained restricted to coastal zones such as Los Frailes. This size-based partitioning suggests coastal habitats function as secondary nursery areas, while insular–pelagic habitats serve as aggregation and transition zones for older juveniles. Combined, these patterns indicate a loss of functional connectivity between habitat types, constraining movements across developmental stages and contributing to ontogenetic truncation in the regional population. The reliance on juvenile habitats and the absence of adults underscore the urgency of strengthening spatial protection and fisheries management to restore connectivity and support recovery of this highly vulnerable species.

1960: Shark and ray consumption has long been a cultural norm in Indonesia’s coastal communities, providing a source of protein and supporting livelihoods tied to marine resources. Domestic consumption focuses mainly on meat, while fins are exported to international markets, reflecting patterns in many developing countries. Although this practice occurs in several regions, Java is notable for its historical role as a marine trade hub. Ports such as Tegal, Surabaya, and Indramayu developed distribution networks that positioned the island as a center of shark and ray trade. This study examines consumption patterns of shark and ray meat in Java through interviews and field observations conducted from April to June 2024. Findings show that most consumers first try these products during adolescence and continue eating them over time. Northern coastal communities, including Tegal, Rembang, Pati, and Surabaya display higher consumption frequency influenced by cultural traditions such as sedekah laut and close access to marine resources. In contrast, Indramayu and Cilacap consume these species less often. Oceanographic conditions shape species distribution and influence consumption behavior. In northern Java, shallow continental shelves and muddy-sandy seabed support demersal species like wedgefish, guitarfish, and stingrays. These species are abundant and processed into smoked or salted products affordable for daily meals. In southern Java, deeper waters support pelagic sharks including silky and shortfin mako sharks which are less integrated into local diets and more often traded for fins. These patterns show how ecological availability, cultural traditions, and economic factors shape shark and ray consumption in Java.

1964: Wedgefish (Rhynchobatus spp.) and Giant Guitarfish (Glaucostegus spp.) are listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN and included in CITES Appendix II. The Java Sea in Indonesia serves as a key habitat for these species, supported by extensive muddy substrates. Along the northern coast of Central Java, from Brebes to Rembang, small- to medium-scale fisheries frequently interact with these taxa. A national production decline of up to 80% in the past decade highlights the need for improved management and conservation measures. Before educational and mentoring interventions were introduced, fishers did not conduct independent data recording or systematic juvenile release, indicating limited awareness of conservation needs. This study supports the development of sustainable conservation and fisheries management for these species in Central Java. Participatory data collection was conducted by captains and crew members in Rembang and Pati Regencies throughout 2023, documenting species identity, total length, capture location and time, and the number of individuals landed or released. A total of individuals were recorded, comprising Guitarfish and Giant Guitarfish. Peak catches occurred between June and October, influenced by the west monsoon. Of all individuals recorded, mostly adults measuring 161–200 cm were landed. 1970: Overfishing has severely depleted marine populations worldwide, including within protected areas, and illegal and unreported fishing remain major drivers of these declines. Large-bodied predators such as sharks are among the most affected, with overexploitation leading to sharp population reductions and ecosystem destabilization. Major barriers to effective marine management include data deficiencies that limit population assessments, insufficient surveillance that allows illegal fishing to persist, and limited capacity in many coastal nations to monitor and protect vulnerable species. Our study addresses these challenges by developing a genomic framework to assess shark population diversity and health while improving fisheries traceability across the Indo-Pacific. We introduce the Reefshark Genomescape—the first genome-wide reference database for Indo-Pacific reef sharks—along with a comprehensive assessment of genetic diversity, structure, and connectivity in two key species. We also demonstrate geographic assignment of fished individuals using population-specific genomic signatures. Grey reef sharks (Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos) show high genetic diversity and strong population structure, including previously undocumented connectivity between the central and western Indian Ocean and clear isolation of Andaman Sea populations. In contrast, silvertip sharks (Carcharhinus albimarginatus) exhibit high connectivity but show genomic signals of declining population health, supporting reconsideration of their IUCN status. Using supervised machine learning we assigned geographic origins of fished grey reef sharks with 96% accuracy. These findings provide essential insight into population health and connectivity while establishing a robust method for origin assignment. By enabling identification of fishing hotspots and detection of illegal fishing, this framework lays the foundation for a broader traceability system.

1972: We analyzed a bp fragment of the mitochondrial ND4 gene in Carcharhinus brevipinna individuals from the Red Sea (Sudan, Eritrea), Western Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and published sequences from Australia and South Africa. Forty-one haplotypes were identified across polymorphic sites. Haplotype (h = 0.550–0.746) and nucleotide (π = 0.0010–0.0015) diversities varied among populations, with the lowest diversity observed in New South Wales and higher diversity in Queensland, the Northern Territory, Gulf of Mexico, western North Atlantic, and South Africa. Red Sea and Northern Territory populations shared nearly identical haplotypes. Despite some haplotype sharing within the Indo-Pacific, AMOVA revealed significant genetic structure among Indo-Pacific populations (φST = 0.02849, p < 0.0001; FST = 0.35459, p < 0.0001) and strong differentiation between Indo-Pacific and Western Atlantic groups. Neighbor-Joining analysis supported two distinct clades corresponding to the Indo-Pacific and Western Atlantic/Gulf of Mexico. These results suggest that the Indian Ocean acts as a substantial barrier to contemporary gene flow, with dispersal largely restricted to shallow continental coasts. Historical demographic analyses indicate population expansion across all sampled regions. Given ongoing fishing pressure in the Red Sea, the protection of nursery habitats is critical for maintaining the long-term viability of these vulnerable populations. This study provides insights into the population structure and evolutionary history of spinner sharks, emphasizing the importance of regional conservation strategies to preserve genetic diversity of the spinner shark populations across the Indo-Pacific and Western Atlantic.
1973: Understanding the movement ecology and threats faced by highly migratory animals is essential for effective management. This is especially true for species like the Endangered oceanic manta ray (Mobula birostris), which have a conservative life history and are vulnerable to population disturbances. Over the last years, focused research, citizen science efforts, and satellite telemetry has led to a better understanding of New Zealand’s M. birostris population and habitat use. Resulting in the NZ Threat Conservation Status upgrade from Data Deficient to Nationally Vulnerable, and 445,546 km² of ocean habitat designated as Important Shark and Ray Areas for foraging and movement. 1,709 verified sightings, including ventral photographic IDs and telemetry data form tags, revealed that M. birostris occur in NZ waters from late austral spring (~November) to late austral autumn (~April). Tagged M. birostris spent most of their time in the top meters, foraging on seasonal krill swarms. Preliminary tag analysis suggests that a seasonal drop in sea temperature triggers a behavioural shift from foraging to migration into the lower latitudes e.g. towards Fiji. A combination of SPLASH-10 and MiniPat satellite tags captured fine and broad scale movements, deployments ranged from to months respectively. MiniPat successfully tracked a return migration of 9,000 km over 10.5 months. Confirming that NZ’s oceanic mantas partake in immense, biannual return migrations navigating through multi-jurisdictional and blue water fisheries. Subsequent analysis of MiniPat tags that exceeded their preprogramed depth strongly suggests negative fisheries interaction and fatality.

1975: The global market demand for products derived from elasmobranchs is a significant factor driving their capture. However, local consumption is often overlooked, despite its crucial role in shaping species exploitation. This is especially true in countries with large populations, where domestic consumption is frequently underestimated. While much research focuses on global demand, the specific drivers of domestic meat consumption remain poorly understood, a critical gap in our understanding of elasmobranch utilization. To address this gap, this study aims to analyze the social-ecological drivers influencing elasmobranch meat utilization in Muncar, Banyuwangi, one of Indonesia's largest elasmobranch landing sites, where local livelihoods are heavily dependent on these species. This study used the Social-Ecological Action Situation (SE-AS) framework as its analytical backbone. Data from stakeholder interviews, alongside landing data and trade analysis, were used to map the emergent phenomena of elasmobranch utilization. Our findings reveal that local demand is primarily driven by multi-generational family enterprises from fishing and processing. This demand is sustained by elasmobranch meat's role as an affordable and traditional protein source, which supports a local circular economy and is reinforced by cultural beliefs, such as the local belief it "warms the body." A better understanding of these drivers and their impact on local elasmobranch utilisation is essential for developing effective, socially acceptable, and sustainable conservation policies for elasmobranchs in Indonesia and in similar coastal communities.

1976: Despite expanding policy and management responses, illegal shark fishing persists worldwide, posing a major challenge to the sustainability of shark populations. In Sri Lanka, a suite of regulatory measures has been introduced to protect sharks, including bans on landing thresher sharks (Alopiidae), whale sharks, and oceanic white-tip sharks. Sri Lanka has also experienced some of the fastest declines in shark landings globally, despite the high socio-economic importance of shark meat consumption and foreign exports, reflecting a complex and rapidly changing fisheries landscape. Yet, despite these complexities, the social context of compliance, particularly the knowledge, perceptions, and motivations of those engaged in illegal fishing, remains poorly understood. Using Sri Lanka’s inboard multiday fleet as a case study, we collected data from three sites historically associated with shark landings. Data were gathered between January and June 2023 through six focus group discussions and surveys with fishers, skippers, and boat owners. Our findings revealed that only 9% of respondents were aware of all banned shark species, 12% reported landing incidentally captured protected sharks, and 47% reported illegal shark landings occur. Thematic analysis identified key drivers of non-compliance, including the economic importance of sharks, reluctance to discard bycatch, insufficient awareness of regulations, and perceived corruption. These findings highlight the critical need to integrate human dimensions into policy and fisheries management if illegal shark fishing is to be addressed effectively. Furthermore, they demonstrate that securing local support is essential for the long-term success and sustainability of shark conservation efforts.

1977: Ratfish are cartilaginous fishes in the family Chimaeriformes that swim using their large, paired pectoral fins. Spotted ratfish (Hydrolagus colliei) undergo diel migration, utilizing nearshore, shallow habitats at night and deeper, offshore habitats during the day, and are known to swim up to km per day. Previous work examining the functional morphology of their pectoral fins showed that muscle mass increases with body mass, while fin aspect ratio is negatively related to body size. Studies of steady, straight-line swimming further demonstrated that as body size increases, pectoral fin amplitude increases while beat frequency decreases. To examine spotted ratfish swimming functions, we measured fin deformation during forward and backward locomotion and station-holding. Ratfish were obtained and housed at Friday Harbor Laboratories (Washington, USA) in a circular mesocosm tank with flow-through seawater. Fish were filmed using a GoPro Hero at an average of frames per second, and fin deformation was quantified using AI-based object detection. We found that as body size (snout-to-vent length) doubled, pectoral fin length increased at a disproportionately faster rate (slope = 1.46), indicating positive allometry. We hypothesize that this positive pectoral fin allometry contributes to increased fin flexibility, facilitating efficient skulling, rowing, and station-holding performance.

1978: Electric rays remain one of the least studied elasmobranch groups in Indian waters, with key gaps in taxonomy, diversity and fishery interactions. This study (2022–2025) used an integrative approach combining COI barcoding, detailed morphological analyses, biological sampling, bycatch monitoring and fisher-dependent surveys to reassess the electric ray assemblage of the Indian EEZ. Molecular data showed clear interspecific divergence (5.5–16.3%) within Narcinidae, supporting the distinctiveness of recognized taxa and revealing cryptic structure in several lineages. Comprehensive field and laboratory work clarified the full Torpediniformes assemblage in India, encompassing species of Narcine, Torpedo, Narke, Heteronarce, Benthobatis and Tetronarce. Three new species—Benthobatis sp. A, Narcine sp. A and Tetronarce sp. A—were identified and are under formal description. Biological data were generated for Narcine timlei (n = 342) and N. dipterygia (n = 54). Species composition was dominated by N. timlei (41.27%), followed by B. moresbyi (28.34%), Torpedo cf. sinuspersici (10.08%), Narke dipterygia (10.31%) and other species (10%). Gear-based catch rates indicated high vulnerability, with N. timlei showing the highest values (6.6/hr in gillnets; 3.5/hr in trawls). Spatial mapping highlighted potential critical habitats, while socio-economic surveys revealed limited utilisation, primarily for fishmeal, with localised medicinal use of Torpedo species in eastern states. Based on species distributions and threat patterns, two candidate Important Shark and Ray Areas were identified off Chennai and Kollam. This study establishes the first integrative, evidence-based framework for Indian electric rays, resolving taxonomic uncertainties and providing essential baselines for biodiversity monitoring, fishery assessments and conservation planning.
1979: The effects of electrical stimulation on shark species have critical implications for the waveform selection of electrical shark deterrents (ESDs). These devices emit strong pulsed waveforms to cause avoidance behaviours in these animals and prevent negative interactions between them and humans (e.g., bites, depredation). Though electrically mediated deterrence is ascribed to electroreceptor overstimulation, it is possible that this is not the primary deterrent effect, and that alternative mechanisms are also present. Electric fields for example also affect the shark nervous system and muscles and may elicit involuntary muscle spasming. Confirming the causes of avoidance behaviours will help inform efforts to overcome the limitations of current ESD technology, which include variable efficacy in reducing predation and a short effective distance. We exposed anaesthetized and free-swimming elasmobranchs and non-electroreceptive teleosts to waveforms systematically varying in key parameters (e.g., frequency, shape) and quantified behavioural and physiological responses (e.g., muscle spasming). Free-swimming experiments followed the procedure of past trials of ESD efficacy, while those on anesthetized animals used accelerometers to quantify muscle spasming during exposure to waveforms. Comparing the field strengths that caused distinct responses across species and experiments allowed us to evaluate the likely mechanisms underpinning them and identify the waveforms which stimulate them best. Deterrence appears to reflect both electrosensory and neuromuscular stimulation, with the relative contribution of each speciesspecific. Future ESD design can be guided now by a clearer understanding of how waveform parameters may influence shark physiology and behaviour.

1980: Sawfishes (Fam. Pristidae) are among the most threatened marine fishes, having declined globally due to high susceptibility to by-catch, low fecundity and trophy taking. Once widespread across countries, they now persist mainly in Northern Australia, which is one of the last strongholds for the four Indo-West Pacific species and a focus of current conservation efforts. Environmental DNA (eDNA) has emerged as a powerful, non-invasive tool for detecting and monitoring sawfish presence in aquatic habitats where traditional survey methods are challenging or ineffective. For this study, eDNA samples were collected from over sites across Northern Queensland and Cape York Peninsula in order to gain a better understanding of how eDNA could aid in sawfish research and conservation in the region. Water samples were filtered through a µm nylon filter, with eDNA extracted from the filters analysed via PCR using species-specific mitochondrial COI primers targeting four species of sawfish. Detection of sawfish eDNA varied across species, with Pristis pristis eDNA being present in most sites (15.6%), followed by Anoxypristis cuspidata (10.8%), and P. zijsron (6%), and no detection for P. clavata. This methodology shows strong promise for identifying critical habitats, optimizing the timing and placement of conservation efforts, and enhancing our overall understanding of sawfish distribution across diverse environments. The results will be discussed in the context of future advancements.

1982: Elasmobranch populations in the Red Sea are declining, largely due to fishing pressure. Despite Saudi Arabia’s 2008 shark fishing ban, enforcement effectiveness remains uncertain, and bycatch from trawl fisheries is largely undocumented. Here, we present a pilot study to assess the feasibility of national-scale monitoring of elasmobranch bycatch in the Saudi Arabian trawl fisheries. Five cameras were deployed on trawlers operating out of the port of Jizan. Onboard cameras captured still images every five seconds, which were manually filtered to only images showing trawl catches with sharks, rays, and other species of interest. Identifications were made to the lowest taxonomic level by two independent reviewers. A total of trawl days were analyzed, covering approximately 1,298 hauls, during which instances of megafauna bycatch were recorded. Nearly all observations (n=453) were elasmobranchs; sea turtles made up the final five records. Within elasmobranchs, rays represented 98.9% of observations, with Rhinoptera spp. representing 78% of elasmobranchs observed. Critically Endangered species, including Rhynchobatus spp. (n=4) and Aetomylaeus vespertilio(n=2) were also detected. Extrapolating our empirical results from only five boats monitored, to the total fleet of approximately boats, indicates that even incidental capture may be unsustainable for some species. These preliminary results demonstrate the effectiveness of onboard camera systems for quantifying bycatch and highlight the presence of species of conservation concern.

1983: Wedgefish and giant guitarfish are key fisheries commodities in Indonesia but are classified as Critically Endangered by the IUCN and listed under CITES Appendix II, underscoring their global conservation priority. Populations have declined sharply due to overfishing, low reproductive capacity, and habitat degradation, while Indonesia remains one of the largest producers and exporters, particularly along the northern coast of Central Java. This situation highlights the urgent need for stricter, science-based regulations supported by reliable data. Community science offers a cost-effective approach for broad-scale fisheries monitoring and conservation engagement. This study evaluated a community science initiative in Rembang, Central Java, one of Indonesia’s major shark and ray landing sites. In 2023, eight industrial-scale vessel captains (>30 GT), designated as “local champions,” were trained and equipped with species identification guides and data collection tools incorporating local names. They documented shark and ray landings and juvenile releases of wedgefish and giant guitarfish, promoting conservation-oriented practices among fishers. A total of specimens were recorded, and juveniles were released back into the ocean with full documentation. Awareness raising efforts achieved positive outcomes but required lengthy negotiations, careful coordination due to limited crew availability, and efficient data collection strategies. Key challenges included improving species identification accuracy, providing regular capacity refreshment, offering consistent mentoring, and developing incentive schemes to sustain motivation. Our experience demonstrates that industrial-scale fishers can contribute meaningfully to shark and ray conservation when supported by sustained engagement strategies, offering a scalable model for similar fisheries worldwide.

1984: Morphological abnormalities in rays are relatively common in the Eastern Pacific, however, little is known about their causes and implications in their populations. Although reports come from isolated cases, one of the most common abnormalities is anophthalmia, a partial or total absence of eyes. Anophthalmia is described to be caused by failures during the developmental stage, and attributable to genetic causes, inbreeding, or due to environmental conditions. Through continuous rays monitoring in El Jobo, a fisherman town located in the north Pacific of Costa Rica, anophthalmia has been frequently observed in different species. Therefore, the present study aims to document the occurrence of anophthalmia across different ray species in El Jobo. From March 2018 to December 2024, rays from El Jobo were captured using hand nets through freediving surveys. On shore, biometrics of rays were taken and then released. Throughout a quantitative approach, the relationship between the presence of anophthalmia and the length, weight, or sex of individuals from different species was assessed. From ray species surveyed, eight presented cases of anophthalmia, and where only in three was previously reported. The most recurrent species were from Urotrygonidae, also exhibiting a high frequency of this abnormality throughout individuals. The present study represents the first documented case of anophthalmia occurring within an assemblage of rays and their populations, showcasing the need of further studies aiming to identify the causes of anophthalmia and implications on the populations health.

1986: Indonesia is one of the world's largest producers of sharks and rays, recording 81,783.20 tons in 2024. Among these, wedgefish (Rhynchobatus spp.) and giant guitarfish (Glaucostegus spp.) are particularly vulnerable, facing high exploitation and Critically Endangered status. On the north coast of Central Java, four wedgefish and two giant guitarfish species are frequently caught as bycatch, primarily for the fin trade. However, fisheries management often relies on aggregated statistics that obscure species-level trends, limiting accurate assessments of population status, exploitation rates, and trade impacts. This lack of robust data constrains policymakers, conservationists, and local communities in designing effective strategies. To address these gaps, the IKAN tool was developed as a digital, co-managed platform to strengthen national monitoring of wedgefish and giant guitarfish. This study evaluates the performance of IKAN in monitoring landings of these species. IKAN integrates an Android-based application with adaptive manual protocols, enabling real-time data collection that enhances accuracy and timeliness, crucial for managing threatened species. The system fosters active participation of fishers, researchers, and stakeholders through standardized protocols, generating credible datasets that support national policy and international reporting, including CITES compliance. Since 2019, IKAN has been implemented across multiple landing sites, demonstrating effectiveness through publicly accessible records of trip data, catch composition, and lengthfrequency distributions. The success of IKAN highlights the potential of technology-driven, collaborative monitoring systems to bridge critical information gaps. Overall, IKAN provides a practical and scalable framework for improving species-specific data collection, offering an evidence-based foundation for future conservation and sustainable management.

1987: Indonesia is one of the world’s largest producers of sharks and rays, and between 2012–2019, its shark and ray meat trade represented a significant share of the global market, valued at $2.2 billion. As species of high economic value, their trade is strictly regulated under international agreements such as CITES. However, shark meat trade chains in Indonesia remain complex, characterized by fragmented product flows, multiple pathways, and governance gaps that hinder conservation and compliance with international regulations. This study aims to map shark meat trade chains in Indonesia, from landing sites to export markets by identifying key actors, product flows, and potential governance issues related to traceability and compliance. Primary data were collected through field observations and interviews at several sites across Indonesia in August 2023, complemented by a literature review. Visual mapping through trade chain diagrams and geographic distribution maps was used to illustrate domestic and international trade pathways. The findings reveal a highly complex trade network involving fishers, local collectors, processors, and exporters, operating across multiple trade pathways. Shark meat products include fresh and salted meat distributed through local markets, national hubs, and export markets. The complexity of trade chains and informal networks contributes gaps in traceability and governance, especially for CITES compliance. This study provides critical insights for more targeted policy interventions, including strengthened monitoring systems, improved traceability, comprehensive data collection, and enhanced multistakeholder collaboration. These efforts are essential for ensuring sustainable shark trade in line with national and international regulations.

1988: Plastic and microplastic (MP) pollution in the marine environment has become a growing global concern due to its impact on marine life and potential risks to human health. Despite the urgency, significant research gaps remain in MP research in Sri Lanka (SL). This ongoing study aimed to investigate MP contamination in the guts of ray fish species that were caught in different parts of the SL sea and were sold at the Paliyagoda central fish market. Sampling was conducted from March to November in 2025, where Neotrygon caeruleopunctata gut samples and Rhinoptera javanica gut samples were analyzed. Stereomicroscope and FTIR spectroscopy were used to identify and analyze the MPs, and results reflect that all the fish samples contain MPs. The mean MP count per fish varied depending on the location where the fish was caught; the seas of Jaffna, Tricomalee, and Galle reported as (70.00 ± 0.00), (51.50 ± 15.67), and (41.29 ± 15.09), respectively. Fibers and fragments were the most abundant MPs, while color-wise, black and red were the abundant in both fish species. The highest MP load was recorded in Neotrygon caeruleopunctata samples that were caught in Trincomalee sea. PET, PVC, PE, and Nylon were the polymer types that were found in Neotrygon caeruleopunctata, and PE and PET were the types that were found in Rhinoptera javanica. These observations demonstrate the impact of MPs on ray species across different coastal areas, highlighting the urgent need for further research on this matter.

1989: Chondrichthyans (Chondrichthyes) are one of the oldest and most distinctive vertebrate lineages, with an evolutionary history exceeding million years. Between 2001 and 2024, the global tally of chondrichthyan species rose from roughly to more than 1,200, reflecting a surge of newly described taxa and distributional records. By collating published literature, visiting marine institutes throughout China, verifying and supplementing public databases, and integrating two decades of field surveys at major fishing ports in mainland China (data current to March 2025), we updated the Chinese chondrichthyan checklist under the current elasmobranch classification. The revised list recognizes species (14 orders, families, genera) occurring in Chinese waters, occupying >20 % of global elasmobranch diversity. Of these, species (59.38 %) are assessed as threatened on the IUCN Red List, a proportion far exceeding the global average of 37.5 %. Jaccard similarity coefficients indicate that China’s chondrichthyan fauna overlaps 61.41 % with Japan’s, 44.39 % with that of Southeast Asia, 21.47 % with Australia, and 13.94 % with New Zealand. These results provide a baseline framework for future taxonomic and ecology studies of Chinese chondrichthyans and furnish essential scientific information for the conservation of Indo-West Pacific elasmobranchs, the sustainable management of fishery resources in Chinese seas, and the implementation of relevant international conventions.

1991: Shallow coastal waters are critical for elasmobranchs, serving as nurseries and foraging habitats, but they face increasing anthropogenic pressures. A small proportion of Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) overlap with MPAs, making these areas a rare opportunity to improve monitoring methods for threatened elasmobranchs and strengthen area-based conservation. We developed and applied a multi-method approach in the shallow waters (0–5 m) of the fully protected Saadiyat Marine National Park in the United Arab Emirates, which overlaps with a designated ISRA. Environmental DNA (eDNA), baited remote underwater videos (BRUVs), and targeted dives were deployed across four seasons to assess elasmobranch diversity, habitat use, and spatial distribution. Ten elasmobranch species were detected, including eight IUCN-listed threatened species, and two key species supporting the ISRA designation: the Critically Endangered Halavi guitarfish (Glaucostegus halavi) and the range-restricted Pakistan whipray (Maculabatis arabica). The complementarity of methods maximized elasmobranch detection rates while providing detailed habitat context: eDNA captured cryptic or transient taxa, BRUVs recorded behavior and relative abundance, and dives enabled in-situ habitat verification. Species-level spatial models showed seasonal variations and habitat associations, identifying sandbanks and macroalgal beds as key areas during cooler months. These results informed priority zones for conservation within the MPA. We propose a scalable framework for elasmobranch monitoring that combines (i) integrated detection using eDNA, BRUVs, and diving; (ii) habitat-based probability maps; and (iii) a standardized, replicable protocol. This approach strengthens the evidence base for elasmobranchs conservation in shallow coastal ecosystems that are ecologically significant but data-deficient.

1993: The Atlantic pygmy devil ray (Mobula hypostoma) remains one of the least documented mobulids, limiting its inclusion in spatial management and conservation planning. To generate evidence needed for candidate Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs), we combined acoustic and satellite telemetry, fecal DNA metabarcoding, citizen-science observations, and field surveys to characterize movements, habitat use, and foraging ecology of M. hypostoma in the northeastern Gulf of Mexico (2019–2025). Seventy-four individuals were acoustically tagged from Sarasota Bay to the Florida Panhandle, revealing strong seasonal connectivity: several subadults completed >1000-km round-trip migrations between Sarasota-Tampa and the Panhandle, with detections extending to Louisiana. Juveniles were more resident along the Panhandle but still ranged 250–300 km, whereas adults were rarely detected, indicating limited nearshore use. Pop-up satellite archival tags (n=11) provided the first depth-use profiles, documenting repeated dives to ~190 m and regular visitation of the DeSoto Canyon, consistent with offshore foraging. Field observations and citizen-science reports revealed predictable seasonal aggregations of juveniles and subadults feeding in surf-zone mysid swarms (Metamysidopsis swifti), corroborated by fecal DNA identifying mysids as dominant prey and fish eggs as a secondary source. Together, these multidisciplinary datasets delineate two spatially significant habitats meeting several ISRA criteria: the Panhandle-DeSoto Canyon as a key foraging area for juveniles and subadults, and the migration corridor linking this region to West Central Florida. These findings provide the first integrated spatial-ecological evidence for M. hypostoma in the region, directly support ongoing ISRA proposals, and underscore the need for coordinated Gulf-wide management.

1994: Fluvitrygon signifer, Fluvitrygon oxyrhynchus, and Urogymnus polylepis are recognized as endemic freshwater stingrays in Southeast Asia, including Indonesia. Despite their protected status in Indonesia, research and documentation on these species are limited compared to other sharks and rays, leading to insufficient protective measures. This semi-investigative study aims to gather basic information and raise public awareness to aid conservation efforts for freshwater stingrays in West Kalimantan, Indonesia. Data were collected through a mixed approach combining qualitative and quantitative methods. Over five months, interviews (N=30), field observations, visual documentation, and focus group discussions (FGD) with key stakeholders were conducted. Although no sightings of Urogymnus polylepis were reported during observations, reports indicate that F. signifer still inhabits the Kapuas Hulu area, and F. oxyrhynchus is found in the tributaries of the Kapuas River. Nonetheless, trade practices for non-consumption purposes, such as for ornamental use, continue to occur. As we sought to gather a collective perspective from key actors, a series of recommendations was generated, including developing a database of freshwater stingray species, increasing monitoring of trade activities, strengthening conservation education programs for fishers and local residents, and establishing a collaborative forum involving academics, government, and local communities. With these steps, conservation efforts for freshwater stingrays are expected to be implemented for sustainable, science-based management in West Kalimantan.

1996: Shark and ray fisheries in Bangladesh are poorly documented, particularly regarding species diversity, composition, trade, and conservation. Between January 2024 and June 2025, elasmobranch landing surveys were conducted at the Chattogram landing site, recorded 2,727 individuals representing species, including rays and sharks. Landings were dominated by six ray species (Gymnura poecilura, Maculabatis gerrardi, Hemitrygon bennettii, Maculabatis pastinacoides, Pateobatis bleekeri, and Glaucostegus granulatus), which comprised 74% of rays landing, and six shark species (Sphyrna lewini, Galeocerdo cuvier, Scoliodon laticaudu, Carcharhinus limbatus, Carcharhinus amboinensis, and Carcharhinus leucas), which accounting for 87% of sharks landing. 11% of rays and 4% of sharks of total landed elasmobranch were identified only to the genus level, underscoring species identification complexity. Trade analysis revealed that Chattogram is a major hub for elasmobranch products, including shark fins with high demand for domestic and international markets. Fins and meat from CITESlisted species (Sphyrna lewini, Carcharhinus leucus, Carcharhinus amboinensis, Carcharhinus limbatus, Glaucostegus typus, Rhina ancylostoma, Glaucostegus granulatus) are frequently exported to Asian countries. The dominance of few high-value ray species (Pateobatis bleekeri, Himantura undulata, Maculabatis pastinacoides, and Gymnure poecilura) is targeted for fresh meat, while ray skins from (Pateobatis bleekeri, Maculabatis pastinacoides, Pateobatis uarnacoides, and Glaucostegus granulatus) are targeted for international trade. These intensive trade raises serious conservation concerns-emphasizes the urgent need for species-specific monitoring, improved fisheries management, and targeted conservation measures to protect threatened and CITES-listed shark and ray populations in Bangladesh.

1997: The establishment of marine protected areas (MPAs) rarely considers the critical habitats of chondrichthyans, despite their high extinction risk. We examined the efficacy of the current network of designated areas in encompassing Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs) in the Mediterranean and Black Seas. We conducted a systematic spatial gap analysis by integrating validated data from multiple sources, including the WDPA, MAPAMED, the Natura 2000 network, the Emerald Network, KBAs, IBAs, and IMMAs. After a rigorous data-cleaning and validation process involving more than national experts, we compiled a final dataset of 4,096 spatial units that integrates all relevant layers. Our evaluation revealed a profound conservation gap. The total ISRA surface area only overlaps with 7.35% of Natura 2000 sites, 3.06% of national MPAs, and a mere 6.24% of Specially Protected Areas of Mediterranean Importance. The majority of these areas lack management plans or measures that benefit chondrichthyans. Furthermore, 18.48% of ISRAs overlap with other biodiversity- or taxon-targeted delineations, such as KBAs, IBAs, and/or IMMAs. Our analysis demonstrates that the current network of protected areas is at high risk of being insufficient to safeguard chondrichthyans in this region. The next step is to consider a prioritisation approach to highlight key areas for expanding the MPA network, to achieve the 30% protection target in an ecologically coherent and effective manner for chondrichthyan conservation. For European Union member states in the region, our results can inform the National Action Plans for implementing the EU Restoration Law, which are currently being developed.

1998: The Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) of the Derawan Islands and their adjacent waters were established to safeguard critical marine habitats, biodiversity and sustainable fisheries. Despite their protected status, fishing activities remain intensive within and around the MPAs, including bycatch of sharks. Since 2022, WWF-Indonesia, has implemented a community-based fisheries bycatch monitoring program. To date, 2,293 fishing trips have been monitored (15,36% trip covered), representing three types of fishing gear. A total of monitored trips recorded shark bycatch. Handlines accounted for the highest number of shark captures, with individuals (70,8%) released alive back into the wild. Gillnets caught five individuals (10,4%) of sharks, all retrieved dead highlighting the urgent need for improved. Longlines captured nine individuals (18.8%), with three sharks recorded alive and released (33%) and six that died (67%), indicating a moderate but still concerning mortality risk. At the species level, Carcharhinus melanopterus was the most frequently recorded species (18 individuals), followed by sixteen other shark species, all categorized as Vulnerable or Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List. Community-based monitoring has generated critical baseline information for improving bycatch mitigation. To increase fishers’ awareness and willingness to report their catches along with evidence of bycatch incidents, there is a need for expanded capacity-building activities. With adequate training, fishers will be better handling sharks as bycatch can be safely released alive. This may include the use of mitigation tools or adjustments to fishing operations, modifying gear-setting depths, selecting alternative fishing grounds, or changing the bait used.
